def: A party's right to reject a prospective juror without stating a reason.

def: To formally offer evidence or testimony for the court's acceptance.

def: To agree formally with the opposing party on a fact or a matter of procedure.
ex: Both sides stipulated to the authenticity of the emails, sparing us a foundation witness.

def: To challenge the credibility of a witness or the reliability of their testimony.
ex: He was impeached with his own prior inconsistent statement to the police.

def: Tending to establish a party's fault or guilt.

def: To bring an accused before a court to hear the charges and enter a plea.

def: A person who gives sworn testimony, especially in a deposition or affidavit.

def: Brought or pursued to harass rather than to obtain genuine relief.

def: The uniting of parties or claims in a single proceeding.

def: Wilful defiance of a court's authority or orders.

def: A party's formal reply to the opponent's answer or reply.
ex: Their rejoinder finally disclosed the indemnity clause they had been hiding.

ex: We were granted surrebuttal to meet the new theory their expert had sprung on us.

def: To deny formally an allegation made by the opposing party.
ex: The defence traversed every material averment in the statement of claim.

def: A judgment against a claimant who fails to make out a case or to proceed.
ex: When their only witness failed to appear, the judge entered a nonsuit.

def: A pretrial application to exclude prejudicial evidence before it reaches the jury.
ex: Our motion in limine kept the prior conviction out of the jury's hearing.

def: To split a trial into separate phases, typically liability and damages.
ex: The court bifurcated the trial so liability could be settled before the costly damages inquiry.

def: To swear in a group of jurors to hear a case.
ex: It took two full days to empanel a jury untainted by the pretrial publicity.

def: Done by or for one party alone, without notice to the other.
ex: She obtained an ex parte freezing order before he could move the funds offshore.

def: Currently under judicial consideration and therefore not open to public comment.
ex: The minister declined to comment while the matter remained sub judice.

def: A conclusion drawn against a party for failing to produce evidence within its control.
ex: His silence at trial invited an adverse inference the jury clearly drew.

def: Tending to prove or disprove a fact in issue.
ex: The photograph was highly probative and its prejudice did not outweigh that value.

def: Sufficient at first sight to establish a fact unless rebutted.
ex: The claimant made out a prima facie case, shifting the burden to the employer.

def: A lawyer's closing address summarising the evidence and argument to the tribunal.
ex: Her summation tied nine days of testimony into a single, damning timeline.

def: The essential grievance at the core of a complaint.
ex: The gravamen of the claim was not the delay but the concealment behind it.

def: To separate claims or parties for independent trial or judgment.
ex: The judge severed the conspiracy count so the weaker fraud charge would not colour it.

def: An event that must occur before a party's contractual duty becomes enforceable.
ex: Closing is subject to a condition precedent that every regulatory approval be obtained first.

def: An event that, if it happens, extinguishes an obligation that has already arisen.
ex: The grant reverts to the donor as a condition subsequent if the land is ever used commercially.

def: The quality that lets the rest of a contract survive even when one clause is struck down.
ex: Thanks to the severability provision, voiding the non-compete left the remaining terms intact.

def: An introductory clause setting out the background and purpose behind an agreement.
ex: The recitals make clear that the parties intended the licence to be worldwide.

def: Standardised clauses inserted routinely near the end of most contracts.
ex: Do not treat the boilerplate as filler: the governing-law clause decides where you will litigate.

def: A clause excusing performance when extraordinary events beyond a party's control intervene.
ex: The supplier invoked force majeure when the port was shut by the embargo.

def: A sum fixed in advance as the agreed measure of loss for a specified breach.
ex: Late delivery triggers liquidated damages of five thousand a day, capped at the contract price.

def: The direct contractual relationship that lets only the parties themselves sue on the contract.
ex: Lacking privity, the subcontractor could not enforce the payment terms against the employer.

def: A provision setting a date on which a right or obligation automatically expires.
ex: The indemnity is subject to a sunset clause and lapses eighteen months after completion.

def: To assume another party's liability so that it bears no loss.
ex: The contractor agreed to hold the owner harmless from any workplace injury claims.

def: The substitution of one party for another whose claim they have satisfied, succeeding to that party's rights; classically an insurer who, having paid the insured, pursues whoever caused the loss.
ex: After paying the claim, the insurer exercised subrogation against the negligent haulier.

def: So grossly unfair that a court will refuse to enforce it.
ex: The arbitration clause was struck out as unconscionable given the stark imbalance in bargaining power.

def: A party's clear refusal to perform its side of the bargain, entitling the other to terminate.
ex: The manufacturer's flat refusal to ship amounted to a repudiation of the whole contract.

def: A breach committed by signalling, before performance falls due, that one will not perform.
ex: Her email disowning the deal was an anticipatory breach, so we terminated at once.

def: A reasonable sum awarded for work done where no price was ever agreed.
ex: With no signed fee schedule, the consultant recovered on a quantum meruit basis.

def: A stipulation making punctual performance a condition, so any delay is a repudiatory breach.
ex: Because time was of the essence, completing a single day late let the buyer walk away.

def: A promise limiting what a party may do, typically after the contract has ended.
ex: The restrictive covenant barred her from soliciting former clients for twelve months.

def: An express exception that removes something from the scope of a broader clause.
ex: We negotiated a carve-out so ordinary-course disclosures fall outside the confidentiality obligation.

def: The threshold of significance that makes a breach or fact legally consequential.
ex: The clause qualifies each warranty by materiality to filter out trivial inaccuracies.

def: The most demanding standard of effort, requiring all reasonable steps even at one's own cost.
ex: A best endeavours obligation may compel you to appeal a refused permit, not merely apply once.

def: The automatic discharge of a contract when an unforeseen event makes performance impossible or radically different.
ex: The hall's destruction by fire frustrated the booking, releasing both sides.

def: The holding of money or documents by a neutral third party until agreed conditions are met.
ex: The deposit sits in escrow and releases only on delivery of clean title.

def: One of several identical copies of a contract, each signed separately but together forming one agreement.
ex: The parties executed the deal in counterpart and exchanged scanned signature pages.

def: The formal witnessing of a signature to confirm a document was duly executed.
ex: The deed failed for want of proper attestation by an independent witness.

def: An upward adjustment to a payment so the recipient nets the intended amount after tax or deductions.
ex: The interest clause includes a gross-up so the lender receives the full coupon free of withholding.

def: A term letting a creditor demand the entire balance at once upon default.
ex: One missed instalment tripped the acceleration clause and the whole loan fell due.

def: The right to reduce a sum owed by netting a cross-claim against the same party.
ex: The buyer exercised set-off, deducting its warranty claim from the final instalment.

def: The party protected by an indemnity and entitled to be reimbursed for covered losses.
ex: As indemnitee, the distributor can recover its defence costs from the manufacturer.

def: A clause that actually creates rights or obligations, as distinct from background recitals.
ex: The recitals set the scene; the operative provisions are where the licence is actually granted.

def: The grace window in which a defaulting party may fix its breach before termination.
ex: The notice starts a thirty-day cure period, after which we may terminate for cause.

def: The bargained-for value each party gives that makes a promise enforceable.
ex: A bare promise to make a gift fails for want of consideration.

def: A provision declaring the written contract the complete and final expression of the deal.
ex: The merger clause shut out the buyer's reliance on oral assurances made during negotiations.

def: The formula binding not only the parties but those who later step into their positions.
ex: The covenant runs to the successors and assigns, so a later purchaser is bound too.

def: A right to end the contract without any breach by the other side.
ex: The client invoked termination for convenience and paid only for work done to date.

def: A promise to extend to one party any better terms later granted to anyone else.
ex: The most favoured nation clause forced the vendor to pass on the discount it had given a rival buyer.

def: A creditor's deliberate choice to hold off enforcing a right it could otherwise assert.
ex: The bank's forbearance on the covenant breach bought the company another quarter.

def: Beyond the legal power or authority of a company or its directors.
ex: The guarantee was struck down as ultra vires, falling outside the company's stated objects.

def: Owing a duty of loyalty and good faith to act in another's interest above your own.
ex: As a director, she stood in a fiduciary relationship to every shareholder.

def: Deferred purchase price tied to the acquired business's future performance.
ex: Half the price sat in an earn-out payable only if revenue hit the agreed milestones.

def: A right forcing minority holders to join a sale approved by the majority.
ex: The drag-along let the founders deliver a clean sale of the entire company.

def: The compulsory buying out of minority shareholders after a takeover crosses a threshold.
ex: Once past ninety percent, the bidder launched a squeeze-out of the remaining holders.

def: A long-term debt instrument, usually secured against a company's assets.
ex: The lender took a debenture over the whole undertaking as security.

def: An existing shareholder's first right to buy new shares before they go to outsiders.
ex: Pre-emption meant the fund had to be offered its pro rata slice first.

def: An undertaking to answer for another person's debt or default.
ex: The parent company's suretyship reassured the bank about the subsidiary's loan.

def: A legally sanctioned pause on enforcing debts against a struggling company.
ex: The moratorium gave the board breathing space to negotiate a rescue.

def: A contractual right to recover money or shares already paid out.
ex: The bonus was subject to clawback if the accounts were later restated.

def: The point at which a contingent right (to shares, options, a pension or a property interest) becomes an absolute, unforfeitable entitlement, whether in stages or all at once.
ex: Her options ran on a four-year vesting schedule with a one-year cliff.

def: Protecting an investor's stake from being watered down by later, cheaper share issues.
ex: The anti-dilution ratchet repriced the fund's shares after the down round.

def: To sell off or dispose of a business, asset, or shareholding.
ex: Regulators required the group to divest its overlapping logistics arm.

def: The transfer of a trade into a fresh subsidiary, often to prepare it for sale.
ex: They executed a hive-down of the trading operations to leave the liabilities behind.

def: A clause limiting a person's freedom to compete or carry on business.
ex: The five-year restraint of trade was unenforceable as far too wide.

def: The intangible value of a business's reputation, brand, and customer base.
ex: Most of the purchase price reflected goodwill rather than hard assets.

def: To cancel a contract and treat it as though it never existed.
ex: The buyer moved to rescind the deal the moment the misstatement surfaced.

def: The introductory clauses of a contract that set out its background and purpose.
ex: The recitals made clear the parties had been dealing with each other for a decade.

def: Security over a shifting pool of assets that fixes onto them on default.
ex: The floating charge covered stock and receivables as they came and went.

def: The ratio of a company's borrowed money to its own equity.
ex: High gearing left the company dangerously exposed when interest rates rose.

def: A significant deterioration that lets a party walk away before a deal closes.
ex: The buyer invoked the material adverse change clause when the target lost its biggest client.

def: A suit a shareholder brings on the company's behalf against those who harmed it.
ex: The minority launched a derivative action against the self-dealing directors.

def: The person who truly enjoys the benefit of shares held in another's name.
ex: Behind the nominee, the fund was the beneficial owner of the entire stake.

def: Legal possession of a freehold estate in land.
ex: Before registration, it was delivery of seisin that actually vested the freehold in the buyer.

def: The interest an owner keeps in land that returns to them once a lesser estate ends.
ex: The landlord sold the reversion, so the ground rents now flow to the new owner.

def: The right to use and enjoy another's property and its fruits without depleting it.
ex: The widow held a usufruct over the vineyard, taking the harvest but never the land itself.

def: A right to enter another's land and take something of value from it, such as timber or game.
ex: Their profit à prendre lets them cut peat on the moor every autumn.

def: Acquiring title to land by occupying it openly and continuously against the owner's rights.
ex: After twelve years farming the strip unchallenged, he claimed it by adverse possession.

def: Disrepair for which a tenant is held liable at the end of a lease.
ex: The landlord served a schedule of dilapidations running to forty thousand pounds.

def: Any form of property capable of being inherited.
ex: The conveyance passed the house together with every hereditament and appurtenance belonging to it.

def: Attached to and passing with a piece of land as a legal accessory.
ex: The parking space is appurtenant to the flat and cannot be sold off separately.

def: Existing as a legal right rather than as a physical thing.
ex: An easement is incorporeal: you own the right of passage, not the soil beneath it.

def: Relating to the owner of land bordering a river or watercourse.
ex: As a riparian owner she was entitled to fish the stretch flowing past her garden.

def: The gradual, natural addition of land by deposits of soil along a shore or bank.
ex: Decades of accretion had quietly pushed the farm's boundary out into the estuary.

def: The sudden loss or shift of land caused by the abrupt action of water.
ex: The flood's avulsion cut a new channel and left half the meadow stranded on the far bank.

def: The enclosed land immediately surrounding a dwelling.
ex: Whether the shed lay within the curtilage decided if planning permission was even needed.

def: The landlord's right to end a lease and retake possession when the tenant breaches it.
ex: Persistent non-payment triggered forfeiture, and the bailiffs changed the locks by noon.

def: The borrower's right to recover mortgaged property by paying off the debt.
ex: Even after default, his equity of redemption survived right up to the moment of sale.

def: A court process by which a lender extinguishes the borrower's interest and takes the mortgaged property.
ex: The bank sought foreclosure once the arrears became hopeless.

def: A right, usually granted for payment, to run cables or pipes across another's land.
ex: The utility pays an annual wayleave for the pylons marching across his pasture.

def: Compensation for the value of occupation recovered from someone wrongfully holding land.
ex: The trespasser was ordered to pay mesne profits for the two years he stayed on.

def: A tenant's right to occupy leased premises without unlawful interference from the landlord.
ex: Cutting off the water was a plain breach of her covenant for quiet enjoyment.

def: The automatic passing of a joint owner's share to the surviving co-owners on death.
ex: Under survivorship, the flat vested wholly in her the moment her partner died.

def: The act of turning a joint tenancy into a tenancy in common, ending the right of survivorship.
ex: A notice of severance meant his half would now pass under his will, not to his co-owner.

def: A property right that binds a purchaser even though it appears nowhere on the register.
ex: Her actual occupation gave her an overriding interest the buyer simply could not ignore.

def: A trust imposed by a court to stop one party unjustly keeping property that belongs to another.
ex: His years of contributions to the mortgage founded a constructive trust in his favour.

def: The land burdened by an easement for the benefit of neighbouring land.
ex: As the servient tenement, his plot must tolerate the drainage pipe running beneath it.

def: A token rent of nominal value used to keep a tenancy legally valid.
ex: The charity holds the hall on a ninety-nine-year lease at a peppercorn rent of one pound a year.

def: A leaseholder's statutory right to buy the freehold or extend the lease.
ex: The flat owners clubbed together to pursue collective enfranchisement of the whole block.

def: A periodic sum charged on freehold land and payable to someone who is not the landlord.
ex: An ancient rentcharge of a few pounds still quietly burdened the title.

def: Capable of being brought to an end or voided if a specified condition occurs.
ex: The gift was defeasible: the land would revert if it ever ceased to be used as a school.

def: An interest in property that is void because it may vest too remotely in the future.
ex: The clause failed for perpetuity, tying up the estate far beyond the permitted period.

def: The grant of property by lease.
ex: The demise took in the flat but expressly excluded the roof space above it.

def: An intrusion onto a neighbour's land by a structure or shifted boundary.
ex: The new extension's encroachment over the party line sparked the entire dispute.

def: A form of freehold ownership of a flat within a building jointly managed by its owners.
ex: They converted the block to commonhold so the residents could run it themselves.

def: A doctrine that enforces a promise about land where someone has relied on it to their detriment.
ex: Having worked the farm for years on his uncle's assurance, he claimed it by proprietary estoppel.

def: The physical conduct or omission that forms the objective element of a crime.
ex: She had the motive, sure, but the file shows no actus reus tying her to the shooting.

def: The first hearing at which an accused is formally read the charges and enters a plea.
ex: He stayed silent at arraignment, so the court entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf.

def: A prosecutor's formal decision to abandon all or part of a case.
ex: The state entered a nolle prosequi on the weapons count once the search was ruled bad.

def: The defendant's own statement of remorse or explanation offered to the court before sentencing.
ex: His allocution was three sentences long and moved no one on the bench.

def: A defense that government agents induced someone to commit a crime he was not predisposed to commit.
ex: The whole case reeks of entrapment; the informant supplied the drugs, the buyer, and the idea.

def: The intent to kill or cause grievous bodily harm that marks a killing as murder.
ex: Prosecutors have to show malice aforethought, not merely that a death occurred.

def: Assisting or encouraging another to commit a crime so as to share in the criminal liability.
ex: She never held the gun, but aiding and abetting exposes her to the same sentence.

def: The ending of a trial before verdict because of a fundamental error or a deadlocked jury.
ex: One holdout forced a mistrial, and the state has already vowed to retry.

def: Guilty knowledge that one's conduct is wrongful or unlawful.
ex: Fraud requires scienter, so his honest-mistake story, if believed, sinks the charge.

def: The crime of inducing another person to commit perjury or another offense.
ex: Coaching the witness to lie turned a weak case into a subornation charge against the lawyer.

def: The carrying away of another's property, an element of larceny and kidnapping.
ex: Even shifting the purse a few inches satisfies asportation for the theft count.

def: A killing committed during a dangerous felony, charged as murder regardless of intent to kill.
ex: The getaway driver never fired a shot, but felony murder puts the clerk's death on him too.

def: A crime whose elements are wholly contained within a more serious charged crime.
ex: The judge instructed the jury on manslaughter as a lesser included offense of murder.

def: Questioning of a suspect who is in custody and not free to leave.
ex: Because it was custodial interrogation, anything he said before the warnings gets thrown out.

def: Emergency conditions that justify a warrantless search or entry.
ex: They claimed exigent circumstances, arguing the evidence was being flushed as they knocked.

def: Evidence derived from an earlier illegal search or seizure and therefore inadmissible.
ex: The confession is fruit of the poisonous tree, tainted by the illegal stop that produced it.

def: A plea by which a defendant accepts conviction without admitting guilt.
ex: He pleaded nolo contendere to keep the conviction from being used against him in the civil suit.

def: The pool of citizens summoned from which a trial jury is chosen.
ex: The venire skewed heavily toward retirees, which worried the defense.

def: A defendant's written promise to appear in court that allows release without posting money.
ex: First offense, strong ties to town, so she walked on her own recognizance.

def: A court order directing an officer to arrest and bring in a named person.
ex: When he blew off the subpoena, the clerk issued a capias that afternoon.

def: A formal request that a jail hold a prisoner for another jurisdiction once his current term ends.
ex: The immigration detainer means he will not walk free even after making bail here.

def: A grand jury's endorsement that the evidence is sufficient to warrant an indictment.
ex: The grand jury returned a true bill on every count the prosecutor presented.

def: The constitutional bar against trying or punishing a person twice for the same offense.
ex: An acquittal ends it; double jeopardy means the state gets no second bite.

def: The principle that genuinely ambiguous criminal statutes are read in the defendant's favor.
ex: Where the statute could cut two ways, lenity tips the reading toward the accused.

def: Describing a crime that is begun or agreed to but not carried through, such as attempt or conspiracy.
ex: These are inchoate offenses; no bank was ever robbed, only planned.

def: The proof that a crime actually occurred, independent of who committed it.
ex: Without a body or any corpus delicti, the confession alone cannot sustain a murder charge.

def: A statement about the cause of one's impending death, admissible despite the hearsay rule.
ex: Her whispered dying declaration naming the shooter came in over a hearsay objection.

def: A spontaneous statement made under the stress of a startling event, admissible as a hearsay exception.
ex: The 911 caller's screaming account qualifies as an excited utterance, not calculated testimony.

def: A jury's acquittal against the evidence because it rejects the law or its application.
ex: Defense counsel cannot openly argue for jury nullification, but the theme hummed under every closing line.

def: A judge's incidental remark that is not essential to the decision and carries no binding force.
ex: Counsel leaned hard on a stray line from the ruling, but it was mere obiter dictum and bound no one.

def: The point of law on which a court's decision actually turns and which later courts must follow.
ex: We spent the afternoon isolating the ratio decidendi from three pages of surrounding commentary.

def: A non-party who, with the court's leave, files argument to assist on a point of broad importance.
ex: Two trade bodies applied to appear as amicus curiae on the data-protection question.

def: With the necessary changes made to fit a different but analogous situation.
ex: The indemnity clause applies to the subcontractor mutatis mutandis.

def: The principle that courts should stand by settled precedent when deciding like cases.
ex: Absent a compelling reason, stare decisis counsels us to follow the 1998 authority.

def: The legal right to bring or be heard in a particular proceeding.
ex: The objector has no locus standi because he suffered no direct loss.

def: With retroactive effect, as though an act had been done at the earlier proper time.
ex: The court entered the corrected order nunc pro tunc to the original filing date.

def: The rhetorical closing passage of a speech or argument, meant to drive the point home.
ex: Her peroration to the jury lasted barely two minutes but left the room silent.

def: To challenge the truth, validity, or integrity of something.
ex: Opposing counsel tried to impugn the witness's motives rather than his account.

def: To assert or allege something formally as a fact in pleadings.
ex: The particulars aver that the notice was served on the third of March.

def: By even stronger reasoning, given that a related weaker case already holds.
ex: If a written notice sufficed there, then a fortiori the signed deed suffices here.

def: For the sake of argument, conceding a point only hypothetically.
ex: Even assuming arguendo that a duty existed, there was no breach.

def: Wilfully disobedient to the authority or orders of a court.
ex: His contumacious refusal to disclose the accounts drew a committal application.

def: Decided in ignorance of a binding authority or statute, and so lacking precedential weight.
ex: We'll argue the earlier ruling was per incuriam because it overlooked the 2004 Act.

def: Provisionally, allowed to stand for now subject to later challenge.
ex: The court admitted the statement de bene esse pending a ruling on privilege.

def: Point by point, dealing with matters one after another in order.
ex: The judgment addresses each ground of appeal seriatim.

def: Ranking equally and without preference among competing claims.
ex: The unsecured creditors rank pari passu in the distribution.

def: The interpretive canon by which general words following a list take their meaning from the listed items' shared class.
ex: Under ejusdem generis, 'other vehicles' after cars and vans won't stretch to aircraft.

def: The rule that an ambiguous term is construed against the party who drafted it.
ex: Any doubt in the exclusion clause falls to be resolved contra proferentem.

def: Among other things, signalling that the items listed are not exhaustive.
ex: The retainer covers, inter alia, drafting, negotiation, and completion.

def: Issued by the court collectively rather than under any single judge's name.
ex: The dismissal came in a short per curiam opinion.

def: Silently, deciding or passing over a point without express discussion.
ex: The earlier panel overruled that line sub silentio, never once mentioning it.

def: The amount of damages or compensation to be awarded, as distinct from liability.
ex: Liability is admitted; we're now fighting purely on quantum.

def: Evasive shifting of position or desertion of a stance one previously held.
ex: The witness's tergiversation under cross-examination destroyed his credibility.

def: The plaintiff's formal reply to the matters raised in the defendant's answer.
ex: Counsel used the replication to plead avoidance rather than merely deny the plea.

def: A defendant's reduction of the plaintiff's claim by a counter-demand arising from the same transaction.
ex: By way of recoupment the buyer set the defective-goods loss against the price sued for.

def: The jurisdiction's continuing control over property that is the subject of a pending suit, and the notice that binds later purchasers.
ex: We filed a lis pendens so no buyer could take the land free of the ownership dispute.

def: The specific factual detail a party must supply to clarify and delimit the case pleaded.
ex: We served a request for further and better particulars of the alleged misrepresentations.

def: A written instruction to the court clerk requesting issue of a writ or other formal step.
ex: Her clerk lodged a praecipe directing the office to enter the appearance.

def: A defendant's written confession of judgment authorising entry against them without contest.
ex: The note contained a cognovit clause, so default judgment issued the moment payment lapsed.

def: An unlawful bargain to fund another's suit in return for a share of the proceeds.
ex: The funding agreement skirted champerty by leaving conduct of the case with the claimant.

def: A discretionary doctrine allowing a court to decline jurisdiction where another forum is clearly more appropriate.
ex: The action was stayed on forum non conveniens grounds in favour of the Singapore courts.

def: The requirement that a controversy be sufficiently developed and concrete before a court will adjudicate it.
ex: The declaratory claim failed for want of ripeness, the threatened harm being wholly contingent.

def: A person appointed to conduct litigation on behalf of a party who lacks capacity.
ex: The court appointed a guardian ad litem to protect the minor's interests in the settlement.

def: By special leave granted to an out-of-jurisdiction lawyer for a single case.
ex: Lead counsel was admitted pro hac vice to argue the motion in the Delaware court.

def: An attempt to impugn a judgment in a separate proceeding rather than by direct appeal.
ex: The debtor's fresh suit was a collateral attack on the default judgment and barred as such.

def: The treatment of an amended pleading as filed at the date of the original for limitation purposes.
ex: The added claim survived because it enjoyed relation back to the writ's original service.

def: A party's failure to advance the action with due diligence, exposing it to dismissal.
ex: Three dormant years led to dismissal for want of prosecution.

def: Spontaneous utterances made in the immediacy of an event, received as an exception to the rule against hearsay.
ex: Her scream of 'he's got a knife' came in as res gestae, since she had no time to concoct anything.

def: An assumption the law treats as established until a party adduces sufficient evidence to displace it.
ex: Legitimacy is only a rebuttable presumption, so the DNA results were enough to overturn it.

def: The degree to which an item of evidence tends to prove a fact genuinely in issue.
ex: The photographs were gruesome, but their probative value on cause of death outweighed the prejudice.

def: The protection shielding materials prepared by or for a lawyer in anticipation of litigation from disclosure to the opponent.
ex: Her handwritten trial strategy falls squarely within the work-product doctrine, so redact it before we produce the file.

def: An itemized schedule identifying withheld documents and stating the basis on which each is claimed to be protected from disclosure.
ex: Their privilege log is so vague we can't tell whether entry forty is genuinely privileged or just embarrassing.

def: To establish the preliminary facts that render a subsequent piece of evidence admissible.
ex: You can't put the ledger in until you lay a foundation through someone who actually kept it.

def: The principle barring extrinsic evidence to contradict or vary the terms of a fully integrated written contract.
ex: The parol evidence rule shuts out his tale of a side deal once the contract says it's the entire agreement.

def: The requirement that the original of a document be produced to prove its contents unless its absence is satisfactorily explained.
ex: Under the best evidence rule, hand up the signed original, not a scan someone retyped afterwards.

def: Evidence of a person's disposition toward certain conduct, offered to suggest they acted in keeping with it.
ex: The Crown wants his prior assaults in as propensity evidence, and I'll fight it tooth and nail.

def: Evidence of other misconduct so strikingly connected to the charge that its probative force overrides the usual bar on character evidence.
ex: Three victims describing the identical modus operandi turned this into classic similar fact evidence.

def: A witness who, once called, shows antagonism to the party calling them and may then be cross-examined by that party.
ex: The moment she recanted on the stand, I applied to treat her as a hostile witness.

def: To establish that an item of evidence is genuinely what its proponent claims it to be.
ex: You have to authenticate the recording before I'll let the jury hear a word of it.

def: The obscuring or removal of privileged or irrelevant material from a document before it is disclosed.
ex: The redaction was so heavy that only the page numbers survived.

def: Conducted privately in the judge's chambers or a closed court, away from the public and sometimes the parties.
ex: The judge reviewed the sensitive files in camera before ruling on the privilege claim.

def: The protection from disclosure of communications made for the dominant purpose of pending or contemplated litigation.
ex: The expert's draft report is covered by litigation privilege because we commissioned it for this very suit.

def: A ground on which a court may withhold relevant material whose disclosure would damage the public interest.
ex: The minister claimed public interest immunity over the informant's identity.

def: A court's acceptance of a notorious or indisputable fact without requiring formal proof of it.
ex: I'll ask the court to take judicial notice that Christmas Day fell on a Sunday that year.

def: A statement describing an event made while the declarant perceives it or immediately afterwards, admitted as a hearsay exception.
ex: Her emergency call narrating the crash as it happened came in as a present sense impression.

def: An earlier account by a witness that conflicts with their present testimony, deployed to undermine credibility.
ex: Confront her with the prior inconsistent statement and watch the whole story unravel.

def: The permitted practice of showing a witness a document to revive their memory of events.
ex: He'd forgotten the figures, so I handed him his diary for refreshing recollection.

def: By word of mouth; given orally in open court rather than on paper.
ex: The tribunal preferred to hear the experts viva voce so it could test them under cross.

def: A court order compelling a person to attend and to bring specified documents or things with them.
ex: We served a subpoena duces tecum on the bank to drag the original ledgers into court.

def: The principle that damages should restore the injured party to the position they occupied before the wrong.
ex: The award aims at restitutio in integrum, so we've costed the repair to put the vehicle back exactly as it was.

def: A deduction from damages reflecting that repair or replacement has left the claimant with something newer or more valuable than what was lost.
ex: The insurer argued betterment, insisting we discount the new roof against the depreciated value of the old one.

def: A sum awarded for injured feelings, grief, or mental suffering rather than for measurable financial loss.
ex: In addition to funeral costs, the widow sought solatium for the anguish of the bereavement.

def: An equitable remedy compelling a wrongdoer to hand over the gains made from the breach.
ex: Rather than prove our own loss, we elected an account of profits to capture everything he earned from the infringing product.

def: The claimant's election to sue for the wrongdoer's gain in restitution instead of for their own loss in damages.
ex: By waiver of tort we can reach the profits from the converted goods rather than merely their market value.

def: An award measured by the benefit the defendant derived from the wrong rather than the harm suffered by the claimant.
ex: Where the loss is negligible, gain-based damages let us strip out the advantage the trespass gave him.

def: A sum representing the hypothetical fee the claimant could have charged to release the defendant from the obligation breached.
ex: The court assessed negotiating damages as the price the parties would reasonably have agreed for relaxing the covenant.

def: Compensation for the lost enjoyment and pleasures of life following a serious injury.
ex: Beyond lost earnings, we're claiming hedonic damages for a man who can no longer walk his daughter down the aisle.

def: Additional losses recoverable only because they attach to an independently actionable head of damage.
ex: The distress claim is parasitic damages, riding on the established property loss rather than standing alone.

def: An award made to affirm and protect a right that has been infringed, independent of any measurable loss.
ex: Even absent financial harm, vindicatory damages mark the court's recognition that a constitutional right was breached.

def: Enhanced compensation reflecting the injury to the claimant's feelings caused by the defendant's malicious or high-handed conduct.
ex: His sneering conduct in the witness box justified aggravated damages on top of the basic award.

def: Insolently contemptuous, describing the high-handed disregard for a claimant's rights that attracts enhanced damages.
ex: The defendant's contumelious refusal to apologise coloured the whole assessment of the award.

def: The reduction in a claimant's ability to enjoy life or use a faculty, compensated as a distinct head of non-pecuniary damage.
ex: The loss of amenity award reflects that she can no longer play the piano she loved.

def: An award made now on the assumption a feared deterioration will not occur, leaving the claimant free to return for more if it does.
ex: We took provisional damages so that, if the epilepsy develops, he can come back for a further sum.

def: The principle that compensation received from independent sources, such as insurance, is not deducted from the damages payable by the wrongdoer.
ex: Under the collateral source rule, his private health payout doesn't reduce what the tortfeasor owes.

def: A restitutionary defence available where the recipient has, in good faith, so altered their circumstances that repaying would be inequitable.
ex: She pleaded change of position, having spent the mistaken payment on a holiday she'd never otherwise have taken.

def: A historic restitutionary claim to recover money the defendant holds but in justice ought to return to the claimant.
ex: We framed the recovery of the misdirected funds as an action for money had and received.

def: The receipt of a benefit at another's expense in circumstances the law treats as unjust, grounding a duty to make restitution.
ex: His retention of the overpayment is textbook unjust enrichment; there was simply no basis for it.

def: A monetary remedy for breach of an equitable duty, assessed by equity's own principles rather than common law rules of damages.
ex: For the trustee's breach we're seeking equitable compensation to restore the fund to what it should have been.

def: The measure of damages taken as the fall in the thing's worth caused by the wrong, rather than the cost of putting it right.
ex: The court preferred diminution in value, awarding the drop in the land's price rather than the exorbitant cost of cure.

def: The measure of damages taken as the expense of remedying the defect or reinstating the position, rather than the loss in value.
ex: He wanted cost of cure to rebuild the wall exactly, but the court thought that wholly disproportionate.

def: An award reversing a transfer of value from claimant to defendant, restoring what the defendant unjustly gained.
ex: Restitutionary damages here strip the benefit he obtained by using our client's land without consent.

def: Damages for the lost opportunity of a favourable outcome, valued by the probability that the chance would have come off.
ex: We're advancing a loss of a chance claim: but for the missed deadline, she had a sixty percent prospect of winning.

def: The annual figure of loss that is multiplied by the appropriate factor to produce a lump-sum award for future losses.
ex: We fixed the multiplicand at his net annual earnings before applying the multiplier for his working life.

def: An award directing damages for future loss to be paid as an index-linked income stream rather than a single lump sum.
ex: Given the lifelong care costs, a periodical payments order suits him far better than a capital sum he might exhaust.

def: In its actual form, describing restitution or transfer of the very asset rather than its money equivalent.
ex: The court ordered the shares returned in specie rather than compensating their value.

def: A loss treated as total because the cost of repair or recovery would exceed the value of the thing saved.
ex: The surveyor declared a constructive total loss, the salvage bill dwarfing what the hull was worth.

def: A sum paid to the claimant on account of the damages likely to be awarded, before final judgment.
ex: We secured an interim payment to fund his rehabilitation while liability was still being fought.

def: The measure of damages that restores a claimant to the position they were in before relying on the defendant, compensating wasted expenditure.
ex: Since the profits were too speculative, we claimed the reliance interest, the money he'd sunk into the aborted venture.

def: Having discharged one's office such that no further authority to act on the matter remains.
ex: Once the tribunal handed down its final award it was functus officio and could not reopen the question of quantum.

def: The measure of respect a reviewing court accords to the findings or discretion of the primary decision-maker.
ex: Given the specialist expertise of the panel, a high degree of curial deference was warranted on the factual findings.

def: A mistake that takes a decision-maker outside the lawful bounds of its power, rendering the decision a nullity.
ex: Because the board misconstrued the eligibility threshold, it committed a jurisdictional error going to the root of its authority.

def: The worsening of an appellant's position as a consequence of that party's own appeal, a result the courts generally forbid.
ex: The prosecution had not cross-appealed, so the court could not increase the sentence without breaching the rule against reformatio in peius.

def: A writ or order staying the enforcement of a judgment pending the outcome of an appeal.
ex: We posted a supersedeas bond to halt execution while the appeal was pending.

def: The quashing of a lower court's judgment for error of law, with the matter remitted for fresh determination.
ex: In civil-law systems the supreme court sits in cassation, correcting points of law rather than reweighing the evidence.

def: The sending back of a matter to a lower court or tribunal for reconsideration in light of the appellate ruling.
ex: Rather than substitute its own decision, the court ordered remittal to a differently constituted panel.

def: A searching form of scrutiny requiring a decision-maker to have genuinely engaged with the relevant evidence and reasoning.
ex: Under hard-look review the agency's cursory treatment of the environmental data could not survive.

def: An attack on the validity of a decision raised in separate proceedings rather than by direct appeal or review.
ex: The defendant mounted a collateral challenge to the byelaw as a defence to the prosecution.

def: The condition of a dispute that has ceased to present a live controversy, depriving the court of a reason to decide it.
ex: The detainee's release raised a question of mootness, though the court heard the appeal on a point of general importance.

def: The principle that a claimant must pursue available alternative avenues of redress before invoking judicial review.
ex: Review was refused for failure to observe the exhaustion of remedies, the statutory appeal being an adequate route.

def: The overturning of a precedent with effect confined to future cases, preserving transactions completed under the old rule.
ex: To avoid disturbing settled conveyances, the court adopted prospective overruling of the discredited principle.

def: Proceedings brought by the Attorney General at the instance of a private individual who lacks standing to sue alone.
ex: Denied sufficient interest of their own, the residents proceeded by way of a relator action.

def: An order capping or extinguishing a party's exposure to adverse costs so as to enable a public-interest challenge.
ex: Without a protective costs order the claimant could not have risked bringing the litigation.

def: An appeal that bypasses an intermediate court to proceed directly to the highest court on a point of general importance.
ex: Given the constitutional dimension, the parties sought a leapfrog appeal straight to the apex court.

def: A document by which the successful party seeks to uphold a decision on grounds other than those given below, or to have it varied.
ex: The respondent's notice contended that the judgment could be affirmed on an alternative basis.

def: The inherent authority of a superior court to police the legality of decisions taken by inferior bodies.
ex: Judicial review is an exercise of the court's supervisory jurisdiction, not an appeal on the merits.

def: The quality of a problem whose many interlocking interests make it ill-suited to bipolar judicial resolution.
ex: The allocation of scarce health resources was too marked by polycentricity for the court to arbitrate.

def: The rule permitting immediate appeal of a discrete ruling that conclusively determines an important issue separate from the merits.
ex: The denial of immunity was appealable at once under the collateral order doctrine.

def: A factual mistake so obvious and consequential as to justify appellate interference with a trial finding.
ex: Absent a palpable and overriding error, the appellate court would not disturb the judge's assessment of credibility.

def: The appearance, judged objectively, of a real possibility that a decision-maker was not impartial.
ex: The adjudicator's undisclosed shareholding gave rise to apparent bias, vitiating the award.

def: The exercise of a power to achieve an end other than that for which it was conferred.
ex: The compulsory purchase was quashed as made for an improper purpose, namely to punish the objectors.

word: error of law on the face of the record
def: A legal mistake apparent from the decision and its stated reasons, reviewable even where no jurisdictional excess is shown.
ex: The tribunal's misdirection was an error of law on the face of the record, plain from its written reasons.

def: Expressly naming one thing implies the deliberate exclusion of others left unmentioned.
ex: They set out the force majeure events exhaustively, so expressio unius bars them from now adding pandemic to the list.

def: A word's meaning is coloured by the neighbouring words it keeps.
ex: Read among 'lodging, board and accommodation', the disputed term takes its sense from its companions under noscitur a sociis.

def: The background of surrounding facts reasonably available to the parties against which the language is construed.
ex: The court read 'delivery' against the factual matrix of a just-in-time supply relationship, not in the abstract.

def: A method of severing an offending restraint by striking out the unenforceable words without redrafting what remains.
ex: The non-compete survives only if the blue-pencil test lets us delete 'or any allied trade' cleanly.

def: A bare promise unsupported by consideration and therefore unenforceable.
ex: Without anything moving from the promisee, his assurance is a nudum pactum we cannot sue on.

def: Demanding the utmost good faith, with a positive duty to disclose all material facts.
ex: Insurance is a contract uberrimae fidei, so the applicant's silence on the prior claim is fatal.

def: A plea that a signed document is fundamentally different in character from what the signer believed, rendering it void.
ex: The elderly guarantor may raise non est factum, having been told he was signing a delivery receipt, not a charge.

def: A bar preventing parties who have dealt on a shared assumption from later denying it to the other's detriment.
ex: Both sides invoiced at the higher rate for years, so estoppel by convention stops the buyer disputing it now.

def: A separate, subsidiary agreement whose consideration is entry into the main contract.
ex: The oral assurance about fuel economy stands as a collateral contract, even though it never made it into the sale document.

def: A stipulation that the contract may be varied only in signed writing, defeating informal amendment.
ex: He claims a phone call raised the fee, but the no-oral-modification clause means only a countersigned addendum counts.

def: The contest over whose standard terms govern when offer and acceptance are exchanged on conflicting pre-printed documents.
ex: In this battle of the forms, the seller's terms prevail as the last shot fired before performance.

def: A party's clear renunciation of its obligations before performance falls due, entitling the other to treat the contract as ended.
ex: Her letter refusing to complete is anticipatory repudiation; we can accept it and sue at once.

def: A stipulation making punctual performance a condition, so that any delay justifies termination.
ex: Serve notice making time of the essence, and a single day's slippage lets us walk away.

def: A test implying a term so obvious that both parties would have testily dismissed a bystander suggesting it be spelled out.
ex: Under the officious bystander test, a duty not to sabotage the works is too plain to need stating.

def: The discharge of a claim by an agreement to accept some substituted performance in place of what was owed.
ex: His cashing the reduced cheque marked 'in full settlement' amounts to accord and satisfaction.

def: A ground for restitution arising where a party receives none of the bargained-for benefit it paid to obtain.
ex: The goods never shipped, so on a total failure of consideration our client recovers the whole deposit.

def: A provision purporting to relieve a party of liability for its own default or negligence.
ex: Their exculpatory clause is read narrowly and will not cover deliberate wrongdoing.

def: The rule striking down a stipulated remedy that is extravagant compared with any legitimate interest in performance.
ex: Because the daily charge dwarfs any conceivable loss, the penalty doctrine renders it unenforceable.

def: The commercial workability a term must supply before a court will imply it into an agreement.
ex: We can imply a right of access on business efficacy grounds, since the maintenance obligation is useless without it.

def: A provision obliging a party to keep paying regardless of any difficulty, defence, or set-off.
ex: Under the hell or high water clause the lessee pays even if the equipment fails entirely.

def: A formal notice that acting on a contract now waives no entitlement to enforce it strictly later.
ex: Accept the late payment under an express reservation of rights so we preserve the termination remedy.

def: A party's clear indication by words or conduct that it will not perform its obligations.
ex: Their email flatly refusing to ship amounts to a renunciation, so we can accept it and sue now.

def: A contractual entitlement of a funder or third party to assume a defaulting party's role rather than let the contract collapse.
ex: Under the direct agreement the bank exercised its step-in rights and installed a replacement contractor.

def: An equitable discretion allowing a party to escape the loss of proprietary or contractual rights triggered by its own default.
ex: The tenant applied for relief from forfeiture, offering to clear all arrears plus the landlord's costs.

def: To both accept a benefit under an instrument and reject its accompanying burdens, which the law forbids.
ex: They can't approbate and reprobate by keeping the goods while disowning the arbitration clause.

def: The binding choice a party must make between two inconsistent rights, such as terminating or affirming after a breach.
ex: Once you've made your election to affirm, you can't later switch and treat the contract as at an end.

def: The measure of damages that puts the innocent party where it would have been had the contract been performed.
ex: The expectation interest captures the profit they'd have earned, not merely what they spent.

def: The requirement that a party seeking to unwind a contract give back any benefits it has itself received.
ex: Rescission is only open to the buyer if it can make counter-restitution of the shares.

def: A defence allowing cross-claims so closely connected to the claim that enforcing payment without accounting for them would be unjust.
ex: We're asserting an equitable set-off, since their defective supply caused the very losses they now sue on.

def: A term providing that variations are effective only if made in writing and signed.
ex: The no oral modification clause defeats their claim that we agreed a discount over the phone.

def: An applicant's promise to compensate the respondent for loss caused by an injunction later found to have been wrongly granted.
ex: The judge required a cross-undertaking in damages before freezing the defendant's accounts.

def: An injunction granted to restrain a wrong that is merely apprehended but has not yet occurred.
ex: Fearing imminent disclosure, we obtained a quia timet injunction before any documents actually leaked.

def: A lease obligation requiring a tenant to keep trading from the premises throughout the term.
ex: The anchor tenant breached its keep-open covenant by shuttering the store two years early.

def: A liquidated sum reflecting a real forecast of anticipated damage and so escaping condemnation as a penalty.
ex: We can defend the charge as a genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than an unenforceable penalty.

def: A trivial non-performance too slight to justify termination or substantial damages.
ex: A two-hour delay is a de minimis breach and won't entitle them to walk away.

def: The rule invalidating arrangements designed to strip assets from an insolvent party's estate on bankruptcy.
ex: The forfeiture-on-insolvency clause offends the anti-deprivation principle and won't bind the liquidator.

def: Closing a deal despite already knowing a representation is false, then suing on the breach afterwards.
ex: The buyer's counsel demanded a pro-sandbagging clause so a defect they already knew about would still support an indemnity claim after completion.

def: A provision that reads materiality qualifiers out of the warranties when quantifying indemnifiable losses.
ex: With the materiality scrape in place, a string of individually trivial compliance lapses aggregated into a claim comfortably above the basket.

def: A stipulation that the buyer relied on no statements beyond those written into the agreement, foreclosing fraud built on extra-contractual assurances.
ex: The anti-reliance clause gutted their pitch-deck fraud theory, since the buyer had disclaimed reliance on anything outside the four corners.

def: A pricing structure that fixes equity value at a pre-signing balance-sheet date with no post-closing purchase-price adjustment.
ex: The sellers pushed for a locked-box, so the price was struck off the March accounts and we owed only a daily accrual through to completion.

def: Post-closing financial statements drawn up to true the price up against agreed working-capital and debt targets.
ex: We are still fighting over the completion accounts because the buyer's accountants quietly restated the inventory provision downward.

def: A covenant obliging the acquirer to take every step, including divestitures and litigation, to secure regulatory approval.
ex: The seller accepted our bid only because we swallowed a hell-or-high-water clause and promised to fight the FTC if it came to that.

def: A takeover defence in which the target sells or options its most prized assets to deter a hostile bidder.
ex: Facing the raider, the board floated a crown-jewel lock-up on the flagship division, betting the suitor only ever wanted that unit.

def: A premium buyback of a hostile holder's accumulated block to make the takeover threat go away.
ex: The founders paid greenmail to see the activist off, and the remaining shareholders promptly sued over the sweetheart repurchase.

def: Buying shares after a deal is announced purely to demand a judicial fair-value determination that beats the deal price.
ex: Hedge funds piled in for appraisal arbitrage, wagering the Chancery Court would peg fair value above the merger consideration.

def: The most exacting standard of review, testing both fair dealing and fair price, applied to conflicted-controller transactions.
ex: Because the controller sat on both sides, the court applied entire fairness and the board's cleansing committee was picked apart.

def: The rule barring a fiduciary from diverting to personal gain a business chance that rightly belonged to the company.
ex: He steered the acquisition into his own vehicle, and the corporate opportunity doctrine handed the resulting profits straight back to the firm.

def: A judicial theory that recharacterises an asset sale as a merger so the buyer inherits the seller's liabilities.
ex: Structuring it as an asset deal did not help; the court found a de facto merger and pinned the tort claims on the acquirer.

def: An acquirer's exposure to the debts and obligations of the business it buys, despite an arm's-length purchase.
ex: The environmental claims followed the plant through the sale under successor liability, wiping out the bargain the buyer thought it had struck.

def: A poison-pill feature that only the incumbent directors who adopted it may redeem.
ex: The dead-hand provision would have frozen the proxy contest, since a freshly elected board could not have pulled the pill, so the court struck it down.

def: A board split into classes with only a fraction standing for election each year, slowing any takeover.
ex: With a staggered board, the activist faced two annual meetings just to win a majority, and the bid lost all its momentum.

def: An undertaking not to buy more shares or launch a bid for an agreed period.
ex: We opened the data room only after they signed a standstill, so the bidder could not flip our diligence into a hostile approach.

def: A clause freeing directors to abandon a signed deal for a superior proposal without breaching their agreement.
ex: When the higher bid landed, the board invoked the fiduciary out, paid the break fee, and switched horses.

def: A first bidder's contractual entitlement to meet the terms of any superior offer before the target may accept it.
ex: The incumbent's matching right meant every time we raised, they simply re-topped us, and the auction quietly died.

def: The portion of sale proceeds that selling owners reinvest as a stake in the buyer's post-deal entity.
ex: The sponsor required thirty percent rollover equity so management kept real skin in the game after the buyout.

def: The thin slice of publicly held shares left outstanding after a leveraged buyout or recapitalisation.
ex: Holders of the stub equity were left riding a wildly levered balance sheet with almost no float to trade against.

def: A refinancing that raises fresh debt to fund a large one-off dividend to shareholders.
ex: The sponsor did a dividend recap, pulling its whole cheque back out while leaving the portfolio company groaning under new leverage.

def: A structure in which the acquirer's shell subsidiary merges into the target, leaving the target alive as a wholly owned subsidiary.
ex: We used a reverse triangular merger to keep the target's licences intact, since it survived and its contracts never triggered an assignment.

def: Insurance kept in force after a deal to answer claims arising from acts before closing.
ex: We bought six-year run-off cover for the departing directors, so their exposure survived the change of control.

def: A limiting phrase confining a warranty to matters within the giver's actual or constructive awareness.
ex: They larded every rep with a knowledge qualifier, so unless we could prove the CFO knew, the warranty simply did not bite.

def: A provision entitling the seller to a share of any quick, richer resale profit the buyer makes.
ex: The council insisted on an anti-embarrassment clause, so when the developer flipped the site within a year it clawed back part of the gain.

def: A loose cluster of activist funds that build stakes in parallel to pressure a target while dodging formal group status.
ex: A wolf pack had quietly gathered fifteen percent between them before any single filing tipped the board off.

def: An indemnity threshold that, once crossed, unlocks recovery of the entire loss rather than only the excess.
ex: With a tipping basket, the buyer just needed claims to nudge past one percent before the whole amount became recoverable from the first dollar.

def: Principle that adequate cautionary language surrounding a forward-looking statement can render alleged misstatements immaterial as a matter of law.
ex: We leaned on the bespeaks-caution doctrine to knock out the projection claims at the pleading stage.

def: The requirement that a plaintiff show the defendant's misrepresentation, and not other market forces, actually caused the claimed investment loss.
ex: Their expert never disentangled the fraud from the sector-wide selloff, so loss causation was fatally thin.

def: Presumption that investors relied on the integrity of a security's market price, sparing them from proving individual reliance in an efficient market.
ex: Class certification rides on fraud-on-the-market, so the defense is throwing everything at market efficiency.

def: Recommending a security while secretly intending to sell one's own holdings into the demand the recommendation creates.
ex: The newsletter's touts read like research until we found he was scalping every stock he pumped.

def: Placing orders one intends to cancel before execution to create a false impression of supply or demand.
ex: Surveillance caught him spoofing the book with large sell orders he yanked the instant the price ticked down.

def: A broker's excessive trading in a client's account driven by commission generation rather than the client's interest.
ex: Her turnover ratio screamed churning; the account traded twelve times over in a single quarter.

def: A person who receives material nonpublic information from an insider and trades or passes it on.
ex: As a remote tippee, he still needed to know the insider had breached a duty for a personal benefit.

def: Basis for insider-trading liability where a person trades on confidential information in breach of a duty owed to the information's source.
ex: The lawyer traded on his own client's takeover, so we charged it under the misappropriation theory rather than the classical one.

def: An offering of securities drawn down from a previously effective shelf registration.
ex: With the shelf already effective, we can price a takedown overnight the moment the window opens.

def: An underwriting in which the bank commits to purchase the entire issue at a fixed price before marketing it.
ex: They offered a bought deal at a two-point discount, so the issuer got certainty and the bank took the placement risk.

def: The process by which underwriters solicit and record investor demand to set the size and price of an offering.
ex: Bookbuilding closed three times covered, so we nudged the price to the top of the range.

def: Doctrine treating ostensibly separate securities offerings as a single offering, potentially defeating a claimed exemption.
ex: We spaced the private placements six months apart to avoid integration with the public deal.

def: Underwriter bidding to support a new issue's market price during distribution, permitted only within strict limits.
ex: The syndicate ran stabilization at the offer price for two sessions before the stock traded free.

def: The return of securities to their home market after being placed with foreign investors in a cross-border offering.
ex: We built in selling restrictions to curb flowback swamping the domestic float.

def: A letter from the issuer's auditors giving underwriters negative assurance on unaudited financial data in an offering document.
ex: We won't close until the accountants deliver a bring-down comfort letter dated the settlement day.

def: An underwriter's or director's defense to statutory liability based on a reasonable investigation supporting belief in the registration statement's accuracy.
ex: Document the diligence calls, because the due-diligence defense lives or dies on what the record shows you actually checked.

def: A pact barring a party from acquiring further shares or launching a bid for a defined period.
ex: Access to the data room was conditioned on a two-year standstill agreement.

def: A poison pill redeemable only by the directors who adopted it, disabling a newly elected board from removing it.
ex: Delaware struck down the dead-hand pill as an impermissible fetter on the incoming board's power.

def: A target's sale or option of its most valuable assets to make itself unattractive to a hostile bidder.
ex: They tried a crown-jewel lockup on the pipeline unit, and the court enjoined it as an unreasonable defensive measure.

def: A friendly investor who takes a substantial minority stake to help a target fend off a hostile suitor short of a full acquisition.
ex: Rather than sell outright, the board placed a blocking stake with a white squire on a long standstill.

def: A dissenting shareholder's statutory entitlement to a judicial determination of the fair value of shares cashed out in a merger.
ex: A cohort of arbitrageurs perfected appraisal rights, betting the court would value the stock above the deal price.

def: A regulatory staff assurance that it will not recommend enforcement against a specifically described course of conduct.
ex: We got a no-action letter blessing the resale structure before anyone touched the shares.

def: The passage of time after issuance that lets restricted securities become freely tradable or an issuer qualify for streamlined registration.
ex: Once the seasoning period ran, the restricted block could dribble out under the volume limits.

def: A prepayment amount compensating lenders for lost future interest when debt is retired ahead of schedule.
ex: Refinancing before the call date meant swallowing a hefty make-whole premium on the whole tranche.

def: An anti-dilution mechanism resetting an earlier investor's conversion price down to the price of a later, cheaper round.
ex: The down round triggered a full ratchet, and the common got crushed on the cap table.

def: An issuer's release of material nonpublic information to favored analysts or investors ahead of the market at large.
ex: The CFO's whisper to two funds on the call was textbook selective disclosure, and the fair-disclosure rules give no quarter.

def: Prearranged buy and sell orders entered to create the false appearance of trading activity in a security.
ex: The pair ran matched orders across two accounts to paint the tape and lure momentum buyers.

def: An insolvency sale negotiated in full beforehand and executed the moment the administrator is appointed.
ex: The buyer wanted a pre-pack so the brand would reopen on Monday without customers ever noticing the administration.

def: A pre-insolvency disposal for significantly less than the asset was worth, liable to be unwound by an office-holder.
ex: Selling the freehold to his brother-in-law for half its value is a textbook transaction at an undervalue.

def: A payment or security given to one creditor shortly before insolvency that unfairly improves its position and can be reversed.
ex: Paying off the overdraft he'd personally guaranteed reeks of a voidable preference.

def: Assets or contracts whose ongoing burdens outweigh their value, which a liquidator may disclaim to shed the liability.
ex: The trustee disclaimed the loss-making lease as onerous property rather than keep bleeding rent.

def: The mandatory netting of mutual debts between an insolvent estate and a creditor so that only the balance is provable or payable.
ex: After insolvency set-off, the supplier's two-million claim nets down to a three-hundred-thousand provable debt.

def: The layer of debt where value breaks in the capital structure, which typically converts to equity in a restructuring.
ex: The mezzanine is the fulcrum security here, so those holders will end up owning the reorganised business.

def: An initial bidder whose agreed offer sets a floor price and bid protections against which rival distressed-sale bids are measured.
ex: We locked in a stalking horse at forty million with a break fee to flush out higher offers at auction.

def: A strategy of buying a troubled company's distressed debt intending to convert it into controlling equity through the restructuring.
ex: That fund isn't chasing a par recovery; this is a loan-to-own play for the whole business.

def: A court's demotion of a creditor's claim below others as a remedy for its inequitable conduct toward the estate.
ex: The insider's loan was equitably subordinated once the court found he'd manipulated the company's finances.

def: The pooling of the assets and liabilities of separate affiliated debtors into a single estate for distribution.
ex: Creditors sought substantive consolidation because the group's intercompany affairs were hopelessly commingled.

def: A court's recasting of a purported loan as an equity contribution, defeating the lender's claim to repayment.
ex: The shareholder advance was recharacterised as equity, so he now ranks behind every genuine creditor.

def: Confirmation of a restructuring plan imposed over the dissent of an entire creditor or shareholder class.
ex: The new plan let us push through a cross-class cram-down of the out-of-the-money shareholders.

def: The principle that no junior class may receive value under a plan until senior dissenting classes are paid in full.
ex: Equity can't keep its shares while bondholders take a haircut; that flatly violates the absolute priority rule.

def: The compensation or safeguards a secured creditor is owed for any decline in its collateral's value during a moratorium.
ex: The lender demanded adequate protection payments to offset the depreciation of the fleet during the stay.

def: A new security interest ranked ahead of existing secured creditors, usually to secure rescue financing.
ex: The rescue lenders insisted on a priming lien over the very collateral the incumbent banks already held.

def: A financing device converting a lender's pre-insolvency debt into new post-filing loans that enjoy priority repayment.
ex: The facility carried a roll-up, quietly elevating the old exposure to super-priority status.

def: The ring-fenced slice of floating-charge realisations reserved by statute for unsecured creditors.
ex: Unsecured creditors will only ever see the prescribed part, capped well below their actual losses.

def: The equitable ordering of a creditor's recourse to funds so a junior creditor with access to only one fund is not prejudiced.
ex: By marshalling, the second lender forced the bank to exhaust the other collateral first.

def: The interval before formal insolvency during which directors' duties shift toward creditors and transactions become vulnerable.
ex: Every payment made in the twilight period will be scrutinised for preference and undervalue.

def: Buying an insolvent company's business cheaply and continuing it through a new entity while dumping the old debts.
ex: Regulators flagged the deal as phoenixing once the same directors reopened under an almost identical name.

def: A liability-management move in which a majority of lenders issue themselves priming debt, subordinating the non-participating minority.
ex: The minority lenders sued after the uptiering shunted them beneath brand-new super-senior paper.

def: A tactic where exchanging bondholders vote to strip protective covenants from the old bonds, coercing holdouts into the swap.
ex: The exchange used exit consents to gut the indenture, so anyone refusing to swap kept only a hollow instrument.

def: A creditor who refuses a consensual restructuring to extract a better individual outcome.
ex: One holdout fund threatened to derail the whole scheme unless it was paid out in full.

def: A doctrine barring appeals against a substantially consummated plan where unwinding it would harm third parties.
ex: The appeal was dismissed for equitable mootness because the plan had already been implemented and the money distributed.

def: A supply clause letting a seller retain ownership of goods until payment, defeating other creditors' claims to them on insolvency.
ex: The supplier invoked its reservation of title clause and reclaimed the unpaid stock from the warehouse.

def: The prolongation of a doomed company's life that swells its debts and destroys further value for creditors.
ex: The claim alleges the directors' deepening insolvency cost creditors millions by trading on a hopeless business.

def: The future interest a grantor automatically retains on conveying a determinable fee, taking effect if the limiting event occurs.
ex: Because the deed granted the land 'so long as it is used for a chapel,' the vendor kept a possibility of reverter.

word: clog on the equity of redemption
def: An improper contractual fetter that impedes or postpones a mortgagor's right to redeem the security.
ex: The option letting the lender buy the property was void as a clog on the equity of redemption.

def: The doctrine treating a purchaser as owner in equity from the moment of exchange, though legal title passes only on completion.
ex: Under equitable conversion the risk of fire passed to the buyer on exchange, so he was well advised to insure at once.

def: A tenant's right to take timber or wood from the land for fuel, repairs, or husbandry.
ex: The lease preserved the farmer's common of estovers for hedging and fencing the holding.

def: A tenant's right to re-enter and harvest the annual crops they sowed after their tenancy has unexpectedly ended.
ex: When the life tenant died mid-season, his executors claimed emblements over the standing wheat.

def: An intangible but inheritable property right in land with no physical existence, such as an easement or rentcharge.
ex: A right of way is a classic incorporeal hereditament, passing with the dominant land on every conveyance.

def: A method of describing land by its boundary lines, natural features, and measured distances.
ex: The old deed described the parcel by metes and bounds, starting at the oak and running thence to the brook.

def: The perpetual, inalienable holding of land by a corporation, historically restricted to stop land escaping feudal incidents.
ex: The medieval statutes of mortmain barred gifts of land to religious houses without royal licence.

def: A collateral provision or condition that, on a stated event, defeats or annuls an estate or interest.
ex: The deed of defeasance rendered the absolute conveyance a mere security, redeemable on repayment.

def: A freehold part of a building that overhangs or sits above land or property belonging to another.
ex: The bedroom extending over the neighbour's passage created a flying freehold that troubled the mortgage lender.

def: The rights of an owner of land abutting a watercourse to use the water and to the flow passing the land.
ex: As a riparian owner, the mill enjoyed the right to the natural flow of the stream undiminished in quantity.

def: A mortgagee's joining of a later advance to an earlier secured one so as to gain priority over an intervening charge.
ex: Lacking notice of the second mortgage, the bank was entitled to tacking of its further advance.

def: Ownerless goods or land that pass to the Crown, typically on an intestacy without kin or from a dissolved company's assets.
ex: When the company was struck off, its freehold vested in the Crown as bona vacantia.

def: A court's power to apply charitable property to a purpose as near as possible to the settlor's original intention once that purpose becomes impossible or impractical.
ex: With the orphanage long since closed, we applied cy-près to redirect the endowment to a children's hospice.

def: A gift made in contemplation of imminent death, conditional on the donor actually dying and revocable until then.
ex: Handing over the key to the deposit box from his hospital bed, he made a valid donatio mortis causa of its contents.

def: Expressing a mere wish, hope, or moral exhortation rather than imposing a binding trust obligation.
ex: The phrase 'in full confidence that she will provide for the children' was precatory, so the widow took absolutely.

def: The bringing of lifetime advances back into account so that an estate is divided equally among those entitled.
ex: The son who received a deposit for his house had to bring it into hotchpot before the residue was split three ways.

def: Distributed so that each branch of a family takes the share its deceased ancestor would have taken.
ex: Because the estate passes per stirpes, the two grandchildren split their late father's one-third between them.

def: Of a trust provision that shields a beneficiary's interest from creditors and bars its voluntary assignment.
ex: The spendthrift clause meant his judgment creditors could not touch the capital, only distributions once actually made.

def: Of a will provision that channels probate assets into an existing trust to be administered under its terms.
ex: Her pour-over will swept every asset that had escaped the living trust straight back into it on death.

def: A trust implied by law that returns beneficial ownership to the person who supplied the property when an express trust fails or title is put in another's name.
ex: Since he paid the whole purchase price but title went into her name alone, a resulting trust arose in his favour.

def: A trust whose terms are communicated to and accepted by a legatee outside the will, enforced although absent from the document itself.
ex: The gift to his solicitor 'absolutely' concealed a secret trust for his mistress, which she proved by the letter he had accepted.

def: Of a will declared orally before witnesses rather than reduced to signed writing.
ex: The soldier's nuncupative will, spoken to two comrades on active service, was admitted despite the absence of any document.

def: Of a will written entirely in the testator's own hand and often valid without attesting witnesses.
