def: A hypothetical, reasonably observant user of the product type against whom design similarity is assessed.
ex: To the informed user, aware of the crowded market, the small differences were enough to distinguish the designs.

def: The condition that a design give the informed user a different overall impression from what already exists.
ex: The design was invalidated for lacking individual character, being too close to a bottle already on the market.

def: The blatant or deliberate quality of an infringement, a factor supporting an award of enhanced damages.
ex: Given the flagrancy of the copying, the court awarded additional damages to mark its disapproval.

def: The reboxing or relabelling of genuine branded goods, often contested when they are parallel-imported.
ex: The brand owner objected to the importer's repackaging, arguing it damaged the mark's reputation.

def: The settling of a dispute by an arbitrator, or the decision itself.
ex: The parties agreed that the arbitrament of a single neutral would be final and beyond appeal.

def: A formal agreement by which parties submit an existing dispute to arbitration and define its terms.
ex: Because no clause covered the quarrel, the states negotiated a compromis specifying the tribunal's mandate.

def: The office or decision of an umpire appointed to resolve a deadlock between arbitrators.
ex: When the two arbitrators split, the dispute passed to the umpirage of the third member.

def: To settle a dispute as an impartial third party chosen by those in disagreement.
ex: A retired judge was retained to arbitrate the shipbuilding claim outside the courts.

def: To reconcile disputing parties by bringing them toward a voluntary settlement.
ex: The commissioner tried to conciliate the union and management before any formal claim was filed.

def: To help opposing parties reach their own agreement without imposing a decision.
ex: She was engaged to mediate the licensing row, steering both sides toward a workable compromise.

def: Describing a mediation style that helps parties find their own solution rather than advising one.
ex: His facilitative approach kept the focus on the parties' interests instead of his own opinion of the merits.

def: Describing a mediation style in which the neutral appraises the merits and predicts likely outcomes.
ex: Frustrated by the impasse, the parties asked for an evaluative session in which the mediator flagged the weakness of the counterclaim.

def: Having the power to settle a question conclusively.
ex: The tribunal held that the choice-of-law clause was determinative of the whole dispute.

def: Intended to placate an opponent and ease a dispute toward resolution.
ex: A conciliatory opening from counsel helped thaw the atmosphere before the mediation began.

def: A neutral third party who helps disputants settle, often by proposing terms.
ex: The statute lets a conciliator suggest settlement terms that a pure mediator would leave to the parties.

def: A neutral who guides discussion so parties can reach their own agreement.
ex: Acting only as a facilitator, she never expressed a view on who was likely to win.

def: The act of intervening between parties to help them resolve differences.
ex: Quiet intermediation by a trusted broker reopened talks that the lawyers had let collapse.

def: A renewal of cordial relations between parties who had been in conflict.
ex: The mediated sessions produced a rapprochement that let the joint venture continue.

def: An easing of hostility between opposing parties.
ex: A fragile detente held long enough for the parties to draft heads of terms.

def: The quality of obligations or benefits being shared reciprocally between parties.
ex: The tribunal stressed the mutuality of the arbitration clause, binding both sides equally.

def: To appease an aggrieved party by conceding something to regain goodwill.
ex: A modest interim payment was offered to propitiate the claimant while the merits were argued.

def: To soothe the anger or resentment of an opposing party.
ex: A carefully worded apology did much to mollify the aggrieved supplier at the mediation.

def: Intended to calm anger and win over an opponent.
ex: His placatory tone drew the temperature out of a hearing that had grown bad-tempered.

def: Aiming to soften a mood or avert conflict.
ex: An emollient remark from the chair defused the exchange before it hardened into a walkout.

def: To intervene on behalf of others in order to reconcile a difference.
ex: A senior partner agreed to intercede between the deadlocked negotiators.

def: The state of not favouring either side in a dispute.
ex: The challenge alleged that a past retainer had compromised the arbitrator's neutrality.

def: A party involved in a dispute.
ex: Each disputant filed a memorial setting out its version of the failed contract.

def: To decide or award something by formal judgment.
ex: The tribunal adjudged the respondent liable for the shortfall in delivered goods.

def: To confirm or approve a decision so as to give it legal force.
ex: Before it could be enforced abroad, the award had to be homologated by the local court.

def: To make a foreign award or judgment enforceable within one's own jurisdiction.
ex: Counsel moved to domesticate the New York award so the assets here could be seized.

def: To detach an arbitration from the law of the place where it is held.
ex: The theory would delocalise the proceedings, freeing the award from the courts of the seat.

def: The idea that an arbitration can float free of the legal system of its seat.
ex: Advocates of delocalisation argue that an award should survive even if the seat's courts annul it.

def: The taking of formal jurisdiction over a matter for decision.
ex: The tribunal declined to take cognisance of claims that fell outside the arbitration clause.

def: A formal statement of disagreement by an arbitrator with the majority's decision.
ex: The party-appointed arbitrator issued a sharp dissent on the calculation of damages.

def: A private meeting between the mediator and one side alone.
ex: In caucus the mediator learned the real figure the seller would accept.

def: A point in a dispute where no further progress seems possible.
ex: With both sides refusing to move on price, the talks reached an impasse.

def: A deadlock in which neither party can advance or force a resolution.
ex: The mediator was brought in to break a stalemate that had stalled the project for months.

def: The tactic of pushing a confrontation to the edge of collapse to extract concessions.
ex: Last-minute brinkmanship nearly wrecked the settlement an hour before the hearing.

def: A contractual mechanism referring an unresolved dispute up to a higher tier of resolution.
ex: The escalation clause required senior executives to meet before either side could arbitrate.

def: Refusing to compromise or change one's position.
ex: The buyer remained intransigent, rejecting every figure the mediator floated.

def: A stubborn refusal to make any concession.
ex: The claimant's intransigence over costs kept a settlement just out of reach.

def: Stubbornly refusing to alter a stance or be persuaded.
ex: Faced with an obdurate respondent, the mediator adjourned to let tempers cool.

def: Unable to be appeased or placated.
ex: The founder's implacable hostility to his former partner doomed every conciliation attempt.

def: Stubbornly resistant to cooperation or authority.
ex: A recalcitrant party who ignores the tribunal's directions risks an adverse costs order.

def: Aggressively defiant and eager to argue.
ex: His truculent conduct at the hearing did his own case more harm than good.

def: Marked by bitterness and sharp resentment.
ex: After an acrimonious exchange over disclosure, the parties agreed to a neutral evaluator.

def: Characterised by opposing parties contesting a matter against each other.
ex: Mediation offers a break from the adversarial posture that litigation forces on the parties.

def: Inclined to bring lawsuits or to dispute matters formally.
ex: An arbitration clause is prized precisely because it keeps a litigious counterparty out of the public courts.

def: Likely to cause disagreement or involving opposing arguments.
ex: The most contentious issue was whether the tribunal had jurisdiction at all.

def: Capable of being defended against objection or attack.
ex: Counsel conceded that the limitation argument was no longer tenable after disclosure.

def: Impossible to defend or maintain against challenge.
ex: The tribunal found the jurisdictional objection untenable and pressed on to the merits.

def: Appearing valid on the surface but lacking real substance.
ex: The respondent raised only a colourable defence, designed to delay rather than to win.

def: Superficially convincing but actually unsound.
ex: The tribunal dismissed the specious argument that silence amounted to consent to arbitrate.

def: Intended to cause delay rather than to advance a matter.
ex: Repeated dilatory applications prompted the tribunal to impose a strict timetable.

def: To obstruct progress by refusing to cooperate or answer.
ex: When the respondent stonewalled on documents, the tribunal drew an adverse inference.

def: To deliberately make something obscure or hard to understand.
ex: The witness seemed to obfuscate rather than explain how the funds had moved.

def: To speak or act evasively to avoid committing oneself to the truth.
ex: Counsel accused the director of prevaricating whenever the dates were put to him.

def: To use ambiguous language to conceal one's real position.
ex: Asked directly whether the goods had shipped, the witness continued to equivocate.

def: To delay a decision or act evasively in order to gain time.
ex: Rather than concede the point, the respondent chose to temporise until the deadline passed.

def: Deserving of blame or responsibility for a wrong done.
ex: The court found the driver blameworthy for pressing on despite the thickening fog.

def: Happening unintentionally, without deliberate purpose.
ex: An inadvertent slip with the scalpel still exposed the surgeon to a negligence claim.

def: A shameful failure to carry out a duty one is bound to perform.
ex: Leaving the scaffolding unsecured overnight was a plain dereliction of the contractor's duty of care.

def: The figure by which an annual loss is multiplied to calculate a lump sum for future damages.
ex: Counsel argued for a higher multiplier given the claimant's long life expectancy.

def: Capable of being made good by an award of money.
ex: Pure emotional distress, absent any physical injury, was not compensable on these facts.

def: Intended to make good a loss rather than to punish the wrongdoer.
ex: The jury awarded compensatory damages for the medical bills and the lost wages.

def: Giving sufficient grounds to sustain a lawsuit.
ex: Mere insulting words, without more, were not actionable as defamation.

def: The closeness of relationship required before a duty of care will be recognised.
ex: The auditors lacked sufficient proximity to the investors to owe them any duty.

def: Operating as the cause of a particular result.
ex: The claimant had to show the defect was causative of, not merely coincident with, the injury.

def: Relating to the connection between a cause and its effect.
ex: The defence broke the causal link by pointing to the claimant's own reckless later choice.

def: To attribute a fault or liability to a person.
ex: The negligence of the delivery driver was imputed to the company that employed him.

def: Causing or likely to cause harm or damage.
ex: The false report was injurious to the surgeon's professional standing.

def: Having a harmful effect, often gradually.
ex: Prolonged exposure to the solvent had a deleterious effect on the workers' lungs.

def: The companionship and support a spouse is entitled to, the loss of which may be compensated.
ex: The husband claimed for loss of consortium after the crash left his wife bedridden.

def: A pathological condition that results from an earlier injury or disease.
ex: Chronic pain was a recognised sequela of the botched operation.

def: The state of being incapacitated by injury or illness.
ex: Permanent disablement entitled him to a substantially larger award.

def: Inability to work or function that results from injury or illness.
ex: Damages reflected two years of total incapacity following the accident.

def: A forecast of the likely course and outcome of an injury or illness.
ex: The neurologist's guarded prognosis heavily influenced the quantum of damages.

def: Tending to injure a person's reputation by a false statement.
ex: The article's defamatory imputation of fraud could not be justified as true.

def: Involving a risk of harm or danger.
ex: Storing the chemicals so carelessly created a hazardous condition on the premises.

def: Involving an inherently high risk of serious harm that no amount of care can eliminate.
ex: Blasting with dynamite was treated as an ultrahazardous activity attracting strict liability.

def: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way.
ex: The owner knew of the dog's propensity to bite yet let it roam free.

def: To bring a nuisance to an end or reduce it.
ex: The council served notice requiring the factory to abate the persistent noise nuisance.

def: Compensation awarded for loss, harm, or injury suffered.
ex: The settlement offered scant recompense for a lifetime of disability.

def: A return or repayment made for a wrong or a service.
ex: The damages were less a requital of the harm than a vindication of the right.

def: Capable of being remedied or put right.
ex: The court held the interference was remediable by an injunction rather than by damages.

def: Showing careless disregard for consequences or danger.
ex: The driver's heedless overtaking on the bend endangered every oncoming car.

def: A person who commits a wrongful or unlawful act.
ex: The statute allows the victim to sue every wrongdoer jointly.

def: Serious and immediate risk of harm or injury.
ex: By ignoring the warning signs the swimmer courted obvious peril.

def: A source of potential danger or harm.
ex: The uncovered pit was an obvious hazard to any lawful visitor.

def: The repayment of money spent or lost by another party.
ex: The insurer sought reimbursement of the medical costs it had already paid out.

def: Fault or negligence that gives rise to legal liability.
ex: The pleadings distinguished mere culpa from the gross fault alleged against the surgeon.

def: Harm, loss, or disadvantage suffered by a person.
ex: The claimant must show some actual detriment flowing from the breach of duty.

def: Tending to cause harm or damage.
ex: The escape of effluent proved detrimental to the neighbouring farmer's crops.

def: Dependence on the truth or care of another's statement or conduct.
ex: The buyer's reliance on the surveyor's negligent report was entirely reasonable.

def: Reparation or compensation made for a wrong or injury.
ex: The company offered to make amends for the pollution by funding a clean-up.

def: Outstandingly bad or shocking in degree.
ex: The hospital's egregious lapses in hygiene amounted to gross negligence.

def: Conspicuously and openly wrong.
ex: The flagrant breach of the guardrail regulations left no room for excuse.

def: So obvious that it can hardly be doubted.
ex: There was a palpable risk of collapse that the engineer simply ignored.

def: Capable of being remedied or compensated by law.
ex: The court doubted that a purely speculative loss was redressable in tort.

def: The action of correcting or making good environmental or physical damage.
ex: The polluter was ordered to fund the remediation of the contaminated land.

def: To feign or exaggerate illness in order to gain compensation.
ex: The insurer alleged the claimant was malingering to inflate his loss-of-earnings claim.

def: Impossible to anticipate or predict.
ex: The freak reaction was so unforeseeable that the harm was held too remote to recover.

def: Able to be reclaimed as damages or compensation.
ex: Purely economic loss is rarely recoverable in a negligence action.

def: Able to be measured or expressed as a definite amount.
ex: The judge distinguished quantifiable pecuniary loss from general damages for pain.

def: To make an injury, condition, or situation worse.
ex: The delayed treatment exacerbated an injury the defendant had already caused.

def: The commission of a civil wrong for which damages may be claimed.
ex: Joint tortfeasance rendered both companies liable for the whole of the loss.

def: To put a person or thing at serious risk of harm.
ex: Leaving the manhole open imperilled every pedestrian on the street.

def: The quality of providing sufficient legal grounds for a claim.
ex: The actionability of the slander depended on proof of special damage.

def: To bring or pursue a claim in a court of law.
ex: The company chose to litigate rather than accept the paltry settlement the insurer had offered.

def: To set out the specific facts or details relied on in a pleading.
ex: The judge ordered the claimant to particularise exactly how each alleged breach had caused the loss claimed.

def: A pleading that admits the opponent's facts but introduces new matter defeating their legal effect.
ex: Rather than deny the debt, the defence proceeded by confession and avoidance, admitting the loan but pleading that it had been repaid.

def: A consent order that stays proceedings on terms recorded in an attached confidential schedule.
ex: The parties settled on the courthouse steps and embodied the deal in a Tomlin order so the payment terms stayed private.

def: A court order imposing an automatic sanction unless a party complies by a specified date.
ex: After repeated delays the master made an unless order, warning that the claim would be struck out unless disclosure was given within fourteen days.

def: A tabular document listing each disputed item alongside the parties' rival contentions and figures.
ex: In the building dispute the surveyor prepared a Scott schedule setting every defect against the cost each side attributed to it.

def: The improper use of court procedure for a purpose other than resolving the genuine dispute.
ex: The second action was struck out as an abuse of process, being a plain attempt to relitigate matters already decided.

def: The rule preventing a party from reopening a particular issue already determined between the same parties.
ex: Issue estoppel barred the defendant from denying negligence, that very question having been resolved against him in the earlier trial.

def: The bar preventing a party from suing again on a claim that has already been adjudicated.
ex: Because judgment had been entered on the identical claim, cause of action estoppel put an end to the fresh writ.

def: Costs a court orders a legal representative to bear personally for improper or negligent conduct of a case.
ex: Counsel's unmeritorious application collapsed so badly that the judge made a wasted costs order against the firm.

def: A settlement offer made without prejudice except as to costs, so it may be shown to the court on the question of costs.
ex: Having beaten its own Calderbank offer at trial, the defendant recovered indemnity costs from the date it was refused.

def: An order compelling a third party mixed up in wrongdoing to disclose the identity of the wrongdoer.
ex: The claimant obtained a Norwich Pharmacal order forcing the platform to reveal who was behind the anonymous defamatory posts.

def: An order permitting a party to enter premises to inspect and preserve evidence at risk of destruction.
ex: Fearing the documents would be shredded, they secured a search order and seized the servers before the defendant was even warned.

def: A warning endorsed on a court order that disobedience is a contempt punishable by imprisonment.
ex: The injunction carried a penal notice, so the director understood that flouting it could land him in prison.

def: An enforcement method by which sums are deducted directly from a judgment debtor's wages.
ex: When instalments went unpaid, the court ordered an attachment of earnings so the money came straight out of his salary.

def: A writ directing an enforcement officer to seize and sell a debtor's goods to satisfy a judgment.
ex: Armed with a writ of fieri facias, the bailiffs arrived to remove goods to the value of the outstanding judgment.

def: A person who conducts legal proceedings on behalf of a party lacking capacity to do so.
ex: As the claimant was a child, his mother acted as his litigation friend throughout the personal injury claim.

def: The historical term for one who brings proceedings on behalf of a minor or person under disability.
ex: Under the old rules an infant sued by his next friend, usually a parent, who took responsibility for the conduct of the action.

def: A person allowed to join existing proceedings because of an interest in their outcome.
ex: The regulator applied to appear as an intervener, arguing that the ruling would affect an entire industry.

def: A lawsuit brought by a representative claimant on behalf of a larger group with the same interest.
ex: Thousands of consumers joined the class action after the defective airbags came to light.

def: The practice of choosing the court or jurisdiction most likely to treat one's claim favourably.
ex: Critics accused the claimant of blatant forum shopping, having filed in the one jurisdiction with the most generous damages.

def: A trivial sum awarded to a claimant who succeeds in law but whose claim the court regards as devoid of merit.
ex: The jury vindicated the libel in principle but signalled its disdain by awarding a penny in contemptuous damages.

def: Tediously long-winded, as of a pleading or submission.
ex: The judge criticised the prolix particulars of claim, which ran to ninety pages where ten would have sufficed.

def: A false statement, made maliciously, that causes economic loss to another.
ex: Telling customers a rival had gone bust was injurious falsehood, and the rival recovered the trade it had lost.

def: A false and malicious assertion disparaging a person's ownership of property, causing loss.
ex: By wrongly registering a charge over the land, the defendant committed slander of title and frustrated the sale.

def: A notice by which a defendant brings a third person into proceedings to seek contribution or indemnity.
ex: The contractor served a third-party notice on its subcontractor, seeking to pass on any liability for the faulty roof.

def: The court procedure for quantifying the costs one party must pay another when they cannot agree.
ex: The bill was wildly inflated, so the paying party insisted the costs go to detailed assessment.

def: The court's immediate quantification of costs at the end of a hearing rather than by a later procedure.
ex: After the short application the judge carried out a summary assessment and ordered four thousand pounds in costs on the spot.

def: A basis of assessing costs under which any doubt about reasonableness is resolved in the receiving party's favour.
ex: The defendant's conduct was so egregious that costs were awarded on the indemnity basis.

def: An arrangement under which a lawyer's fee is payable only if the case succeeds.
ex: Unable to fund the claim herself, she instructed solicitors under a conditional fee agreement.

def: The percentage uplift a lawyer may charge on winning a case funded by a conditional fee agreement.
ex: On top of the base costs the firm claimed a success fee reflecting the risk it had run.

def: A funding arrangement under which the lawyer's fee is a share of any damages recovered.
ex: Under the damages-based agreement the firm would take twenty-five per cent of whatever the client won.

def: A court's dispensation excusing a party's failure to comply with a rule, order, or deadline.
ex: Having missed the deadline for its witness statements, the defendant applied for relief from sanctions.

def: The process by which the court approves the parties' projected litigation costs in advance.
ex: At the case management conference the parties exchanged budgets so the judge could undertake costs budgeting.

def: Service of court documents by an alternative method permitted where the ordinary method is impracticable.
ex: As the defendant was evading the process server, the court allowed substituted service by email.

def: A final injunction granted at trial that permanently restrains or compels conduct.
ex: Having proved a continuing nuisance, the claimant obtained a perpetual injunction against the noisy factory.

def: A writ enforcing a judgment for possession by authorising officers to remove occupiers from land.
ex: When the squatters ignored the order, the owner enforced it with a writ of possession.

def: An order requiring someone who owes money to the judgment debtor to pay it instead to the creditor.
ex: Learning that the debtor's bank held a healthy balance, the creditor obtained a third party debt order against the bank.

def: The lodging of a disputed sum with the court, historically as a protected settlement offer.
ex: The defendant made a payment into court, gambling that the claimant would recover no more at trial.

def: A formal demand that another party clarify or elaborate on its statement of case.
ex: The defence was so vague that the claimant served a request for further information to pin down the allegations.

def: A denial in a pleading that fails to advance any positive case in answer to the allegation.
ex: A bare denial will not do; the defence must say why the sum is not owed.

def: The legal basis on which the amount of compensation for a wrong is calculated.
ex: The measure of damages for the defective goods was the difference between their actual and their warranted value.

def: The distinct categories under which items of loss are claimed.
ex: Her schedule broke the claim down into heads of loss: lost earnings, care costs, and future treatment.

def: A defamation defence asserting that statements of fact are true and that comments on them are fair.
ex: The newspaper met the libel with a rolled-up plea, standing by both its facts and its opinions.

word: damages in lieu of an injunction

def: A monetary award granted in equity as a substitute for restraining or compelling conduct.

def: A claim brought by a defendant against a third party or a co-defendant within existing proceedings.

def: A concise written outline of the submissions a party intends to make at a hearing.

def: A formal written demand for payment of a debt, non-compliance with which can found insolvency proceedings.

def: Disclosure of documents ordered before proceedings are issued to help a prospective claimant assess its case.

def: A formal request that another party admit specified facts or documents so they need not be proved at trial.

def: The remedy of a court order requiring a party to do or refrain from doing something.

def: A remedy requiring the return of particular property to the person entitled to it.

def: To bring profits or capital held abroad back to the home country.

def: The attaching of a credit to a dividend to reflect corporation tax already paid on the underlying profits.

def: Liable to be levied or demanded, as of a tax or duty.

def: The public treasury or the body of state revenue.

def: The act of levying a tax, duty, or other charge.

def: To nullify a tax advantage obtained through an abusive arrangement.

def: Existing only as an assumed figure for the purpose of calculating tax, rather than as an actual receipt.

def: A relief that defers a gain by transferring it to the recipient of a gifted asset.

def: Granted as a favourable exception to the strict statutory position.

def: A relaxation of the strict tax rules granted by the revenue authority outside legislation.

def: A reduction in the recorded value of an asset, sometimes with tax consequences.

def: To designate tax revenue for a particular purpose.
ex: The government earmarked the levy's proceeds for social care, at least on paper.

def: Describing an asset with a predictable useful life of fifty years or less, treated specially for gains.
ex: As a wasting asset, the vintage car fell outside the charge to capital gains tax altogether.

def: The charge arising when a company leaves a group still holding assets transferred to it tax-free within that group.
ex: The share sale triggered a degrouping charge on the property that had been moved between the subsidiaries.

def: Describing an arrangement that exploits the tax rules in a way Parliament never intended.
ex: The general anti-abuse rule bites only on arrangements that are abusive rather than merely tax-efficient.

def: The quality of being contrived and lacking genuine commercial substance.
ex: The sheer artificiality of the circular payments persuaded the judge to disregard them entirely.

def: The system under which taxpayers calculate and report their own liability.
ex: Under self-assessment, the onus falls on the taxpayer to declare the gain and pay on time.

def: The application of disposal proceeds into new qualifying assets, often in order to defer a gain.
ex: Reinvestment of the whole proceeds in a replacement building rolled the gain over in full.

def: To prove a statement or accusation wrong by argument or evidence.
ex: Defence counsel refuted the identification by producing timestamped footage placing her client miles away.

def: To prove a person or argument decisively wrong.
ex: The expert's calculations confuted the prosecution's theory of how the fire had started.

def: To assert or confirm the truth or reliability of something from personal knowledge.
ex: No colleague was willing to vouch for the accuracy of the ledger entries under oath.

def: To question someone closely and often aggressively to extract information.
ex: The detectives interrogated the suspect for six hours before any solicitor arrived.

def: Relating to the scientific analysis of physical evidence for use in court.
ex: Forensic analysis of the fibres tied the coat to the scene of the burglary.

def: The forensic study of firearms, projectiles, and the marks they leave.
ex: Ballistics matched the recovered round to a pistol registered in the defendant's name.

def: The smallest possible trace or amount, especially of evidence.
ex: The judge dismissed the charge, finding not a scintilla of evidence linking the two men.

def: A formal withdrawal of an earlier statement or testimony.
ex: The key witness's recantation on the stand collapsed the entire prosecution case.

def: To formally withdraw a statement, allegation, or admission.
ex: Under cross-examination she retracted her earlier claim to have seen him at the door.

def: A person who lies under oath.
ex: Once exposed as a perjurer, the witness's every prior answer was thrown into doubt.

def: To alter a document or record fraudulently so as to deceive.
ex: The auditor found that invoices had been falsified to conceal the missing funds.

def: The fraudulent alteration of a document or record.
ex: The charge rested on the deliberate falsification of the timesheets.

def: To invent false evidence or a false account with intent to deceive.
ex: Counsel alleged the officer had fabricated the confession after the interview ended.

def: Something invented in order to deceive, especially false evidence.
ex: The alibi turned out to be a complete fabrication supported by a forged receipt.

def: To interfere with evidence, a witness, or a document so as to alter or corrupt it.
ex: The seal was intact, ruling out any suggestion that someone had tampered with the sample.

def: An open and frank admission or declaration.
ex: His avowal of responsibility, made freely at the police station, was later ruled admissible.

def: To deny any knowledge of, responsibility for, or connection with something.
ex: The company disavowed the emails, insisting they were sent without authority.

def: A denial of knowledge, responsibility, or connection.
ex: His disavowal of the signature was undermined by three earlier documents bearing the same hand.

def: To declare or admit openly and without shame.
ex: She avowed her part in the scheme but denied any intent to defraud.

def: Legally capable of being required to give evidence.
ex: A spouse was not a compellable witness for the prosecution on that particular charge.

def: The extent to which a witness can lawfully be forced to testify.
ex: The argument turned on the compellability of a co-accused who had already pleaded guilty.

def: The quality of being genuine and of undisputed origin.
ex: The authenticity of the disputed will was tested by handwriting experts on both sides.

def: The quality of being real and not counterfeit or forged.
ex: Counsel challenged the genuineness of the signature on the loan agreement.

def: Relating to or constituting evidence.
ex: The court held a separate evidentiary hearing to decide whether the recording could be admitted.

def: Providing or serving as evidence.
ex: The photograph had real evidential value once its provenance was established.

def: Serving to test, prove, or establish a fact.
ex: The document was tendered for its probatory force on the question of intent.

def: A person who makes a solemn affirmation instead of swearing an oath.
ex: As an affirmant, the witness solemnly affirmed rather than swore on the Bible.

def: A person who witnesses and certifies a signature or document.
ex: Each attestant to the will confirmed that the testator had signed in their presence.

def: One who attests or bears witness to the execution of a document.
ex: The deed failed for want of a second attestor to the grantor's signature.

def: With no part concealed or blacked out.
ex: The court ordered production of the unredacted contract so the pricing terms could be seen.

def: To make a person appear guilty of a crime by evidence or suggestion.
ex: He refused to answer questions that might incriminate him in the fraud.

def: Conformity to truth; habitual truthfulness.
ex: The whole case hinged on the veracity of a single informant.

def: Untruthfulness; a tendency to lie.
ex: The judge remarked on the witness's evident mendacity when confronted with the records.

def: Given to lying; not truthful.
ex: The tribunal found the claimant's account to be mendacious and self-serving.

def: Truthful and corresponding to fact.
ex: Expert evidence confirmed that the recording was a veridical account of the exchange.

def: Beyond doubt or reproach and not open to being discredited.
ex: The provenance of the ledger was unimpeachable, having been held by the bank throughout.

def: The quality of being believable or trustworthy as a witness.
ex: Repeated inconsistencies destroyed the complainant's credibility in the eyes of the jury.

def: To undermine the credibility or reliability of a witness or account.
ex: Cross-examination sought to discredit the expert by exposing his undisclosed fee.

def: Tending to confirm or support other evidence.
ex: The phone records were corroborant of the victim's timeline.

def: Not able to be denied or disputed.
ex: DNA on the weapon provided incontrovertible proof of contact.

def: Impossible to disprove or contradict.
ex: The paper trail was irrefutable, and the defence conceded the point.

def: The quality of being clear, logical, and convincing.
ex: The cogency of the circumstantial case persuaded the jury despite the lack of a confession.

def: Strongly indicating guilt or wrongdoing.
ex: The most damning evidence was an email in which he priced the bribe.

def: Serving one's own interests, especially in a way that lacks independent support.
ex: The court gave little weight to his self-serving account of the meeting.

def: To prevent evidence from being disclosed or admitted at trial.
ex: The defence moved to suppress the confession as the product of an unlawful arrest.

def: The prevention of evidence from being disclosed or used.
ex: Suppression of the search results followed from the officers' failure to obtain a warrant.

def: Operating to keep improperly obtained evidence out of a trial.
ex: Under the exclusionary rule, the seized documents could not be put before the jury.

def: To edit a document by concealing or removing sensitive parts before disclosure.
ex: The firm redacted the clients' names before serving the file on the regulator.

def: To conceal one's true motives or knowledge by deception.
ex: She dissembled about her whereabouts until confronted with the toll records.

def: Involving secret cooperation for a deceitful or fraudulent purpose.
ex: The transaction was collusive, staged solely to put the assets beyond the creditors' reach.

def: The process by which an offender gradually stops committing crime.
ex: Sentencing policy increasingly aims to support desistance rather than merely to punish.

def: The public condemnation of criminal conduct expressed through the imposition of a sentence.
ex: The judge stressed denunciation, saying the term had to mark society's revulsion at the offence.

def: The prevention of further offending by removing an offender's ability to reoffend, typically through imprisonment.
ex: The lengthy tariff was justified largely on grounds of incapacitation, given his record of violence.

def: The restoration of an offender to a law-abiding life through treatment, training, or supervision.
ex: The programme's emphasis on rehabilitation cut reoffending sharply among released prisoners.

def: Fixed in length and known at the point of sentencing.
ex: He received a determinate sentence of eight years, half of which was to be served in custody.

def: Having no fixed end date, with release depending on an assessment of risk.
ex: An indeterminate sentence for public protection left him wholly reliant on the Parole Board.

def: Not involving imprisonment.
ex: Given the strength of her mitigation, the bench imposed a non-custodial penalty of unpaid work.

def: A court-imposed requirement to remain at a specified address during set hours.
ex: The order combined an electronically monitored curfew with a rehabilitation requirement.

def: A formal expression of disapproval delivered by an authority.
ex: The youth was given a reprimand rather than being charged for the first minor offence.

def: A judicial warning or reproof, sometimes given in place of a formal penalty.
ex: The sheriff dismissed the accused with an admonition, taking a lenient view of the lapse.

def: Relating to punishment or to the system of penalties for crime.
ex: Reformers argued that the penal regime did little but warehouse the poor.

def: The study of the punishment of crime and the management of prisons.
ex: Modern penology questions whether ever longer tariffs deter offending at all.

def: Relating to prisons and imprisonment.
ex: Critics decried the carceral drift of the new sentencing guidelines.

def: A judicial inquiry, held before a coroner, into the cause of a sudden or suspicious death.
ex: The inquest returned a verdict of unlawful killing, prompting a fresh police investigation.

def: An official who investigates deaths that are violent, sudden, or of unknown cause.
ex: The coroner adjourned the hearing pending the outcome of the criminal trial.

def: The lawful disinterment of a body, often to obtain forensic evidence.
ex: The court ordered an exhumation so that a fresh toxicology analysis could be carried out.

def: The scientific analysis of poisons and drugs, often used to establish a cause of death.
ex: The toxicology report revealed a lethal concentration of the sedative in her blood.

def: A medical examination of a corpse to determine the cause of death.
ex: The postmortem established that the victim had been strangled before the fire was set.

def: The act of exposing oneself to prosecution through one's own statements.
ex: He invoked the privilege against self-incrimination and declined to answer the detective's questions.

def: The formal and often prolonged questioning of a suspect by investigators.
ex: A confession obtained through oppressive interrogation risks being ruled inadmissible.

def: To charge someone formally with a serious crime.
ex: The grand jury voted to indict the officer on two counts of manslaughter.

def: To surrender a suspect to another jurisdiction to face prosecution there.
ex: The court agreed to extradite him once assurances were given that no death penalty would be sought.

def: A second trial of a case, ordered after a mistrial or a successful appeal.
ex: The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction as unsafe and ordered a retrial.

def: A warrant issued directly by a judge, usually for the arrest of someone who has failed to appear.
ex: When the defendant absconded mid-trial, the judge issued a bench warrant for his arrest.

def: The feigning of illness or incapacity, sometimes to avoid trial or punishment.
ex: The psychiatrist ruled out malingering, finding the symptoms wholly genuine.

def: The process by which a jury considers the evidence in private to reach a verdict.
ex: After two days of deliberation, the jury remained hopelessly deadlocked.

def: Any circumstance that increases the seriousness of an offence and the appropriate sentence.
ex: The use of a weapon was treated as a serious aggravation lifting the case above the custody threshold.

def: To clear someone of blame or suspicion.
ex: The fresh alibi evidence finally vindicated the wrongly convicted man after fifteen years.

def: The principle that any doubt must be resolved in favour of the accused.
ex: Applying in dubio pro reo, the tribunal acquitted where the evidence fell short of certainty.

def: A person who incites another to commit an offence in order to secure their prosecution.
ex: The defence alleged that an agent provocateur had lured him into the drug deal.

def: Not of sound mind, and therefore not legally responsible.
ex: The court found him non compos mentis at the time of the killing and ordered hospital treatment.

def: A period of court supervision served in the community instead of, or after, custody.
ex: He was placed on probation with a condition of intensive drug treatment.

def: An official act remitting the penalty for a crime and, sometimes, the conviction itself.
ex: Decades later, a posthumous pardon acknowledged the miscarriage of justice.

def: A judge's review of the evidence and directions on the law given to the jury before they retire.
ex: Defence counsel complained that the summing-up had badly understated the alibi.

def: A person who flees to evade arrest or prosecution.
ex: As a fugitive from justice, he forfeited any right to challenge the order in his absence.

def: A characteristic method of operating that links a series of offences to a suspect.
ex: The burglaries shared a modus operandi distinctive enough to point to a single hand.

def: A person who personally saw the events in question and testifies to them.
ex: Eyewitness identification is notoriously fallible and demands a careful warning to the jury.

def: The doctrine that evidence obtained unlawfully may be barred from trial.
ex: Under the exclusionary rule, the illegally seized documents were kept from the jury.

def: Relating to the bringing and conduct of a prosecution.
ex: The decision not to charge fell squarely within the ambit of prosecutorial discretion.

def: Denoting a system in which the judge actively investigates the facts rather than umpiring.
ex: Continental, inquisitorial procedure gives the judge a far more searching investigative role.

def: Relating to or consisting of evidence given orally by a witness.
ex: The case rested on testimonial evidence unsupported by any documents or forensics.

def: Denoting evidence, such as models or diagrams, used to illustrate testimony.
ex: The prosecution used demonstrative exhibits to walk the jury through the layout of the scene.

def: Interfering improperly with evidence, witnesses, or jurors.
ex: He faced a further charge of witness tampering after contacting the complainant before trial.

def: The act of impeding the administration of justice.
ex: Lying to detectives about the weapon amounted to obstruction and drew a consecutive sentence.

def: The covert interception of telephone communications to gather evidence.
ex: Evidence obtained through unauthorised wiretapping was ruled inadmissible at trial.

def: The capturing of communications in the course of their transmission.
ex: The interception of his messages required a warrant signed personally by the Secretary of State.

def: Arising as a minor accompanying consequence of a breach, such as the cost of returning defective goods.
ex: Alongside the price difference, the buyer recovered incidental expenses for storing and reshipping the rejected consignment.

def: To withdraw from or go back on an agreement or previously adopted position.
ex: Once the contract was signed the vendor could not resile from the price merely because the market had moved.

def: To fail to honour a promise or commitment one has made.
ex: When the contractor reneged on the completion date, the employer treated the delay as a repudiatory breach.

def: The state of performance having become excessively burdensome or unfeasible through unforeseen events.
ex: The seller pleaded commercial impracticability after the sole refinery supplying the compound was destroyed.

def: The condition of a contractual obligation that can no longer be performed at all.
ex: Supervening impossibility discharged the hire agreement when the music hall burned down before the concert.

def: The judicial rewriting of a contract to reflect the parties' true agreement.
ex: The court ordered reformation of the deed so that it recorded the boundary the parties had actually agreed.

def: The passing or expiry of a period of time, by which a contract may come to an end.
ex: The lease determined by effluxion of time, so no notice of termination was required.

def: To repudiate or renounce a contract, treating it as no longer binding.
ex: On reaching majority the minor promptly disaffirmed the loan agreement he had signed the year before.

def: The cancelling or bringing to an end of a right, obligation, or debt.
ex: Payment in full operated as an extinguishment of the guarantor's residual liability.

def: The relinquishment of a contract or right, often inferred from a party's conduct.
ex: Prolonged mutual inactivity led the tribunal to find an abandonment of the arbitration agreement.

def: Relating to or effecting the setting aside of a contract.
ex: The pursuer sought rescissory damages to restore the position that would have existed had the deal never been struck.

def: A concession granting the other party extra time or leniency without giving up one's rights.
ex: The bank's indulgence over the missed payment was expressly stated not to prejudice its right to call in the loan.

def: A reduction, especially the measure of damages based on lost value.
ex: Damages were assessed by the diminution in the property's value rather than the far greater cost of rebuilding.

def: The failure to carry out an obligation that the contract requires.
ex: Persistent nonperformance of the delivery schedule entitled the buyer to terminate and source elsewhere.

def: The election to keep a contract on foot despite having grounds to end it.
ex: His continued acceptance of benefits amounted to an affirmance, extinguishing any right to rescind.

def: Capable of being justified so as to relieve a party of liability for nonperformance.
ex: The force majeure clause rendered the delay excusable, so no damages flowed from the missed shipment.

def: Capable of being prevented, so that any resulting loss is not recoverable.
ex: The rule against recovering avoidable loss required the claimant to have sourced a substitute promptly.

def: Able to be brought to an end, especially by notice.
ex: The distribution agreement was terminable on ninety days' notice without any need to show cause.

def: Insufficiency, notably of damages as a remedy so as to justify specific performance.
ex: The inadequacy of damages for a unique painting persuaded the court to order specific performance.

def: A claim for the reasonable value of goods supplied where no price was fixed.
ex: Having delivered the materials under an incomplete contract, the supplier recovered on a quantum valebat basis.

def: Capable of being set aside or annulled.
ex: A contract induced by misrepresentation is rescindable at the innocent party's option.

def: Not capable of being justified or explained away.
ex: The deliberate diversion of materials was an inexcusable breach for which no clause offered relief.

def: Incapable of being cured or put right.
ex: The loss of the launch window was irremediable, so damages, not repair, were the only recourse.

def: Reasonably capable of being anticipated at the time of contracting.
ex: Only losses that were foreseeable when the contract was made fell within the recoverable head of damage.

def: A failure to perform a legal or contractual duty, especially to pay.
ex: On the borrower's default the lender was entitled to accelerate the loan and enforce its security.

def: Based on conjecture rather than proof, and so not recoverable as damages.
ex: The claim for lost future contracts was dismissed as too speculative to be quantified.

def: Capable of being ascribed to a particular cause, such as the breach.
ex: Only the losses attributable to the defective valve, not the pre-existing wear, were recoverable.

def: Of a contract, made up of separable obligations that can be performed and paid for in parts.
ex: Because the supply contract was divisible, the seller could recover for the instalments already accepted.

def: To give up gains wrongfully obtained.
ex: The court made the fiduciary disgorge the secret profit he had made by diverting the contract.

def: To lose a right, sum, or property as a consequence of breach or default.
ex: The buyer who repudiated forfeited the ten per cent deposit paid on exchange.

def: The failure to reveal a material fact one was bound to disclose.
ex: Nondisclosure of the pending litigation gave the purchaser grounds to rescind the share sale.

def: The process of assessing the monetary amount of a claim or loss.
ex: Liability was admitted, leaving only the quantification of damages for the expert to address.

def: Of a remedy, compelling a party to act or refrain rather than merely to pay money.
ex: An injunction is a coercive remedy, backed ultimately by the court's power to punish for contempt.

def: To bring a contract to an end automatically because an unforeseen event makes performance radically different.
ex: The outbreak of war frustrated the charterparty, discharging both sides from further performance.

def: To declare a contract or transaction void and of no legal effect.
ex: The court annulled the agreement once it found that consent had been procured by duress.

def: Not significant enough to affect the substance of the bargain or justify termination.
ex: The shortfall was immaterial, so the buyer had to accept the goods and sue only for the small difference.

def: The benefit a party expected to receive, used as the measure of expectation damages.
ex: Damages were set to protect the claimant's expectancy, putting it in the position performance would have achieved.

def: To recover or make good a loss or outlay.
ex: The claimant sought to recoup the wasted expenditure incurred in reliance on the abandoned deal.

def: To restore a contract, right, or position to its former state.
ex: On payment of the arrears the tenant applied to reinstate the lease and obtain relief from forfeiture.

def: To divide loss or liability proportionately between parties.
ex: The court apportioned the damages to reflect the buyer's own failure to mitigate.

def: Capable of being lessened or avoided by taking reasonable steps.
ex: Because the loss was readily mitigable, the seller could not recover the portion a substitute sale would have avoided.

def: The temporary transfer of an employee to another department, employer, or role for a fixed period.
ex: Her three-month secondment to the Brussels office counted towards her continuous employment for redundancy purposes.

def: An employee who has been temporarily assigned to work elsewhere while remaining employed by the original firm.
ex: The tribunal had to decide whether the secondee remained an employee of the sending company or of the host.

def: A temporary period of mandatory leave during which an employee is retained but not required to work.
ex: Thousands of staff were placed on furlough rather than made redundant during the downturn.

def: The practice of holding a second job, usually in the evenings and often without the main employer's knowledge.
ex: His contract's exclusivity clause expressly prohibited moonlighting for a competitor.

def: A worker who continues working during a strike, or who takes a striker's place.
ex: Union members jeered the blacklegs who crossed the picket line each morning.

def: The stationing of striking workers outside a workplace to protest and discourage others from entering.
ex: The injunction limited peaceful picketing to six people at each factory gate.

def: An employer's exclusion of workers from the workplace during an industrial dispute to force acceptance of terms.
ex: When negotiations collapsed, management responded to the overtime ban with a lockout.

def: A person hired or induced to work in place of employees who are on strike.
ex: Bringing in agency strikebreakers only hardened the union's resolve.

def: Habitual or persistent absence from work without good reason.
ex: The disciplinary policy set clear trigger points for managing chronic absenteeism.

def: The practice of attending work while unwell or beyond required hours, often reducing genuine productivity.
ex: A culture of presenteeism meant staff came in sick rather than risk their attendance record.

def: A person who supplies and supervises casual labour, especially in agriculture, subject to licensing to prevent exploitation.
ex: The unlicensed gangmaster was prosecuted for withholding wages from migrant fruit pickers.

def: A person or firm engaged by a main contractor to perform part of the work under a separate arrangement.
ex: Whether the courier was a genuine subcontractor or a worker determined his holiday-pay entitlement.

def: The reassignment of an employee to a different role, often to avoid redundancy.
ex: The employer must consider redeployment into suitable alternative vacancies before dismissing for redundancy.

def: The formal process of managing an employee's departure from an organisation.
ex: Proper offboarding ensured the departing manager returned all confidential files and revoked her system access.

def: Improper or unacceptable behaviour by an employee that may justify disciplinary action.
ex: Repeated lateness amounted to misconduct, but not the gross misconduct needed for summary dismissal.

def: Deliberate refusal to obey a lawful and reasonable instruction from a superior.
ex: His flat refusal to attend the meeting was treated as insubordination warranting a final warning.

def: Treating a person less favourably on grounds of a protected characteristic.
ex: A dress code that penalised only female staff was found to be indirectly discriminatory.

def: An employee working through an initial trial period before permanent appointment is confirmed.
ex: As a probationer, she could be dismissed on shorter notice if her performance fell short.

def: A structured arrangement combining paid employment with training towards a recognised qualification.
ex: The apprenticeship agreement gave the trainee greater protection against dismissal than an ordinary contract.

def: A worker who has completed an apprenticeship and is qualified in a trade but not yet a master.
ex: After qualifying as a journeyman electrician, he was entitled to the higher collectively agreed rate.

def: To pay someone for work or services rendered.
ex: The contract failed to specify how the on-call hours would be remunerated.

def: A sum of money given for service, or a lump sum paid on leaving employment.
ex: New rules require that a customer's gratuity be passed to staff in full.

def: A benefit or privilege attached to a job in addition to normal pay.
ex: A company car and private healthcare were the principal perquisites of the senior role.

def: A voluntary payment made for services on which no fee is legally set.
ex: The non-executive received only a modest honorarium rather than a salaried wage.

def: A position that carries pay or status but requires little or no actual work.
ex: Critics dismissed the advisory post as a sinecure created to reward a political ally.

def: To motivate someone to act by offering a reward, typically financial.
ex: The bonus scheme was designed to incentivise retention over short-term sales.

def: An extended period of leave from work, whether paid or unpaid, for rest, study, or travel.
ex: Her contract allowed an unpaid sabbatical after five years without loss of seniority.

def: The state of having lost a close relative, giving rise to entitlements to leave.
ex: Parents now have a statutory right to bereavement leave following the death of a child.

def: The reduction of a workforce to cut costs, especially through dismissals.
ex: The wave of retrenchment across the sector triggered mass collective consultation obligations.

def: The deliberate reduction of the number of employees to lower costs.
ex: The downsizing programme was structured to qualify each departure as a genuine redundancy.

def: The restructuring of a workforce to what management deems an optimal size, usually a euphemism for cuts.
ex: Employees saw through the talk of rightsizing and braced for redundancies.

def: Support given to departing employees to help them find new employment.
ex: The settlement included six months of outplacement counselling and CV coaching.

def: To accept or overlook conduct that might otherwise justify disciplinary or legal action.
ex: By taking no action for months, the employer was held to have condoned the earlier breach.

def: A contractual restriction barring a departing employee from approaching the employer's clients or staff.
ex: The non-solicitation covenant was enforceable because it was limited to clients he had personally handled.

def: The party who transfers a business or undertaking, with the workforce passing to another under transfer regulations.
ex: On the sale, the transferor was obliged to inform and consult the affected employees.

def: The party who takes over a business, inheriting its employees on their existing terms.
ex: The transferee could not lawfully harmonise contracts simply because of the transfer.

def: Making one employee redundant so that another whose role has disappeared can take the vacated position.
ex: The employer's failure to consider bumping rendered the selection unfair.

def: The withdrawal by an employer of a trade union's status for collective bargaining.
ex: Derecognition of the union removed its statutory right to be consulted over pay.

def: An arrangement for pooling and distributing tips and service charges among staff.
ex: Running a compliant tronc allowed the restaurant to share gratuities fairly and tax-efficiently.

def: The trend towards replacing secure permanent jobs with temporary or insecure work.
ex: The union blamed the casualisation of the sector for eroding sick pay and pensions.

def: The class of workers whose employment is insecure, low-paid, and lacking in benefits.
ex: Gig platforms have swollen a precariat with no guaranteed hours or holiday entitlement.

def: A period during which an employee is provided no work and no pay while the contract continues.
ex: After four weeks of lay-off, the workers became entitled to claim a redundancy payment.

def: To reduce the level of skill required for a job, often through automation or reorganisation.
ex: Automating the assessments would deskill the role and undermine the case for its higher grade.

def: To strike out an unenforceable part of a restrictive covenant while leaving the rest intact.
ex: The court could blue-pencil the excessive geographic limit but not rewrite the clause.

def: The reduction of an employee to a lower rank, grade, or pay, sometimes as a disciplinary sanction.
ex: Imposing a demotion without a contractual right to do so risked a claim of constructive dismissal.

def: A worker who discloses information about wrongdoing and gains protection against reprisal.
ex: As a whistleblower, she was shielded from dismissal for reporting the safety breaches.

def: Adverse treatment of an employee in response to their asserting a protected right or complaint.
ex: His sudden exclusion from meetings looked like retaliation for the grievance he had filed.

def: To move an employee to a different role or location rather than dismiss them.
ex: The company tried to redeploy the affected staff before confirming any redundancies.

def: To work a second job in addition to one's main employment, often covertly.
ex: He was disciplined for moonlighting as a consultant for a rival firm.

def: Expressed or calculated as a total over a full year, especially of working hours or pay.
ex: Under the annualised hours scheme, staff worked longer in peak months and less in quiet ones.

def: A standardised contract offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, leaving the weaker party no scope to negotiate its terms.
ex: The court scrutinised the exclusion clause more closely because the policy was one of adhesion drafted entirely by the insurer.

def: The requirement that an acceptance correspond exactly to the terms of the offer for a contract to be formed.
ex: Because the buyer's reply added a delivery condition, the mirror image rule meant it operated as a counteroffer rather than an acceptance.

def: Exaggerated or vague sales talk that no reasonable person would treat as a binding statement of fact.
ex: The seller's boast that the machine was the finest in the trade was mere puffery and gave rise to no actionable misrepresentation.

def: To profess or claim to be or do something, without necessarily being so in fact.
ex: The document purported to assign the copyright, but the assignor in truth had no title to convey.

def: To show or make evident, especially an intention.
ex: The parties' course of dealing evinced a clear intention to be legally bound despite the absence of any signed agreement.

def: To become a party to an existing agreement by formally consenting to its terms.
ex: A new lender may accede to the facility agreement by executing a short deed of accession.

def: To take effect or operate, typically so as to benefit someone.
ex: The restrictive covenant was drafted to inure to the benefit of the developer's successors in title.

def: An ambiguity not apparent on the face of a contract's wording but emerging when it is applied to the facts.
ex: The reference to the warehouse concealed a latent ambiguity, since the seller owned two, and extrinsic evidence was admitted to resolve it.

def: The whole of a written document considered on its own, without reference to outside material.
ex: Applying the four corners rule, the judge refused to look beyond the deed to imply an obligation the parties had never written down.

def: The gradual writing off of an intangible asset or the spreading of a loan's repayment over its term.
ex: Stripping out amortization of the acquired patents lifts the segment's reported margin by four points.

def: The release of a borrower from a debt by setting aside enough assets to cover it.
ex: Rather than refinance, the treasury team funded a defeasance portfolio of government bonds to retire the old notes.

def: A contractual right to reclaim money already paid out, often bonuses after misconduct or a restatement.
ex: The compensation committee triggered the clawback provision and recovered three years of the ousted CFO's incentive pay.

def: A binding condition in a loan agreement that the borrower must keep, such as a maximum leverage ratio.
ex: A single quarter of soft sales pushed them within a whisker of breaching the interest-coverage covenant.

def: A claim or liability attached to an asset, such as a lien or mortgage, that limits its free use.
ex: Due diligence turned up an undisclosed encumbrance on the warehouse, so we escrowed part of the purchase price.

def: A charge recognizing that an asset is worth less on the books than its carrying value.
ex: The collapse of the Asian unit forced a nine-figure goodwill impairment that wiped out full-year profit.

def: The ability to meet long-term obligations and keep total assets above total liabilities.
ex: Liquidity was fine, but the pension shortfall raised real questions about the group's long-run solvency.

def: Ranking below other claims for repayment if the borrower defaults.
ex: Holders of the subordinated notes recovered pennies on the dollar once the senior lenders were made whole.

def: A distinct slice of a financing or security carrying its own risk and return profile.
ex: Investors piled into the senior tranche while the equity tranche took the first losses.

def: The charging of interest at rates that are illegally or unconscionably high.
ex: The payday lender's effective annual rate crossed into usury and drew a regulator's suit.

def: An unsecured bond backed only by the issuer's general creditworthiness rather than specific collateral.
ex: With no assets to pledge, the firm raised the cash through a ten-year debenture priced off its credit rating.

def: The process of matching two sets of records so that any differences are identified and explained.
ex: The bank reconciliation flagged a six-thousand-dollar gap that turned out to be a duplicated supplier payment.

def: A reduction in the recorded value of an asset to reflect a fall in its worth.
ex: Slow-moving stock forced a hefty inventory write-down that dragged the quarter into the red.

def: To reduce the amount of debt a company or household carries.
ex: Management spent two years deleveraging the balance sheet before it dared to fund growth again.

def: The gradual increase of a bond's book value toward par, or growth in value over time.
ex: The discount bond was bought below face, and the accretion is booked as income each period until maturity.

def: The reduction in existing shareholders' ownership caused by issuing new shares.
ex: Founders resisted the round because the dilution would drop their combined stake below fifty percent.

def: To record a cost as an asset on the balance sheet rather than expensing it at once.
ex: They chose to capitalize the software build and amortize it over five years instead of taking the whole hit now.

def: The pledging of an asset as security for a loan without giving up possession of it.
ex: The hedge fund's hypothecation of client securities to its prime broker became a flashpoint after the collapse.

def: The profit a monetary authority earns from issuing currency that costs less to produce than its face value.
ex: A shift to digital cash would quietly erode the central bank's seigniorage revenue.

def: The share of a fund's profits paid to its managers as their performance reward.
ex: Most of the partner's take-home came not from salary but from carried interest on the funds she ran.

def: The pace at which a company uses up its cash reserves before turning profitable.
ex: At the current burn rate they have eleven months of runway, so the next raise cannot slip.

def: An expense or revenue recognized when it is earned or incurred rather than when cash changes hands.
ex: We booked an accrual for the unpaid December bonuses so the cost lands in the year it was earned.

def: The postponement of recognizing revenue or expense to a later period.
ex: The upfront license fee sits as deferred revenue and unwinds through the deferral schedule over the contract.

def: A potential obligation that will crystallize only if some future event occurs.
ex: The pending lawsuit is disclosed as a contingent liability rather than booked, since the outcome is still uncertain.

def: An amount set aside in the accounts for a probable future liability or loss.
ex: The bank raised its loan-loss provision sharply as defaults crept up across the mortgage book.

def: A formal revision of previously issued financial statements to correct a material error.
ex: A restatement of two years' revenue sent the stock down twenty percent and triggered a shareholder suit.

def: Cosmetic moves near a reporting date to make the numbers look stronger than they really are.
ex: Selling losers on the last trading day is classic window dressing to prettify the fund's year-end holdings.

def: Valued at current market prices rather than at original cost.
ex: On a mark-to-market basis the trading book showed a loss the day prices gapped down.

def: The offsetting of mutual amounts owed so that only a single balance changes hands.
ex: After netting the intercompany payables and receivables, only a small residual had to be wired.

def: A reduction applied to the value of collateral or the amount a creditor is repaid.
ex: Lenders accepted a thirty percent haircut on the bonds to keep the company out of formal bankruptcy.

def: A negotiated restructuring of a troubled loan to avoid outright default or bankruptcy.
ex: The bank's special-situations team ran the workout, stretching maturities in exchange for a slice of equity.

def: The premium paid over the fair value of a target's net assets, booked as an intangible.
ex: Most of the acquisition price landed on the balance sheet as goodwill, a number auditors test yearly for impairment.

def: The minimum return a project or investment must clear to be worth funding.
ex: The expansion pencilled out at nine percent, below the board's twelve percent hurdle rate, so it was shelved.

def: Wrongful or unlawful conduct by an official or person in a position of trust.
ex: The inquiry found no criminal malfeasance, only a pattern of sloppy oversight.

def: Acting in a transaction to benefit oneself rather than the organization one represents.
ex: Routing contracts to his own firm was textbook self-dealing, and the audit committee flagged it.

def: The use of governance mechanisms to insulate management from removal or challenge.
ex: Analysts saw the poison pill as pure board entrenchment, protecting incumbents rather than shareholders.

def: Strict adherence to honesty and ethical principles in one's dealings.
ex: Regulators expect absolute probity from anyone signing off on the accounts.

def: The total pay and benefits an employee or director receives for their work.
ex: The remuneration committee capped executive payouts after the shareholder revolt.

def: The responsible oversight and careful management of assets entrusted to one's care.
ex: Institutional investors are under pressure to show active stewardship of the companies they hold.

def: The minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting's decisions to be valid.
ex: Two directors dialed in late, so we didn't have a quorum to approve the resolution.

def: To withdraw oneself from a decision because of a potential conflict of interest.
ex: He recused himself from the vote since his brother-in-law owned the target company.

def: To give formal approval that makes a decision or agreement official.
ex: Shareholders will ratify the auditor's appointment at the annual meeting.

def: A commitment to compensate another party for a specified loss or liability.
ex: Directors won't join the board without an indemnity covering suits arising from their decisions.

def: The threshold at which an item is significant enough to affect a reasonable person's decisions.
ex: Below the materiality threshold, the misstatement didn't warrant a restatement.

def: A formal declaration certifying that something is accurate or that controls are sound.
ex: Management's attestation on internal controls now sits alongside the audited accounts.

def: Beyond the legal powers granted to a company or its officers.
ex: The court voided the guarantee as ultra vires, since the charter never authorized it.

def: A defensive tactic that makes a hostile takeover prohibitively costly for the acquirer.
ex: The board adopted a poison pill overnight to fend off the raider's creeping stake.

def: A lucrative payout guaranteed to an executive if they lose their job after a takeover.
ex: His golden parachute was worth three years' salary the moment the deal closed.

def: A board structure where only a fraction of directors face election each year, slowing any takeover.
ex: With a staggered board, an activist would need two annual cycles to win control.

def: A lawsuit brought by a shareholder on the company's behalf against its own directors.
ex: Minority holders launched a derivative action to recover the sums lost to self-dealing.

def: A deal between a company and an insider or affiliated entity, requiring extra scrutiny.
ex: Every related-party transaction over a set size now needs independent-committee sign-off.

def: The real economic interest in an asset, regardless of whose name legally holds it.
ex: Regulators traced beneficial ownership through three shell companies before finding the actual controller.

def: A voting threshold well above a simple majority required to pass certain decisions.
ex: Amending the bylaws needs a two-thirds supermajority, not a simple show of hands.

def: The compulsory buyout of minority shareholders once an acquirer crosses an ownership threshold.
ex: After hitting ninety percent, the bidder moved to a squeeze-out of the remaining holders.

def: The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its goals.
ex: Expanding into that market sits well outside our stated risk appetite.

def: The exposure that remains after controls and mitigations have been applied.
ex: Even with the new safeguards, the residual risk of fraud is higher than the board is comfortable with.

def: The level of risk present before any controls are taken into account.
ex: Cash-heavy operations carry high inherent risk, so the audit focuses there first.

def: The tendency to take greater risks when shielded from the consequences of failure.
ex: Bailing out the traders would create a moral hazard the whole desk would exploit.

def: The danger that one failure cascades to bring down an entire market or system.
ex: Their exposure was small alone, but tangled counterparties turned it into systemic risk.

def: The assumption that a business will remain financially viable for the foreseeable future.
ex: The auditors attached a going-concern warning, spooking lenders overnight.

def: Splitting a task among several people so no one person controls a whole risky process.
ex: Poor segregation of duties let the same clerk both approve and pay the invoices.

def: The ethical climate set by senior leaders that shapes conduct throughout an organization.
ex: You can write all the policies you like, but a rotten tone at the top undoes them.

def: A legal presumption that directors' informed, good-faith decisions won't be second-guessed by courts.
ex: The business judgment rule shielded the board even though the acquisition later flopped.

def: A director's obligation to put the company's interests ahead of any personal gain.
ex: Steering the contract to his wife's firm was a plain breach of the duty of loyalty.

def: A campaign to win shareholder votes in order to replace directors or force a change.
ex: The activist launched a proxy contest to seat three of its own nominees.

def: A provision that shields a party from liability if specified conditions are met.
ex: Forward-looking statements fall within a safe harbor as long as risk factors are disclosed.

def: A control or measure that reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk.
ex: Collateral is the main mitigant against the borrower defaulting.

def: The danger that the other side of a contract fails to meet its obligations.
ex: We cap counterparty risk by refusing to trade with anyone below an A rating.

def: The cutting out of intermediaries between a producer and the end customer.
ex: The disintermediation of our distributors let us sell direct and capture the margin they used to take.

def: A self-reinforcing loop in which each success feeds and accelerates the next.
ex: Every new seller brings buyers, and more buyers pull in more sellers, so the flywheel keeps gaining speed.

def: To strip a product of differentiation until it competes on price alone.
ex: Once every vendor offered the same features, the whole market commoditized almost overnight.

def: A discipline of relentless small, incremental improvements to a process.
ex: The line workers flag tiny inefficiencies every week, and that kaizen mindset is why we run so lean.

def: The amplification of small demand swings as they ripple up a supply chain.
ex: A minor dip in retail orders left the factory drowning in cancelled components a month later, a textbook bullwhip effect.

def: The relocation of operations to a nearby country rather than a distant one.
ex: We are nearshoring assembly to Mexico to shave weeks off transit times.

def: A unit separated from its parent to operate or be sold on its own.
ex: The semiconductor carve-out will list as a standalone company by the third quarter.

def: The value of keeping future choices open rather than committing now.
ex: Leasing instead of buying preserves optionality if the market suddenly turns.

def: Reducing earnings or ownership per share.
ex: Issuing new stock to fund the acquisition would be dilutive to existing holders.

def: Cash or reserves held ready to deploy when the moment is right.
ex: We are sitting on plenty of dry powder for when valuations finally come back to earth.

def: To trim and streamline a portfolio or footprint for efficiency.
ex: We rationalized the product line from forty items down to twelve.

def: How well a business can protect its position against competitors.
ex: The tech is clever, but I am not convinced of its defensibility once the giants notice.

def: To adjust an organization or cost base to the level actually needed.
ex: After the merger we right-sized the combined headcount to match real demand.

def: To turn a strategy or idea into concrete, working processes.
ex: The vision deck is inspiring, but nobody has operationalized a single step of it yet.

def: A small initial market secured as a foothold for wider expansion.
ex: We will win the dental clinics first, then use that beachhead to move into wider healthcare.

def: An unserved gap in a market where no competitor is yet established.
ex: There is real white space in mid-market pricing that nobody has bothered to fill.

def: A related market or capability a business can plausibly expand into.
ex: Payments is a natural adjacency for us given how much transaction data we already hold.

def: The revenue and cost tied to a single unit of what a business sells.
ex: Growth looks great, but the unit economics fall apart once you factor in returns.

def: The elapsed time between placing an order and receiving it.
ex: With lead times stretching to sixteen weeks, we had to order components far ahead.

def: Delivering inputs exactly when needed so inventory is kept minimal.
ex: Our just-in-time system kept warehouses lean until the port strike broke everything.

def: Extra inventory held to absorb unexpected demand or supply shocks.
ex: We doubled safety stock on critical parts after last year's shortage.

def: The chain of dependent tasks that sets a project's minimum duration.
ex: Permitting is on the critical path, so any delay there pushes the whole launch back.
