ex: The stylised logo functioned as an indicium of origin recognised throughout the market.

def: An arrangement by which similar marks are used in parallel under agreed conditions to avoid conflict.
ex: The parties signed a coexistence agreement delimiting the territories in which each mark would be used.

def: From the very beginning, used to describe something treated as invalid or valid from its inception.
ex: Because the parties never had capacity to contract, the agreement was void ab initio.

def: Made or done in good faith, without fraud or deception.
ex: He was a bona fide purchaser for value and took the property free of the earlier charge.

def: Done in bad faith, with dishonest intent or knowledge of wrongdoing.
ex: The court found that the transfer was made mala fide to defeat the claims of creditors.

def: Denoting legal work undertaken without charge for the public good.
ex: The firm requires each associate to complete fifty hours of pro bono work every year.

def: Existing in fact, whether or not by legal right.
ex: Although never formally appointed, he acted as the de facto director of the company.

def: Existing by right or according to law, whether or not that is the position in fact.
ex: She remained the de jure owner even after losing physical possession of the land.

def: Calculated in proportion to a relevant total, such as a share or a period of time.
ex: Dividends are payable pro rata according to each shareholder's holding.

def: Let the buyer beware, the principle that a purchaser buys at their own risk absent a warranty.
ex: The doctrine of caveat emptor placed the onus on the buyer to inspect the property before completion.

def: Of its own unique kind and not fitting into any existing category.
ex: The database right is a sui generis form of protection distinct from copyright.

def: Between the parties, denoting a hearing at which both sides are present and heard.
ex: The interim order was later reconsidered at an inter partes hearing.

def: Given as a favour or gesture of goodwill rather than out of any legal obligation.
ex: The company made an ex gratia payment to the injured worker without admitting liability.

def: In the place of a parent, describing a person who assumes parental responsibility for a child.
ex: During the school trip the teachers stood in loco parentis to the pupils.

def: The principle that a person who willingly consents to a risk cannot later sue for resulting harm.
ex: The defence of volenti non fit injuria failed because the claimant had not truly consented to the danger.

def: The principle that negligence may be inferred where the accident speaks for itself.
ex: Since a swab was left inside the patient, the claimant relied on res ipsa loquitur.

def: The rule that no one may be a judge in their own cause, requiring an impartial decision-maker.
ex: Because the chairman had a financial interest, the decision offended nemo judex in causa sua.

def: The principle that agreements must be kept and are binding on the parties who make them.
ex: Under the maxim pacta sunt servanda, the state was obliged to honour the treaty.

def: The principle that there can be no punishment without a pre-existing law creating the offence.
ex: Retrospective criminal liability would violate nulla poena sine lege.

def: The burden of proof, namely the duty to establish the facts alleged.
ex: In criminal cases the onus probandi rests firmly on the prosecution.

def: The maxim that the burden of proof lies on the party who asserts, not on the one who denies.
ex: The tribunal reminded the applicant that ei incumbit probatio qui dicit governs who must prove the claim.

def: At the outset or threshold of proceedings, typically of a preliminary objection or motion.
ex: Counsel raised a motion in limine to exclude the disputed evidence before trial.

def: So trivial or minor that the law will not take account of it.
ex: The court dismissed the encroachment as de minimis and refused any remedy.

def: In agreement on the same thing, denoting the meeting of minds needed to form a contract.
ex: Because the parties were never ad idem on price, no binding contract arose.

def: The maxim that ignorance of the law is no excuse for breaking it.
ex: The defendant's plea that he did not know the regulation failed, since ignorantia juris non excusat.
syn: ignorance of the law is no excuse

def: A judge's incidental remark that is not essential to the decision and carries no binding authority.
ex: The observation was mere dictum and did not bind the courts that followed.

def: An authoritative decree or order issued by a person having the power to enforce it.
ex: The regulator cannot rewrite the parties' bargain by fiat.

def: Of an order, taking effect only after a specified period unless cause is shown to the contrary.
ex: The decree nisi would be made absolute after six weeks.

def: Simply and unconditionally; without qualification or added condition.
ex: The obligation was to deliver the goods simpliciter, not upon any precondition.

def: Used to introduce a doubtful point or an open question of law for consideration.
ex: Quaere whether the same principle applies to a gratuitous bailee.

def: Official approval or sanction giving something the authority to proceed.
ex: The scheme could not go ahead without the minister's imprimatur.

def: Signs, marks or indications from which the existence of a fact may be inferred.
ex: The document bore all the indicia of a validly executed deed.

def: A person who has made and left a valid will.
ex: The testator revoked all previous wills in the opening clause.

def: A woman who has made and left a valid will.
ex: The testatrix appointed her two daughters as her executrices.

def: Having died without leaving a valid will.
ex: Because he died intestate, his estate passed under the statutory rules.

def: A document executed to add to, vary or partly revoke an existing will.
ex: She added a codicil leaving a modest legacy to her carer.

def: A person who holds property under a usufruct.
ex: As usufructuary she was entitled to the harvest but not to fell the timber.

def: A charge or security over property that remains in the debtor's possession.
ex: The landlord's hypothec secured the arrears of rent over the tenant's goods.

def: A civil wrong giving rise to an obligation to make reparation, especially in civil-law systems.
ex: Under Scots law the claim sounded in delict rather than in contract.

def: The formal act of freeing a person from slavery or bondage.
ex: The deed of manumission granted the bondsman his liberty.

def: A person appointed to manage the affairs or property of one unable to do so.
ex: A curator was appointed to administer the estate of the incapacitated heir.

def: The right of the firstborn, especially the eldest son, to inherit the whole estate.
ex: Under the old rule of primogeniture the younger sons took nothing.

def: In accordance with or under the authority of a specified statute, contract, or provision.
ex: Pursuant to clause 12.3, the tenant shall give three months' written notice of any assignment.

word: without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing
def: Introducing specific examples that do not limit the broad scope of a general provision just stated.
ex: The Company shall keep proper records and, without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing, shall retain all invoices for six years.

def: Introducing a clarification that makes explicit something intended to be implied, removing any possible ambiguity.
ex: For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this clause obliges the Buyer to purchase further stock.

def: Conditional upon or qualified by another provision, which takes priority in the event of conflict.
ex: Subject to clause 5, the Licensee may sub-license the software to its affiliates.

def: Except as otherwise provided in a specified place, used to carve out an exception to a general rule.
ex: Save as expressly set out in Schedule 2, all warranties are excluded to the fullest extent permitted by law.

def: Except that, introducing a single qualification to an otherwise general statement.
ex: The terms of the previous lease shall continue to apply, save that the annual rent is increased to £45,000.

def: Introducing a proviso that imposes a condition or qualification on the preceding words.
ex: The Employer may vary duties, provided that any change is reasonable and consistent with the Employee's status.

def: To the extent that, limiting a provision so it applies only within the stated bounds.
ex: This clause applies only insofar as it does not conflict with any mandatory provision of the Consumer Rights Act.

def: Limiting the operation of a provision so that it applies only within specified boundaries.
ex: The indemnity applies only to the extent that the loss was caused by the Contractor's negligence.

def: In conformity with the requirements or procedure laid down in a specified provision or instrument.
ex: Notice shall be served in accordance with clause 20 and shall be deemed received on the next business day.

def: Concerning or relating to a specified matter, used to define the subject a provision addresses.
ex: The Seller shall have no liability in respect of any claim notified more than 18 months after Completion.

def: Concerning or as regards a specified matter, used to delimit the scope of an obligation.
ex: The Company gives no warranty with respect to the future profitability of the business.

def: As a result of or by reason of the operation of a specified provision, right, or fact.
ex: The claimant acquired the easement by virtue of long uninterrupted use of the private roadway.

def: Because of or on account of a specified cause, used to attribute a consequence to it.
ex: The Landlord may forfeit the lease by reason of the tenant's persistent failure to pay rent.

def: Taking into account or giving due consideration to specified factors when reaching a decision.
ex: The court determined the reasonable notice period having regard to the employee's length of service and seniority.

def: By that very fact or act, indicating that a consequence follows automatically from a stated circumstance.
ex: A material breach does not ipso facto terminate the contract; the innocent party must elect to accept it.

def: By means of this present document or clause, used to give immediate operative effect to a declaration.
ex: The Assignor hereby assigns to the Assignee all its right, title and interest in the copyright.

def: In this document or clause, used to point to something contained within the instrument itself.
ex: The definitions set out herein apply throughout this Agreement unless the context otherwise requires.

def: Of this document or clause, used to refer back to the instrument or a part of it.
ex: The recitals form part hereof and are to be read together with the operative provisions.

def: Under or in accordance with the terms of this document, used to refer to rights or obligations it creates.
ex: Any sums payable hereunder shall be paid in cleared funds within 30 days of invoice.

def: To the thing just mentioned, used to refer back to a previously identified item or document.
ex: The Company shall execute the transfer and all documents ancillary thereto.

def: In the thing just mentioned, used to refer to something contained in a document, place, or provision already identified.
ex: The lease demised the flat together with the fixtures and fittings therein.

def: Under or in accordance with the document or provision just mentioned.
ex: The parties referred to the earlier deed and the obligations arising thereunder.

def: Mentioned or referred to earlier in the same document, used to point back to a previously stated matter.
ex: The aforesaid sum shall be held on trust for the beneficiaries named in the Schedule.

def: Referring to a person or thing already specifically identified earlier in the document.
ex: The Tenant shall keep the said premises in good and substantial repair throughout the term.

def: Of the kind or the particular one already mentioned, used to refer back precisely without repeating a defined term.
ex: Where the Buyer requests a variation, such variation shall not take effect until agreed in writing.

def: Introducing a recital that states the background facts and intentions leading up to an agreement.
ex: Whereas the Seller is the registered proprietor of the Property, the parties have agreed as follows.

def: Marking the transition from the recitals to the operative provisions of an agreement.
ex: Now, therefore, in consideration of the mutual covenants set out below, the parties agree as follows.

def: Introducing the value or promise given in exchange that makes a contract binding.
ex: In consideration of the sum of £1, the Guarantor agrees to guarantee the Tenant's obligations.

def: Imposing a binding obligation or duty on a party to do or refrain from doing something.
ex: The Contractor shall complete the works by the date specified in the Schedule.

def: Indicating that whichever of two or more stated alternatives applies is to be selected according to the circumstances.
ex: The notice shall be given to the Buyer or the Seller, as the case may be.

def: Governing the position solely between the named parties, without affecting the rights of others.
ex: As between the Contractor and the Sub-contractor, responsibility for site safety rests with the Contractor.

def: Introducing examples that illustrate but do not restrict the scope of a general word or category.
ex: The Company shall not disclose any Confidential Information, including without limitation client lists and pricing.

def: Signalling that the following items are non-exhaustive examples and do not narrow the preceding general term.
ex: Losses recoverable include but are not limited to lost profits, wasted expenditure and reputational harm.

def: Qualifying a definitions clause so that a defined meaning applies except where the surrounding text demands a different reading.
ex: In this Agreement, unless the context otherwise requires, the singular includes the plural.

def: Limiting a definition or rule so that it operates only in relation to the specified provision or context.
ex: For the purposes of this clause, "Group Company" means any subsidiary of the Parent.

def: In a way that makes each obligor liable both individually for the whole and together with the others.
ex: The Guarantors are jointly and severally liable for the whole of the outstanding debt.

def: Introducing a specific instance that must not be read as narrowing a broader obligation already stated.
ex: Without limiting clause 4, the Supplier shall comply with all applicable data protection laws.

def: In the proper manner and in accordance with the required formalities or authority.
ex: The Agreement was duly executed by a director of the Company and witnessed accordingly.

def: Introducing the concluding attestation clause of a deed, confirming that the parties have signed it.
ex: In witness whereof the parties have executed this Deed on the date first above written.

def: Treated by the drafting as being the case, whether or not it is so in fact, in order to fix a legal consequence.
ex: A notice sent by first-class post is deemed to have been received on the second business day after posting.

def: Selecting, from two or more stated dates or events, the one that occurs first.
ex: The option lapses on completion of the sale or on 31 December, whichever is the earlier.

def: Formal written questions served on an opposing party that must be answered under oath during discovery.
ex: The defendant's evasive answers to the interrogatories prompted a motion to compel.

def: A procedure by which a stakeholder facing rival claims to property forces the claimants to litigate between themselves.
ex: The bank issued interpleader proceedings so that the competing claimants to the fund could resolve their dispute.

def: A procedure allowing a defendant to bring a third party into the action who may be liable for the claim.
ex: Through impleader, the contractor joined its subcontractor as a party liable to indemnify it.

def: A court's reduction of an excessive jury award, offered to the claimant as an alternative to a new trial.
ex: Finding the damages grossly disproportionate, the judge ordered a remittitur to a fifth of the verdict.

def: A court's increase of an inadequate jury award, offered to the defendant to avoid a new trial.
ex: The trial court applied an additur, raising the paltry award to a figure supported by the evidence.

def: The formal resolution of a dispute by a judge or other tribunal.
ex: The complex accounting issues were referred for adjudication by a specialist referee.

def: Lacking any serious legal merit or arguable basis.
ex: The appeal was struck out as frivolous and an abuse of the court's process.

def: To enrol and swear in a jury for the trial of a case.
ex: Once the jury had been impanelled, the judge delivered his opening directions.

def: The process of discrediting a witness's credibility, typically through prior inconsistent statements.
ex: Cross-examining counsel secured the witness's impeachment by producing his contradictory earlier statement.

def: An action to recover possession of goods wrongfully taken or detained.
ex: The owner brought replevin to recover the machinery seized by the former lessee.

def: An action for the wrongful detention of goods and their recovery or value.
ex: He sued in detinue after the bailee refused to return the deposited artworks.

def: Concerning a judgment that authoritatively states the parties' legal rights without ordering enforcement.
ex: The company sought declaratory relief establishing that the disputed clause was unenforceable.

def: Of a sum, fixed or ascertainable by calculation rather than requiring assessment.
ex: The contract stipulated liquidated damages of a set amount for each week of delay.

def: Of damages awarded to punish and deter rather than merely to compensate.
ex: The jury awarded exemplary damages to mark its disapproval of the defendant's oppressive conduct.

def: Of negligence on a claimant's part that contributed to the harm and reduces recoverable damages.
ex: The award was cut by a third to reflect the claimant's contributory negligence.

def: The statutory period within which a claim must be brought, after which it becomes time-barred.
ex: The defence pleaded that the claim was statute-barred, the limitation period having long expired.

def: To formally start a legal action by filing a claim form at court.
ex: If the debt remains unpaid by Friday, we will issue proceedings in the County Court without further notice.

def: The court document that starts a civil claim and sets out the remedy the claimant seeks.
ex: The claim form must be served on the defendant within four months of the date it is issued.

def: A formal court document such as a claim, defence or reply that sets out a party's position.
ex: The judge criticised the claimant for advancing an argument that appeared nowhere in its statement of case.

def: To formally deliver court documents to the other party so that the action can proceed.
ex: We served proceedings on the company's registered office by first-class post on Monday.

def: To lodge at court a document responding to a claim and stating which allegations are denied.
ex: The defendant has fourteen days to file a defence or risk judgment in default.

def: A judgment entered for the claimant because the defendant failed to respond in time.
ex: Because no acknowledgment of service was filed, we obtained default judgment for the full sum claimed.

def: A document that a party may withhold from inspection because it attracts legal privilege.
ex: Advice from counsel is a privileged document and need not be produced to the other side.

def: To put forward evidence to the court in support of a case.
ex: The defence sought to adduce fresh evidence of an alibi at a late stage.

def: A witness permitted to give opinion evidence on a matter within their specialist expertise.
ex: Each party instructed an expert witness on the standard of care in orthopaedic surgery.

def: The set of facts that entitles a party to bring a claim against another.
ex: The cause of action in negligence accrued when the claimant first suffered loss.

def: Describing a claim that can no longer be pursued because the limitation period has expired.
ex: The defendant pleaded that the claim was statute-barred and applied to strike it out.

def: An application made to the court without informing the other party in advance.
ex: A freezing order is usually sought by a without notice application to preserve the element of surprise.

def: A court order preventing a party from dealing with or dissipating its assets before judgment.
ex: We secured a worldwide freezing order over the defendant's bank accounts.

def: A court order determining which party must pay the legal costs of the proceedings.
ex: The judge made a costs order requiring the losing party to pay 80 per cent of our client's costs.

def: A formal offer to settle made under the rules that carries automatic costs consequences if refused and not beaten.
ex: The claimant beat its own Part 36 offer at trial and was awarded enhanced interest and indemnity costs.

def: To resolve a dispute by agreement between the parties without proceeding to trial.
ex: The parties settled out of court on the morning of the hearing.

def: To voluntarily bring one's own claim to an end before it is decided.
ex: The claimant chose to discontinue the action but remained liable for the defendant's costs to date.

def: Damages for losses that cannot be calculated precisely, such as pain and suffering.
ex: General damages for the whiplash injury were assessed at £4,500.

def: Damages for specific, quantifiable financial losses actually incurred.
ex: Special damages included lost earnings and the cost of private physiotherapy.

def: To take reasonable steps to reduce the loss caused by another party's breach or wrong.
ex: The claimant failed to mitigate its loss by refusing a comparable replacement contract.

def: The court's permission required before an appeal against a decision may proceed.
ex: The judge refused leave to appeal, so we renewed the application to the Court of Appeal.

def: To decide an appeal in favour of the appellant and set aside or vary the decision below.
ex: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and remitted the case for a fresh trial.

def: To reject an appeal and uphold the decision of the lower court.
ex: The appeal was dismissed and the original judgment stood.

def: To cancel or nullify a judgment or order made by a court.
ex: The defendant applied to set aside the default judgment on the ground of a real prospect of defending.

def: To take legal steps to compel a losing party to comply with a judgment, usually to pay the sum owed.
ex: Having won at trial, the claimant instructed enforcement agents to enforce the judgment against the debtor's goods.

def: A hearing at which the court gives directions to prepare the case efficiently for trial.
ex: At the case management conference the judge set a timetable for disclosure and witness statements.

def: Decided on the substance of the legal and factual issues rather than on a technicality.
ex: The claim was dismissed on the merits, so the same dispute cannot be relitigated.

def: A charter under which a shipowner agrees to carry a specified cargo between named ports for an agreed freight, retaining possession and control of the vessel.
ex: Under the voyage charter, the owners bore the cost of bunkers and port charges, not the charterers.

def: A charter under which a charterer hires a fully crewed vessel for a defined period, directing its commercial employment while the owner retains navigational control.
ex: The time charter allowed the charterers to trade the vessel worldwide within Institute Warranty Limits.

def: A charter under which the charterer takes full possession, control and management of the vessel, crewing and operating it as if the owner for the charter period.
ex: On a bareboat charter, the charterers were responsible for insuring and manning the ship throughout the demise.

def: A party who charters in a vessel and then sub-charters it out, so acting as owner towards the sub-charterer without holding legal title.
ex: The disponent owners sought to pass the charterers' claim up the chain to the head owners.

def: A document issued by a carrier acknowledging receipt of goods for shipment, serving as evidence of the contract of carriage and, when negotiable, as a document of title.
ex: The bank refused to release funds because the bill of lading was claused and therefore not clean.

def: A bill of lading bearing no clause or notation expressly declaring a defective condition of the goods or their packaging.
ex: A clean bill of lading was a condition of payment under the documentary credit.

def: A bill of lading endorsed with a remark noting that the goods or packaging were received in defective or damaged condition.
ex: The mate's notation that the drums were leaking rendered it a claused bill, rejected by the receiving bank.

def: A document whose transfer operates to pass constructive possession of, and the right to claim delivery of, the goods it represents.
ex: Because a straight bill of lading is not a document of title, indorsement did not transfer the right to delivery.

def: A non-negotiable transport document that evidences the contract of carriage and receipt of goods but is not a document of title, so goods are delivered to the named consignee without its surrender.
ex: They used a sea waybill to avoid the delays caused by bills of lading arriving after the ship.

def: A provisional document signed by the ship's mate acknowledging receipt of cargo on board, later exchanged for the bill of lading.
ex: Any remarks as to apparent condition were first entered on the mate's receipt before the bill was drawn up.

def: A principle of maritime law under which loss or expenditure voluntarily and reasonably incurred to save a common maritime adventure is shared rateably among all interests benefited.
ex: The jettison of deck cargo to refloat the vessel was declared general average and apportioned among ship, cargo and freight.

def: A partial loss of, or damage to, a ship or cargo that is borne solely by the owner of the affected interest and not shared among the adventure.
ex: Water damage to a single consignment, having conferred no common benefit, fell as particular average on that cargo owner alone.

def: An extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally and reasonably made for the common safety of the maritime adventure, which grounds a claim in general average.
ex: There is a general average act only where the sacrifice is voluntary; loss by fortuitous accident does not qualify.

def: A specialist who investigates a general average or insurance loss and prepares the statement apportioning contributions among the interested parties.
ex: The average adjuster's statement allocated the salvage costs across hull, cargo and bunkers in proportion to their saved values.

def: A body of internationally accepted rules, incorporated into charterparties and bills of lading, that governs the adjustment of general average.
ex: The bill of lading provided that general average would be adjusted in London according to the York-Antwerp Rules 2016.

def: An undertaking given by cargo interests to pay their due general average contribution, taken so that goods may be released before the adjustment is complete.
ex: Cargo was delivered only against an average bond and a cash deposit or underwriters' guarantee.

def: The deliberate throwing overboard of cargo or ship's equipment to lighten or save the vessel in time of peril.
ex: The jettison of the heaviest containers was a classic general average sacrifice for the common safety.

def: The period allowed to the charterer under a voyage charter for loading and discharging the cargo without additional payment.
ex: Laytime commenced once a valid notice of readiness had been tendered and the vessel was an arrived ship.

def: A payment made by the owner to the charterer as a reward for completing loading or discharge in less than the allowed laytime.
ex: Having finished loading a day early, the charterers claimed despatch money at half the demurrage rate.

def: A formal notification by which the master informs the charterer that the vessel has arrived and is ready in all respects to load or discharge, so that laytime may begin.
ex: The notice of readiness was invalid because the vessel had not yet passed her cargo inspection.

def: A vessel that has reached the agreed destination in the charter such that it is legally in a position to tender a valid notice of readiness and start laytime.
ex: Under a port charter, the vessel became an arrived ship only when it reached a position within the port at the charterers' disposal.

def: A port which, at the relevant time, a vessel can reach, use and leave without being exposed to danger that cannot be avoided by good navigation and seamanship.
ex: The charterers were in breach of the safe port warranty by ordering the vessel to a berth where she grounded at low water.

def: The fitness of a vessel in all respects — hull, equipment, crew and cargoworthiness — to encounter the ordinary perils of the contemplated voyage.
ex: The owners' duty was to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage.

def: An international regime governing carriers' rights and liabilities under bills of lading, allocating risk and capping liability per package or unit of weight.
ex: Liability was limited under the Hague-Visby Rules to the higher of the package or kilogramme figure.

def: An unjustified departure by a vessel from the contractual or customary route of the voyage, which may deprive the carrier of contractual defences.
ex: The unauthorised deviation to load additional cargo displaced the exceptions clause and left the owners fully liable.

def: A clause in a bill of lading or charterparty permitting the carrier to depart from the direct route, call at additional ports, or take other specified steps without it constituting a breach.
ex: The owners relied on the liberty clause to justify bunkering at an intermediate port.

def: The remuneration payable to a carrier or shipowner for the carriage of goods by sea.
ex: Freight was deemed earned on shipment and was payable whether or not the cargo was lost in transit.

def: Damages payable by a charterer who fails to load a full and complete cargo, representing the freight lost on the space left unfilled.
ex: Having shipped only 8,000 of the 10,000 tonnes contracted, the charterers were liable in deadfreight for the shortfall.

def: The right of a shipowner to retain possession of cargo until outstanding freight, demurrage or general average contributions are paid.
ex: The owners exercised their contractual lien on cargo for unpaid demurrage before allowing discharge.

def: A privileged charge that attaches to a vessel from the moment a claim arises and travels with the ship regardless of any change in ownership until enforced or extinguished.
ex: The crew's claim for unpaid wages ranked as a maritime lien and took priority over the mortgagee.

def: The detention of a ship by order of an admiralty court to found jurisdiction or provide security for a maritime claim.
ex: They obtained the arrest of the sister ship to secure their bunker claim.

def: An admiralty proceeding brought against the ship or other maritime property itself, rather than against a person, allowing its arrest as security.
ex: The claimants commenced an action in rem against the vessel to enforce their maritime lien.

def: Another vessel in the same beneficial ownership as the ship connected with a claim, which may be arrested in its place to obtain security.
ex: Where the offending vessel had left the jurisdiction, the claimant arrested a sister ship instead.

def: The reward payable to those who voluntarily and successfully save maritime property in danger, or the service of doing so.
ex: The tug owners claimed salvage for refloating the grounded tanker before it broke up.

def: A standard salvage agreement, based on the 'no cure, no pay' principle, under which the reward is fixed later by arbitration in London.
ex: The master signed Lloyd's Open Form as the casualty drifted towards the reef.

def: The fundamental principle of salvage law that a salvor earns a reward only if the salvage operation produces a useful result.
ex: Operating on a no cure, no pay basis, the salvors recovered nothing when the vessel ultimately sank.

def: A payment, exceptionally recoverable by a salvor who has prevented or minimised environmental damage even where no property is saved, departing from the no cure, no pay rule.
ex: Although the vessel was lost, the salvors recovered special compensation for averting a major oil spill.

def: The international rules prescribing steering, sailing and signalling conduct to prevent collisions at sea, breach of which bears on the apportionment of fault.
ex: The vessel was held two-thirds to blame for crossing ahead in breach of the collision regulations.

def: A collision for which both vessels are at fault, so that liability is apportioned between them in proportion to their respective degrees of blame.
ex: In this both-to-blame collision, damages were divided 60/40 according to the vessels' relative culpability.

def: A mutual association of shipowners providing protection and indemnity cover against third-party liabilities not met by ordinary hull insurance.
ex: The P&I club issued a letter of undertaking to secure the cargo claim and avoid arrest of the ship.

def: An undertaking given to a carrier, typically to secure delivery of cargo without production of the original bill of lading or a clean bill, promising to hold the carrier harmless from resulting liability.
ex: The receivers gave a letter of indemnity, backed by a first-class bank, so the cargo could be delivered against it.

def: The wrongful dispossession of a person from the seisin of their freehold land.
ex: The squatter's occupation amounted to a disseisin of the registered proprietor.

def: A former feudal tenure of land held in return for agricultural or monetary services rather than military ones.
ex: Free and common socage became the residual form of tenure after military tenures were abolished.

def: A former tenure of land held at the will of the lord according to the custom of the manor and evidenced by a copy of the court roll.
ex: Copyhold tenure was finally enfranchised and converted to freehold in the early twentieth century.

def: A nominal payment reserved as rent or consideration to render an agreement legally binding.
ex: The charity holds the hall on a 99-year lease at a peppercorn rent.

def: The interest that remains in and returns to a grantor upon the natural determination of a determinable estate.
ex: When the land ceased to be used for worship, the possibility of reverter took effect and the estate returned to the donor's heirs.

def: A settlement of land upon a person and a specified line of their descendants that restricts alienation.
ex: The ancestral estate was tied up in an entail preventing any heir from selling it.

def: A gift of real property made by will.
ex: By the devise in clause 4 the testator left the farmhouse to his eldest son.

def: The person to whom real property is given by a will.
ex: As devisee of the cottage, she took the freehold subject to the outstanding mortgage.

def: The state of dying without having made a valid will disposing of one's property.
ex: On intestacy the estate is distributed according to the statutory order of entitlement.

def: The compulsory taking of private property by the state, generally on payment of compensation.
ex: The landowners challenged the expropriation of their fields for the new motorway.

def: The party who grants a lease of property.
ex: The lessor covenanted to keep the building's structure in good repair.

def: The party to whom a lease of property is granted.
ex: The lessee is obliged to yield up the premises in good condition at the end of the term.

def: A lease carved out of and shorter than the grantor's own leasehold interest.
ex: The tenant granted an underlease of the upper floors without the landlord's consent, breaching the alienation covenant.

def: The gradual retreat of water leaving previously submerged land, which accrues to the adjoining owner.
ex: As the lake receded by reliction, the exposed shore became part of the neighbouring estate.

def: The failure of a specific legacy because its subject matter no longer forms part of the testator's estate at death.
ex: The gift of 'my car' failed by ademption because the testator had sold the vehicle before dying.

def: Denoting property that has a tangible physical existence, such as land or goods.
ex: The house and its grounds are corporeal property, unlike the covenants that burden them.

def: A civil-law perpetual or long-term right to use and enjoy another's land subject to payment of rent.
ex: Under the emphyteusis the tenant could improve and even alienate the land while the ground rent continued.

def: The legal process of transferring ownership of land or property from a seller to a buyer.
ex: She handles residential conveyancing and can usually take a straightforward sale to completion in six weeks.

def: The legal right to ownership and possession of a piece of land or property.
ex: Before exchange we must be satisfied that the seller can show good title to the whole site.

def: Ownership that is free from defects and can be safely relied upon by a buyer and their lender.
ex: The unregistered deeds gap meant the seller could not deduce good title, so the transaction stalled.

def: A formal legal document that is signed, witnessed and delivered to transfer property or create binding obligations.
ex: The transfer must be executed as a deed and witnessed by an independent adult.

def: The deed by which legal ownership of registered land passes from the seller to the buyer.
ex: Once both parties have signed the transfer deed, we can submit the application to register the buyer as proprietor.

def: A loan secured against property, giving the lender rights over it if the borrower fails to repay.
ex: The buyer's mortgage offer is valid for three months, so we should aim to complete well within that window.

def: A registered charge that gives a lender an enforceable security interest over the borrower's land.
ex: We must redeem the existing legal charge before the new lender's charge can take first priority.

def: To pay off the outstanding mortgage debt in full so that the lender's charge is released.
ex: On completion the seller's solicitor will use the sale proceeds to redeem the mortgage and remove the charge.

def: The point at which the parties become legally bound to the sale and neither can withdraw without penalty.
ex: On exchange of contracts the buyer paid a ten per cent deposit and completion was fixed for the 28th.

def: The party selling land or property in a conveyancing transaction.
ex: The vendor is unwilling to reduce the price despite the adverse survey findings.

def: The party buying land or property in a conveyancing transaction.
ex: As purchaser, your client takes the property subject to the tenant's existing lease.

def: The state of a property being empty of occupiers and belongings so the buyer can take it over on completion.
ex: The contract requires the seller to give vacant possession, so all tenants must have left before completion.

def: A contract granting exclusive possession of property for a fixed term in return for rent.
ex: The commercial lease runs for fifteen years with rent reviews every five years.

def: The person who grants a lease and owns the reversion of the property.
ex: Under the lease the landlord is responsible for insuring the structure and recovering the premium from the tenant.

def: The person who holds property under a lease and is entitled to possession for the term.
ex: The tenant is in arrears of three months' rent, so forfeiture is now an option.

def: A mechanism in a lease for adjusting the rent at set intervals, usually to open market value.
ex: The upward-only rent review has pushed the annual rent well above current market levels.

def: A lease provision allowing a party to terminate the lease before the end of the term on a specified date.
ex: The tenant exercised the break clause on the fifth anniversary, giving the required six months' notice.

def: To grant a lease of part or all of premises to another party while retaining the head lease.
ex: The tenant wants to sublet the upper floors but the lease prohibits underletting of part.

def: A payment made by a tenant to cover the landlord's costs of maintaining the common parts and structure.
ex: The service charge has risen sharply this year to fund major works to the roof.

def: A periodic sum payable by a long leaseholder to the freeholder under the terms of the lease.
ex: The escalating ground rent doubles every ten years, which lenders now regard as onerous.

def: Land whose ownership and interests are recorded at the Land Registry under a unique title number.
ex: For registered land, the title register is conclusive evidence of who owns the property.

def: The public body that records the ownership of land and the interests affecting it.
ex: We submitted the application to the Land Registry to register the transfer and the new charge.

def: The official record for a registered property showing its ownership, description and any burdens.
ex: The title register lists a mortgage in the charges section that must be discharged on completion.

def: The official map identifying the extent and boundaries of a registered property.
ex: The title plan does not include the strip of land at the rear, so ownership of it is unclear.

def: A type of easement entitling a person to pass over another's land along a defined route.
ex: The property enjoys a right of way over the shared driveway to reach the public road.

def: The dividing line that marks the extent of one owner's land from the neighbouring land.
ex: The parties disagree about where the boundary runs, so we have instructed a surveyor to prepare a plan.

def: Enquiries made to public authorities to reveal matters affecting a property before purchase.
ex: The local authority searches revealed a proposed road scheme that could affect the value.

def: Formal questions raised by a buyer's solicitor to clarify or resolve issues with the seller's title.
ex: We raised requisitions on title about the missing planning consent for the loft conversion.

def: A document setting out the final sums due between the parties on completion of a transaction.
ex: The completion statement shows the balance payable after deducting the deposit and apportioning the rent.

def: A part-payment, usually ten per cent, paid by the buyer on exchange as security for completing.
ex: If the buyer fails to complete, the seller may forfeit the deposit and resell the property.

def: A form of co-ownership in which owners hold the whole together and the survivor takes the deceased's share.
ex: As joint tenants, on the husband's death the property passed automatically to his wife by survivorship.

def: A form of co-ownership in which each owner holds a distinct share that passes under their will.
ex: They hold as tenants in common in equal shares, so each can leave their half to whomever they choose.

def: Consent from the local planning authority required before carrying out most development of land.
ex: The sale is conditional on the buyer obtaining planning permission for a change of use to residential.

def: A clause in a lease obliging a party to keep the premises in a specified state of repair.
ex: Under a full repairing and insuring lease the tenant bears the entire cost of maintaining the building.

def: A formal notice by which a landlord or tenant ends a periodic tenancy on a specified date.
ex: The landlord served a valid notice to quit, requiring the tenant to give up possession by month's end.

def: An organisation that exercises functions of a public nature and is therefore amenable to judicial review.
ex: The regulator is a public body and its licensing decisions may be challenged in the Administrative Court.

def: A body whose functions are of a public nature and which is required to act compatibly with Convention rights.
ex: As a public authority, the local council must not act in a way incompatible with the applicant's human rights.

def: Not authorised or permitted by law.
ex: The court declared the detention unlawful and ordered the claimant's immediate release.

def: Describing a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable public body could have made it, following the Wednesbury case.
ex: The claimant contended that refusing the licence on those facts was Wednesbury unreasonable.

def: The obligation on a decision-maker to explain the basis of its decision so that fairness and lawfulness can be assessed.
ex: The tribunal breached its duty to give reasons, leaving the parties unable to understand why it had ruled as it did.

def: A court order stating the legal position or rights of the parties without compelling any specific action.
ex: The claimant sought a declaration that the policy was incompatible with the right to family life.

def: The preliminary filter at which a judge decides whether a judicial review claim is arguable enough to proceed.
ex: The claim was refused at the permission stage because the ground was held to be unarguable.

def: To allow a judicial review claim to proceed to a substantive hearing.
ex: The judge granted permission on two of the four grounds and refused the remainder.

def: The set of steps parties are expected to follow, including a letter before claim, before issuing judicial review proceedings.
ex: We complied with the pre-action protocol by sending a letter before claim inviting the authority to reconsider.

def: A pre-action letter setting out the proposed challenge and inviting the public body to respond before proceedings begin.
ex: Our letter before claim gave the department 14 days to withdraw the decision or face judicial review.

def: The rights set out in the European Convention on Human Rights and given effect in domestic law by the Human Rights Act.
ex: The applicant argued that the search violated her Convention rights to privacy.

def: The statute that incorporates Convention rights into domestic law and requires public authorities to act compatibly with them.
ex: The claim was brought under section 6 of the Human Rights Act against the police force.

def: The most common form of delegated legislation, made by a minister under statutory authority.
ex: The new charges were introduced by a statutory instrument laid before Parliament in March.

def: To restrict a statutory discretion unlawfully by adopting a rigid policy and refusing to consider individual cases.
ex: By applying a blanket rule, the board had fettered its discretion and failed to consider the applicant's circumstances.

def: The factors a decision-maker is legally required to take into account when exercising a statutory power.
ex: The decision was flawed because the minister failed to take relevant considerations into account.

def: A residual power of the Crown exercised by the executive that does not derive from statute.
ex: The decision to deploy troops was taken under the prerogative power rather than any Act of Parliament.

def: To send a matter back to the original decision-maker for reconsideration according to law.
ex: The court quashed the refusal and remitted the application to the tribunal for a fresh hearing.

def: A person directly affected by a judicial review claim who is joined to the proceedings alongside claimant and defendant.
ex: The developer was named as an interested party in the challenge to its planning permission.

def: The full hearing at which the merits of a judicial review claim are argued and determined.
ex: Having obtained permission, the parties prepared their bundles for the substantive hearing.

def: The formal ending of a parliamentary session without dissolving the legislature.
ex: The prorogation was quashed as unlawful because it frustrated Parliament's constitutional functions without justification.

def: To discontinue a session of a legislature without dissolving it.
ex: The Crown may prorogue Parliament on the advice of ministers, bringing the session to a close.

def: The supreme authority of a state to govern itself and make binding law free from external control.
ex: Parliamentary sovereignty means that no court may strike down a validly enacted statute.

def: A direct vote by the electorate on a specific constitutional or political question.
ex: The territory's status was settled by plebiscite, with a clear majority favouring independence.

def: A general vote by the electorate on a single political or legislative proposal.
ex: The constitutional amendment required approval by referendum before it could take effect.

def: The manipulation of electoral boundaries to favour one party or group over another.
ex: The court invalidated the map as unconstitutional gerrymandering designed to dilute minority votes.

def: The unequal distribution of representation so that some votes carry more weight than others.
ex: Gross malapportionment left rural districts with far greater voting power than crowded urban ones.

def: To prohibit or forbid something, especially an organisation, by law.
ex: The Home Secretary moved to proscribe the group as a terrorist organisation.

def: To depart from or partially repeal a right, rule or standard.
ex: No state may derogate from the absolute prohibition on torture, even in wartime.

def: A discretionary power historically vested in the Crown and exercised without statutory authority.
ex: The making of treaties remains an exercise of the royal prerogative, subject to limited judicial review.

def: The formal withdrawal of a region or state from a larger political union.
ex: The constitution contained no lawful mechanism for the unilateral secession of a province.

def: The tactic of prolonging debate to obstruct or delay a legislative decision.
ex: A determined filibuster kept the bill from coming to a vote for weeks.

def: A procedure for ending debate and forcing an immediate vote in a legislative body.
ex: Only a supermajority could invoke cloture and bring the filibuster to an end.

def: The act of rendering a law or act legally void or of no effect.
ex: The state claimed a right of nullification, refusing to enforce the federal statute within its borders.

def: A form of government in which power rests with a small privileged group.
ex: Critics warned that concentrating authority in a handful of families amounted to an oligarchy.

def: A system of government in which one person holds unlimited power.
ex: The abolition of checks on the ruler transformed the republic into an autocracy.

def: The exercise of absolute power in an oppressive and arbitrary manner.
ex: The separation of powers was conceived as a bulwark against despotism.

def: The legislative imposition of punishment on a named person without a judicial trial.
ex: The constitution forbids any bill of attainder that would punish an individual by statute.

def: A formal parliamentary procedure by which members demand an explanation from a minister.
ex: The opposition's interpellation forced the minister to justify the emergency decree before the chamber.

def: The principle that the numerical majority is entitled to prevail in political decision-making.
ex: Entrenched rights temper majoritarianism by shielding minorities from the untrammelled will of the majority.

word: without prejudice save as to costs
def: Describing a Calderbank offer whose contents remain privileged until the substantive issue is decided but may then be shown to the court on the question of costs.
ex: This offer is made without prejudice save as to costs and may be referred to on the issue of costs at the conclusion of the trial.

def: Letters written on an open basis that may be placed before the court, as distinct from privileged without-prejudice communications.
ex: Unless expressly marked without prejudice, this letter is open correspondence and may be produced to the court.

def: A formal pre-action letter setting out the claim and demanding a remedy before court proceedings are issued.
ex: Should we not receive your substantive response to this letter before action within 14 days, our client will issue proceedings without further reference to you.

def: A standard opening by which a firm of solicitors identifies the client whom it represents.
ex: We act on behalf of Mrs Patel in connection with the boundary dispute at 14 Elm Road.

def: A formula by which a lawyer relays the client's account of events without personally vouching for its truth.
ex: We are instructed that your client attended the site on 3 March and removed the fencing without consent.

def: A connector used to refer back to an earlier letter, meeting or conversation.
ex: Further to our telephone conversation of yesterday, I now set out our client's position in writing.

def: A client-letter opener introducing formal advice on the matter in hand.
ex: I write to advise you on the merits of the claim and on the likely costs of proceeding to trial.

def: A conventional formula introducing documents physically enclosed with a letter.
ex: Please find enclosed a copy of the executed lease for your records.

word: should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact
def: A conventional closing formula inviting the recipient to seek clarification.
ex: Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact the writer.

word: we should be grateful if you would
def: A formal and courteous way of making a request in professional correspondence.
ex: We should be grateful if you would confirm your client's position by return.

def: A courteous closing indicating that the writer believes the explanation is now complete.
ex: I trust this clarifies matters, but do let me know if you require anything further.

def: A phrase signalling that the action requested must be taken immediately.
ex: We ask that you revert to us as a matter of urgency, given the imminent hearing.

def: At an appropriate but unspecified later time.
ex: We will write to you again in due course, once counsel's advice has been received.

def: A deferential formula introducing a legal argument in a skeleton argument or written submission.
ex: It is respectfully submitted that the judge below erred in law in construing clause 7 of the lease.

def: A pleading connector introducing an argument advanced in addition to, or as an alternative to, the preceding one.
ex: The notice was invalid; further or alternatively, it was served out of time.

def: In pleading usage, meaning in these circumstances or given the matters already stated.
ex: In the premises, the Claimant is entitled to damages for breach of contract.

def: A defence formula denying every allegation that has not been specifically admitted.
ex: Save as expressly admitted herein, the Defendant denies each and every allegation in the Particulars of Claim.

def: To require the opposing party to prove an allegation strictly rather than admitting or denying it.
ex: The Defendant does not admit the alleged loss and puts the Claimant to strict proof thereof.

def: A pleading formula by which a party neither admits nor denies an allegation, thereby requiring it to be proved.
ex: As to paragraph 5, the Defendant is unable to admit or deny the matters alleged and makes no admissions.

word: by reason of the matters aforesaid
def: A causal connector in pleadings meaning because of the matters already set out.
ex: By reason of the matters aforesaid, the Claimant has suffered loss and damage.

word: particulars of which are as follows
def: A phrase introducing an itemised list of the details supporting an allegation.
ex: The Defendant was negligent, particulars of which are as follows.

def: A pleading formula giving notice of a document or fact that will be relied on at trial.
ex: For its full terms and effect, the Claimant will rely on the agreement at trial.

def: The concluding part of a pleading setting out the remedies sought from the court.
ex: The prayer for relief seeks damages, interest pursuant to statute, and costs.

def: A formal opening address by counsel to a senior judge at the outset of submissions.
ex: May it please your Lordship, I appear for the Claimant and my learned friend appears for the Defendant.

def: A courteous advocacy formula prefacing an assertion of what the law or the facts require.
ex: In my respectful submission, the authority relied upon by my friend is distinguishable on its facts.

def: The conventional way in which a barrister refers to opposing counsel in court.
ex: My learned friend has, with respect, misstated the effect of the 1996 Act.

def: An advocacy hedge that politely signals firm disagreement, often more emphatic the more courteous it sounds.
ex: With the greatest respect, that submission cannot be reconciled with the decision in Pepper v Hart.

def: A formula by which counsel identifies the solicitors or client on whose behalf they appear.
ex: I am instructed by the Respondent, and I am grateful to your Lordship for accommodating this application.

word: if I may take your Lordship to
def: An advocacy formula directing the judge to a particular document or passage in the bundle.
ex: If I may take your Lordship to page 47 of the bundle, the relevant clause appears at the foot of the page.

word: unless I can assist the court further
def: A closing formula by which counsel signals that their submissions are at an end.
ex: Those are my submissions and, unless I can assist the court further, that concludes my argument.

def: A courtesy used by counsel to acknowledge the court's rulings, guidance or indulgence.
ex: I am grateful, my Lord; I shall move directly to the question of quantum.

def: The arbitrator or panel of arbitrators determining a dispute referred to arbitration.
ex: The Tribunal is respectfully invited to dismiss the counterclaim in its entirety.

def: The initiating document by which a claimant commences arbitral proceedings under most institutional rules.
ex: The Claimant filed its Request for Arbitration with the Secretariat on 12 January.

def: The legal, as opposed to merely physical, place of an arbitration, which fixes the governing procedural law.
ex: The parties have agreed that the seat of the arbitration shall be London, notwithstanding that hearings may be held in Paris.

def: A deferential arbitration formula introducing the responding party's argument to the Tribunal.
ex: The Respondent respectfully submits that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over the additional claims.

def: A formal connector meaning as a result of what has just been stated.
ex: The condition precedent was not satisfied; accordingly, no obligation to make payment arose.

def: A connector introducing an argument that holds regardless of whether the preceding point succeeds.
ex: The notice was valid; in any event, any defect was waived by the Defendant's subsequent conduct.

word: for the reasons set out above
def: A connector referring back to arguments already made as the basis for a conclusion.
ex: For the reasons set out above, the application should be dismissed with costs.

def: The imposition and compulsory collection of a tax, or the sum so raised.
ex: The government introduced a temporary levy on windfall profits in the energy sector.

def: An additional charge or tax imposed on top of an existing liability.
ex: Late filers incurred a surcharge of five per cent on the outstanding balance.

def: The deduction of tax at source from a payment before it reaches the recipient.
ex: Cross-border royalties were subject to a fifteen per cent withholding at source.

def: The transfer of money, especially foreign income brought into a jurisdiction where it may become taxable.
ex: Non-domiciled residents are taxed only on the remittance of their overseas earnings.

def: Tax that remains unpaid after its due date.
ex: Interest continued to accrue on the arrears until the debt was finally cleared.

def: Capable of being subtracted from gross income in computing taxable profit.
ex: Only expenses incurred wholly for the trade are deductible against its profits.

def: Permitted by the tax code as a deduction against income.
ex: The tribunal held that the entertainment costs were not an allowable expense.

def: Liable to be evaluated and charged to tax.
ex: The premium formed part of the tenant's assessable income for the year.

def: Subject to a tax charge.
ex: The disposal of the shares gave rise to a chargeable gain of forty thousand pounds.

def: Subject to taxation.
ex: After deducting allowances, her taxable income fell within the basic-rate band.

def: The recognition of income or expense when it is earned or incurred rather than when cash changes hands.
ex: On the accrual basis, the interest is taxed in the year it arises, not when it is received.

def: The systematic writing-off of the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life.
ex: The amortisation of the acquired goodwill was deductible under the intangibles regime.

def: The allocation of the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life for tax or accounting purposes.
ex: Accounting depreciation is added back and replaced by statutory capital allowances.

def: The division of income or a tax base between jurisdictions or persons.
ex: The multinational's profits were divided among the states by a formulary apportionment.

def: A statutory release from a tax that would otherwise apply.
ex: Charities enjoy a broad exemption from tax on income applied for charitable purposes.

def: A repayment of tax that has already been paid.
ex: Overpaying through the year, she was entitled to a rebate once the return was filed.

def: A reduction in tax liability granted by statute.
ex: Business asset disposal relief reduced the rate charged on the entrepreneur's gain.

def: An amount of income or expenditure that may be set against tax.
ex: Each taxpayer may earn up to the personal allowance before any income tax is due.

def: The postponement of a tax liability to a later period.
ex: The rollover allowed a deferral of the gain until the replacement asset was sold.

def: The deferral of a gain achieved by reinvesting the proceeds in a qualifying replacement asset.
ex: By claiming rollover relief, the farmer postponed tax on the sale of the old land.

def: The adjustment of a tax base or allowance to reflect inflation.
ex: Indexation allowance stripped out the inflationary element of the company's gain.

def: A graduated reduction of a relief or allowance as a value rises.
ex: The annual allowance is subject to a taper for individuals with very high incomes.

def: The refusal by the revenue authority to permit a claimed deduction.
ex: The disallowance of the interest deduction substantially increased the assessment.

def: The illegal non-payment or underpayment of tax.
ex: Concealing the offshore accounts amounted to deliberate evasion and attracted criminal charges.

def: The cancellation or waiver of a tax or penalty otherwise due.
ex: The authority agreed a partial remission of the penalty given the reasonable excuse.

def: The connection between a taxpayer and a jurisdiction sufficient to justify taxation.
ex: A warehouse in the state created enough nexus to trigger a sales-tax obligation.

def: A system that attributes corporation tax paid to shareholders as a credit against tax on their dividends.
ex: Under the imputation system, franked dividends carried a credit for the underlying tax.

def: The designation of tax revenue for a particular category of expenditure.
ex: The earmarking of the levy for social care reassured a sceptical public.

def: A duty charged on certain goods produced or sold within a country.
ex: Excise on tobacco and alcohol remains an important source of indirect revenue.

def: A tax or duty, especially one levied on imported goods.
ex: Merchants complained that the new impost eroded the margins on imported wine.

def: The compulsory levying of a payment such as a tax, or the payment so demanded.
ex: The pamphleteers denounced the ship money as an unlawful exaction by the Crown.

def: A payment made by one state or person to another as a levy or tax.
ex: The conquered provinces were required to render an annual tribute to the empire.

def: A tax charged on goods, transactions or documents.
ex: Stamp duty is charged on the transfer of land above the threshold.

def: A legal process by which a debtor's wages or funds are attached to satisfy a tax debt.
ex: Following the judgment, the authority sought garnishment of the taxpayer's bank balance.

def: A monetary sanction imposed for a breach of tax obligations.
ex: Careless inaccuracy in the return exposed the taxpayer to a penalty of thirty per cent.

def: The ultimate distribution of a tax's economic burden among those who actually bear it.
ex: Although employers remit the contribution, its incidence often falls on workers' wages.

def: Of a tax, taking a larger proportion of income from lower earners than from higher earners.
ex: Consumption taxes are widely criticised as regressive because the poor spend a larger share of income.

def: Of a tax, rising in rate as the taxable amount increases.
ex: A progressive income tax charges higher marginal rates on successive bands of income.

def: The degree to which a tax system's rates rise with income.
ex: Flattening the higher bands would markedly reduce the progressivity of the system.

def: The responsiveness of tax revenue to growth in the underlying tax base or economy.
ex: Strong wage growth improved the buoyancy of income-tax receipts.

def: The corporate restructuring by which a company relocates its tax residence to a lower-tax jurisdiction.
ex: Congress tightened the rules to deter inversion through nominal foreign mergers.

def: An entity used to channel income through a jurisdiction so as to obtain a tax advantage.
ex: The holding company was a mere conduit interposed to access the treaty benefits.

def: An entity whose income is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than at entity level.
ex: As a pass-through, the partnership itself paid no tax and its profits were taxed on the partners.

def: Relating to government revenue, taxation and public finance.
ex: The measure was introduced for fiscal reasons rather than any economic purpose.

def: Taxation levied directly on the income, profits or gains of the person or entity that ultimately bears the burden.
ex: Corporation tax and income tax are the principal forms of direct taxation borne by the group.

def: Taxation charged on transactions or consumption and collected by an intermediary who passes the cost on to the final consumer.
ex: VAT and excise duties are the main heads of indirect taxation affecting the retail division.

def: The lawful arrangement of one's affairs to minimise the tax due, though it may be challenged where it defeats the purpose of the legislation.
ex: The scheme was marketed as legitimate tax avoidance but was struck down under the anti-abuse rule.

def: The rules governing the prices charged on transactions between associated enterprises within a multinational group.
ex: The transfer pricing adjustment increased the UK subsidiary's taxable profits by several million pounds.

def: The standard requiring that intra-group transactions be priced as if the parties were independent and dealing on open-market terms.
ex: The pricing failed the arm's length principle because no unconnected buyer would have paid such a royalty.

def: A deduction from taxable profits given for qualifying capital expenditure on assets such as plant and machinery.
ex: The new production line qualified for a first-year capital allowance of one hundred per cent.

def: The amount of profit, after statutory adjustments to the accounting figure, on which tax is actually charged.
ex: Disallowable entertainment costs must be added back in computing the taxable profit.

def: The total amount of income, assets or transactions on which a particular tax is levied.
ex: Broadening the tax base allowed the government to lower the headline rate.

def: Tax deducted at source from a payment such as interest, dividends or royalties and remitted to the authority by the payer.
ex: A fifteen per cent withholding tax was deducted from the cross-border royalty payment.

def: The imposition of comparable taxes by two or more jurisdictions on the same income or gain of the same taxpayer.
ex: A treaty credit was available to relieve the double taxation of the branch profits.

def: A bilateral agreement allocating taxing rights between two states and providing relief from double taxation.
ex: Under the double tax treaty, the withholding rate on dividends was reduced to five per cent.

def: A fixed place of business through which a foreign enterprise's activities are wholly or partly carried on, creating a taxable presence in that state.
ex: The dependent agent's habitual authority to conclude contracts created a permanent establishment in France.

def: The jurisdiction with which a person or company is sufficiently connected to be liable to tax on its worldwide income there.
ex: The company's tax residence turned on where its central management and control were exercised.

def: The gain arising on the disposal of an asset that is subject to capital gains tax after deducting allowable costs and reliefs.
ex: The sale of the warehouse produced a chargeable gain of two million pounds.

def: An item of expenditure that the legislation permits to be set against income or gains in computing the tax charge.
ex: Interest incurred wholly for the trade is an allowable deduction against trading profits.

def: Expenditure that, though charged in the accounts, cannot be deducted in computing taxable profits.
ex: Client entertaining is disallowable expenditure and must be added back to the accounting profit.

def: The VAT a business incurs on its purchases, which it may generally recover from the revenue authority.
ex: The developer could not recover the input tax attributable to its exempt residential lettings.

def: The VAT a business charges on its taxable supplies of goods and services to its customers.
ex: Output tax on the quarter's sales exceeded recoverable input tax, so a payment was due.

def: Describing a taxable supply charged to VAT at nil per cent, so that related input tax remains recoverable.
ex: Most food and children's clothing are zero-rated, allowing the supplier to reclaim its input tax.

def: A supply on which no output tax is charged and for which the supplier cannot recover the related input tax.
ex: Because insurance is an exempt supply, the broker could not reclaim VAT on its overheads.

def: A tax charged on the production or sale of specific goods such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel.
ex: Excise duty on the imported spirits was payable when the goods left the bonded warehouse.

def: A tax charged on certain documents or transactions, notably transfers of land and, historically, of shares.
ex: Stamp duty land tax was payable on the acquisition of the commercial premises.

def: A statutory provision empowering the revenue authority to counteract tax advantages arising from abusive arrangements.
ex: The general anti-abuse rule allowed HMRC to disregard the artificial steps inserted to create a loss.

def: The principle that a transaction is taxed according to its true commercial reality rather than its legal labelling.
ex: Applying substance over form, the tribunal treated the loan as a disguised distribution of profits.

def: A low-taxed foreign subsidiary whose profits may be attributed to and taxed in the hands of its parent under anti-deferral rules.
ex: The diverted profits fell within the controlled foreign company charge and were apportioned to the UK parent.

def: The excessive funding of a company by intra-group debt rather than equity, often to strip taxable profits through deductible interest.
ex: The thin capitalisation rules restricted the interest deduction to an arm's length amount.

def: The reduction of a country's tax base through the shifting of profits to lower-tax jurisdictions.
ex: The OECD's project targets base erosion and profit shifting by multinational groups.

def: The relocation of taxable profits from high-tax to low-tax jurisdictions, typically through intra-group pricing or financing.
ex: Routing royalties through a low-tax holding company was a classic instance of profit shifting.

def: A jurisdiction offering very low or nil taxation and often secrecy, used to reduce a group's overall tax burden.
ex: The intangibles were parked in a tax haven to shelter the licensing income from tax.

def: A mechanism allowing losses of one company in a group to be surrendered to and set against the profits of another.
ex: The loss-making subsidiary surrendered its trading losses to the parent by way of group relief.

def: A relief deferring the tax on a gain where the disposal proceeds are reinvested in qualifying replacement business assets.
ex: By reinvesting in new premises, the company claimed rollover relief and deferred the chargeable gain.

def: A relief that reduces the tax otherwise due according to how long an asset was held or how long the donor survived after making a gift.
ex: Taper relief reduced the inheritance tax on the lifetime gift because the donor survived six years.

def: The purposive approach under which a series of preordained, self-cancelling steps in a tax scheme is viewed as a single composite transaction.
ex: Under the Ramsay principle, the court disregarded the circular payments and taxed the true end result.

def: Arrangements, often using loans or trusts, that channel reward for employment in a form intended to escape income tax and national insurance.
ex: The loan scheme was attacked as disguised remuneration and the sums were treated as taxable earnings.

def: An arrangement agreed in advance with a tax authority fixing the transfer pricing method for specified intra-group transactions.
ex: The group secured an advance pricing agreement to give certainty over its intercompany royalty rate.

def: The total amount of tax that a person or company is legally obliged to pay for a given period.
ex: After reliefs, the group's corporation tax liability for the year fell to under a million pounds.

def: The formal determination by a tax authority of the amount of tax due from a taxpayer.
ex: The taxpayer appealed the assessment on the ground that the profits had been overstated.

def: The transaction or occurrence that triggers a liability to a particular tax.
ex: The surrender of the life policy was the chargeable event giving rise to the income tax charge.

def: Relating to or arising from a delict.
ex: The parties disputed whether the claim sounded in contract or in delictual liability for negligent misstatement.

def: Failing to exercise the standard of care that a reasonable person would have shown.
ex: The surgeon was found negligent for leaving a swab inside the patient after the operation.

def: An unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or with a public right.
ex: The persistent fumes from the factory amounted to a private nuisance affecting the neighbouring householders.

def: Defamation expressed in a permanent form, typically written, printed or broadcast.
ex: Because the statement appeared in print, the claim was pleaded in libel rather than slander.

def: Defamation expressed in a transient form, typically spoken words or gestures.
ex: The remarks made aloud at the meeting founded an action in slander, which generally requires proof of special damage.

def: A statement whose defamatory meaning arises only from extrinsic facts known to those to whom it is published.
ex: By way of innuendo the claimant argued that readers aware of his profession would understand the words as an accusation of fraud.

def: The making of false and malicious statements intended to damage a person's reputation.
ex: The politician denounced the leaflet as a calumny designed to destroy his standing before the election.

def: To speak falsely or maliciously of a person so as to injure their reputation.
ex: He sued the columnist who had traduced him as a swindler before a national readership.

def: To defame or disparage a person by making abusive or belittling statements.
ex: The broadcast sought to vilify the claimant as corrupt, and the jury awarded substantial damages.

def: A false statement that denigrates another's goods, title or business, causing economic loss.
ex: The rival's advertisement amounted to malicious disparagement of the claimant's products.

def: The tort of knowingly making a false representation intending that another rely on it to their detriment.
ex: The investor recovered in deceit after showing that the promoter had lied about the company's turnover.

def: The failure to perform an act that one is under a legal duty to do.
ex: Liability for pure nonfeasance is rare, since the common law seldom imposes a duty to act positively.

def: A direct and unjustified interference with another's person, land or goods.
ex: Walking across the fenced field without permission constituted a trespass to land actionable without proof of damage.

def: A person who enters land or interferes with property without lawful authority or permission.
ex: An occupier owes even a trespasser a limited duty in respect of dangers of which he is aware.

def: The tort of dealing with another's goods in a manner inconsistent with that person's rights of ownership.
ex: By selling the borrowed equipment as his own, the defendant committed conversion and was liable for its full value.

def: The historical form of action for damages for the wrongful conversion of goods.
ex: At common law an owner deprived of his chattel would bring trover to recover its value.

def: The person to whom goods are entrusted under a bailment.
ex: As bailee of the vehicle, the garage bore the burden of explaining how it came to be damaged.

def: The intentional and unlawful application of force to another person.
ex: Even the slightest unwanted touching may amount to a battery if it is hostile and without consent.

def: The tort or crime of maliciously maiming or disabling another person.
ex: The old law of mayhem addressed injuries that deprived a man of the limbs needed to defend himself.

def: Describing a duty for which a party remains liable even where performance is entrusted to another.
ex: An employer's nondelegable duty to provide a safe system of work cannot be discharged merely by hiring a competent contractor.

def: The causal link between the defendant's breach and the claimant's damage.
ex: Even a clear breach of duty is not actionable unless causation is established on the balance of probabilities.

def: The extent to which a reasonable person could have anticipated the harm that occurred.
ex: The reasonable foreseeability of the injury determined both the existence of a duty and the scope of liability.

def: Being the direct and effective cause of an injury in an unbroken sequence of events.
ex: The court identified the driver's inattention as the proximate cause of the collision.

def: Describing a later event that intervenes so as to break the chain of causation.
