def: One of the three roughly equal three-month periods into which a pregnancy is divided.
ex: Nausea usually eases once a woman moves into the second trimester.

def: The descent of the foetal head into the pelvis in the weeks before labour, easing pressure on the ribs.
ex: After the lightening, she found it easier to breathe but needed to pass urine more often.

def: The upper rounded part of the uterus, farthest from the cervix, palpated to gauge growth.
ex: She measured from the fundus to the pubic bone to check the baby was growing as expected.

def: The point at which the widest part of the presenting foetal head has passed into the pelvic brim.
ex: On palpation the head was two-fifths palpable, indicating good engagement.

def: The crown of the foetal head, whose presentation is the most favourable position for birth.
ex: With the vertex presenting and the head well flexed, labour was allowed to continue.

def: Relating to the head; used of a foetus lying head-downwards ready for birth.
ex: By thirty-seven weeks the foetus had turned to a cephalic lie.

def: A soft, temporary swelling on the foetal scalp caused by pressure during labour.
ex: The caput felt on vaginal examination made it harder to identify the exact position of the head.

def: The amniotic fluid surrounding the foetus within the membranes.
ex: When the membranes ruptured, the liquor was clear and there was no sign of concern.

def: The dark green, sticky first stool passed by a newborn, sometimes seen in the liquor during labour.
ex: The presence of meconium in the liquor prompted closer monitoring of the foetal heart.

def: The process of artificially starting labour rather than waiting for it to begin on its own.
ex: Because she was well past her due date, an induction of labour was offered.

def: A tear or jagged wound in the tissues, such as a perineal tear sustained during birth.
ex: She sustained a minor perineal laceration that was repaired shortly after delivery.

def: The natural rotation of the foetal head after it is born, realigning it with the shoulders.
ex: Following restitution, the midwife guided the delivery of the anterior shoulder.

def: The gradual return of the uterus to its non-pregnant size after birth.
ex: Daily palpation showed steady involution, with the fundus descending as expected.

def: The period of about six weeks after childbirth during which the mother's body recovers.
ex: Careful observation during the puerperium helps detect problems such as infection early.

def: The production and secretion of milk from the breasts to feed an infant.
ex: The lactation consultant helped her find a comfortable position for feeding.

def: The way a baby takes the breast into the mouth to feed effectively.
ex: A poor latch was causing her nipples to become sore, so we adjusted the baby's position.

def: The white, waxy coating that protects the skin of the foetus in the womb and may remain at birth.
ex: There was still a little vernix in the baby's skin creases, which we left in place.

def: The fine, soft hair that covers a foetus and is often still present on a preterm baby.
ex: The preterm infant was covered in fine lanugo across the shoulders and back.

def: A soft membranous gap between the bones of a newborn's skull that later closes.
ex: The anterior fontanelle felt soft and flat, which was a reassuring finding.

def: A dangerous lack of oxygen supply to the tissues, of particular concern around the time of birth.
ex: The team was prepared to act quickly to prevent asphyxia if the baby did not breathe at once.

def: The condition of being born before the completion of thirty-seven weeks of gestation.
ex: The complications of prematurity meant the baby needed care in the neonatal unit.

def: The stage at which a foetus is developed enough to be capable of surviving outside the womb.
ex: The parents were counselled sensitively about viability given the very early gestation.

def: A lack of normal muscle tone, as when the uterus fails to contract firmly after birth.
ex: Uterine atony was suspected when the fundus felt soft and bleeding continued.

def: The premature separation of a normally sited placenta from the wall of the uterus.
ex: Sudden abdominal pain and bleeding raised concern about a placental abruption.

def: The slipping down of a body part from its normal position, as when the umbilical cord descends ahead of the foetus.
ex: A cord prolapse is an emergency because pressure on the cord can compromise the baby.

def: Difficult or obstructed labour, such as when the shoulders fail to deliver easily after the head.
ex: The midwife called for help and began manoeuvres the moment shoulder dystocia was recognised.

def: A transient drop in the foetal heart rate seen on the trace, which may be a sign of stress.
ex: Repeated late decelerations on the trace prompted the midwife to escalate to the obstetric team.

def: A grating, crackling or grinding sensation felt or heard when roughened articular surfaces or fractured bone ends move against each other.
ex: Palpating the arthritic knee, she detected coarse crepitus as the patient slowly flexed the joint.

def: A bony outgrowth or spur that forms at the margins of a joint in response to degenerative change.
ex: The lateral radiograph revealed marginal osteophytes bridging two adjacent vertebral bodies.

def: Inflammation at the site where a tendon, ligament or joint capsule inserts into bone.
ex: Achilles enthesitis is a hallmark of the spondyloarthropathies and often heralds ankylosing spondylitis.

def: Inflammation of the synovial membrane lining a joint, typically producing swelling, warmth and effusion.
ex: Ultrasound confirmed active synovitis with hypervascularity on power Doppler in the affected wrist.

def: An abnormal layer of inflammatory granulation tissue that invades and erodes cartilage and bone in rheumatoid arthritis.
ex: Histology of the resected joint showed aggressive pannus overgrowing the denuded articular cartilage.

def: Active resorption and dissolution of bone tissue, often seen around loosened prostheses or in malignancy.
ex: Periprosthetic osteolysis around the acetabular cup necessitated a complex revision arthroplasty.

def: A fragment of dead bone that has become separated from healthy bone, characteristic of chronic osteomyelitis.
ex: Surgical debridement removed the avascular sequestrum harbouring the persistent infection.

def: A sheath of new bone laid down by the periosteum around a sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
ex: The radiograph showed a dense involucrum encasing the necrotic diaphyseal sequestrum.

def: Inflammation of the periosteum, the fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of bone.
ex: Repetitive loading in the recruit produced tibial periostitis, presenting as shin pain on exertion.

def: Inflammation of a tendon together with its surrounding synovial sheath.
ex: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the first dorsal compartment tendons at the radial styloid.

def: A degenerative or overuse disorder of a tendon characterised by pain, swelling and impaired function.
ex: Chronic Achilles tendinopathy responded better to eccentric loading than to corticosteroid injection.

def: Inflammation of the fascia, the connective-tissue sheet enveloping muscles and other structures.
ex: Plantar fasciitis classically produces sharp inferior heel pain worst with the first steps of the morning.

def: Inflammation of a bursa, the fluid-filled sac that cushions bone from overlying soft tissue.
ex: Olecranon bursitis produced a tense, fluctuant swelling over the point of the elbow.

def: Softening and degeneration of articular cartilage, most often affecting the undersurface of the patella.
ex: Arthroscopy graded the chondromalacia of the patellar facet as fibrillation with early fissuring.

def: Inflammation or avascular disturbance affecting both bone and its overlying cartilage, often near a growth centre.
ex: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle can shed a fragment into the joint as a loose body.

def: A skeletal disorder of low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration that increases fragility and fracture risk.
ex: Postmenopausal osteoporosis had rendered her vertebrae susceptible to atraumatic compression fractures.

def: The formation and development of bone tissue.
ex: Osteogenesis imperfecta arises from mutations affecting type I collagen, yielding brittle bones.

def: A bone-forming cell that synthesises and secretes the organic matrix which subsequently mineralises.
ex: Parathyroid hormone given intermittently stimulates osteoblast activity and bone formation.

def: A large multinucleated cell responsible for the resorption of bone tissue.
ex: Bisphosphonates suppress osteoclast-mediated resorption, tilting the balance toward bone retention.

def: A mature bone cell embedded within a lacuna in the mineralised matrix that senses mechanical strain.
ex: Osteocytes act as the mechanosensory network orchestrating skeletal adaptation to loading.

def: A small beam-like strut of cancellous bone forming the internal lattice that resists mechanical stress.
ex: In osteoporosis the trabeculae thin and lose their connectivity, weakening the vertebral body.

def: The elongated cylindrical shaft or central portion of a long bone.
ex: The transverse fracture traversed the mid-diaphysis of the femur.

def: The flared region of a long bone between the shaft and the growth plate, rich in trabecular bone.
ex: Acute osteomyelitis in children characteristically seeds the vascular metaphysis of long bones.

def: The rounded end of a long bone, separated from the shaft by the growth plate until skeletal maturity.
ex: A slipped capital femoral epiphysis displaces the femoral head posteroinferiorly on the neck.

def: The cartilaginous growth plate near the end of a growing long bone where longitudinal growth occurs.
ex: Fractures traversing the physis risk premature closure and subsequent limb-length discrepancy.

def: The tough vascular connective-tissue membrane covering the outer surface of bone except at joints.
ex: Elevation of the periosteum by pus produced the classic radiographic sign of an involucrum.

def: The thin cellular membrane lining the inner medullary cavity and trabecular surfaces of bone.
ex: Remodelling proceeds along the endosteum as osteoclasts widen the marrow cavity with age.

def: A bony outgrowth or process that serves as a site of tendon or muscle attachment and has its own ossification centre.
ex: Traction on the tibial tuberosity apophysis underlies the adolescent condition of Osgood-Schlatter disease.

def: A fibrous joint in which two bones are united by an interosseous ligament or membrane.
ex: A high ankle sprain disrupts the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and often requires screw fixation.

def: A slightly movable cartilaginous joint in which the bones are joined by fibrocartilage.
ex: Widening of the pubic symphysis beyond ten millimetres suggests an unstable pelvic ring injury.

def: A ball-and-socket synovial joint permitting movement in multiple planes, such as the hip or shoulder.
ex: The glenohumeral enarthrosis sacrifices bony stability for an exceptional range of movement.

def: The surgical fusion of a joint to relieve pain or provide stability.
ex: When arthroplasty is unsuitable, ankle arthrodesis remains a durable option for end-stage arthritis.

def: The surgical reconstruction or replacement of a joint to restore movement and relieve pain.
ex: Total hip arthroplasty transformed the management of disabling coxarthrosis.

def: A surgical procedure in which a bone is cut to shorten, lengthen or realign it.
ex: A high tibial osteotomy redistributes load away from the arthritic medial compartment of the knee.

def: Surgical removal of the vertebral lamina to decompress the spinal cord or nerve roots.
ex: Decompressive laminectomy relieved the neurogenic claudication caused by lumbar canal stenosis.

def: Surgical excision of part or all of an intervertebral disc, usually to relieve nerve compression.
ex: Microdiscectomy removed the herniated fragment impinging on the traversing S1 nerve root.

def: Aspiration of fluid from a joint with a needle, for diagnosis or therapeutic relief.
ex: Urgent arthrocentesis of the hot swollen knee yielded turbid fluid teeming with crystals.

def: A partial or incomplete dislocation in which the joint surfaces remain in some contact.
ex: Atlantoaxial subluxation is a feared complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

def: Abnormal separation of two normally adjacent bones or of the parts of a single bone.
ex: Diastasis of the distal tibiofibular joint widened the ankle mortise on the weight-bearing film.

def: Describing a fracture in which the bone is broken into three or more fragments.
ex: The comminuted calcaneal fracture from the fall demanded meticulous reconstruction of the joint surface.

def: The forcible tearing away of a fragment of bone at the site where a tendon or ligament attaches.
ex: A sudden hamstring contraction caused an avulsion of the ischial tuberosity apophysis in the sprinter.

def: Denoting an incomplete fracture in which one cortex breaks while the other bends, typical of children.
ex: The child's forearm showed a greenstick fracture with an intact but bowed volar cortex.

def: The bridging tissue, initially cartilaginous and later ossified, that forms at a fracture site during healing.
ex: Abundant callus visible at six weeks confirmed that the fracture was uniting satisfactorily.

def: The healing of a fracture in a deformed, angulated or rotated position.
ex: The neglected distal radius fracture healed in malunion, leaving a prominent dorsal deformity.

def: The failure of a fractured bone to heal within the expected time, with no prospect of doing so without intervention.
ex: The atrophic nonunion of the scaphoid required bone grafting and rigid internal fixation.

def: A permanent shortening and fixed tightening of muscle, tendon or other soft tissue producing joint deformity.
ex: Dupuytren contracture progressively flexed the ring and little fingers into the palm.

def: A fine, involuntary, spontaneous twitching of a group of muscle fibres visible beneath the skin.
ex: Widespread fasciculations with wasting raised the spectre of motor neurone disease.

def: The breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing myoglobin and other contents into the circulation, threatening the kidneys.
ex: After the crush injury, rising creatine kinase and dark urine signalled rhabdomyolysis.

def: Any primary disease of muscle tissue characterised by weakness, usually of the proximal muscles.
ex: Statin-induced myopathy typically presents with proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase.

def: Inflammation of muscle tissue, whether autoimmune, infectious or drug-induced.
ex: Myositis ossificans denotes heterotopic bone formation within a muscle after blunt trauma.

def: A progressive, usually inherited disorder marked by degeneration and weakening of muscle tissue.
ex: Duchenne muscular dystrophy stems from mutations abolishing functional dystrophin.

def: An excessive outward curvature of the thoracic spine producing a rounded or hunched back.
ex: Multiple osteoporotic wedge fractures had accentuated the patient's thoracic kyphosis.

def: A break in the continuity of a bone.
ex: The X-ray confirmed a fracture of the distal radius following the fall.

def: A fracture in which the broken bone does not pierce the skin.
ex: She sustained a closed fracture of the tibia, so there was no wound to dress.

def: A fracture in which the broken bone breaks through the skin, carrying a high risk of infection.
ex: The open fracture was irrigated in theatre and covered with a sterile dressing.

def: A fracture in which the bone is broken into three or more fragments.
ex: The comminuted fracture of the femur required internal fixation with a plate and screws.

def: An incomplete fracture in which the bone bends and cracks on one side, seen mainly in children.
ex: The paediatric registrar diagnosed a greenstick fracture of the forearm in the six-year-old.

def: A thin, incomplete crack in a bone that may not be visible on initial imaging.
ex: A hairline fracture of the scaphoid was only picked up on the repeat X-ray two weeks later.

def: A fracture in which the bone fragments have moved out of their normal alignment.
ex: The displaced fracture needed manipulation under anaesthetic to restore alignment.

def: A fracture that occurs in bone weakened by underlying disease such as cancer or osteoporosis.
ex: A pathological fracture through the vertebra raised suspicion of metastatic disease.

def: The complete displacement of a bone from its normal position in a joint.
ex: The anterior shoulder dislocation was reduced in the emergency department under sedation.

def: To realign the ends of a broken bone into their correct position.
ex: The orthopaedic team reduced the fracture and applied a backslab.

def: An injury caused by the stretching or tearing of a ligament.
ex: She has a grade two ankle sprain and should rest, ice and elevate the joint.

def: An injury caused by the overstretching or tearing of a muscle or tendon.
ex: The patient presented with a hamstring strain sustained while sprinting.

def: A band of fibrous tissue that connects two bones and stabilises a joint.
ex: An MRI scan showed a complete rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament.

def: A tough band of tissue that attaches muscle to bone.
ex: The Achilles tendon had ruptured and required surgical repair.

def: Firm connective tissue that cushions joints and covers the ends of bones.
ex: Years of running had worn away the cartilage in his knee joint.

def: A degenerative joint disease caused by the breakdown of cartilage and underlying bone.
ex: Osteoarthritis of the hip left her with pain and stiffness on walking.

def: An autoimmune disease causing chronic inflammation of the joints, typically symmetrically.
ex: Her rheumatoid arthritis was managed with methotrexate and regular monitoring.

def: The full extent to which a joint can be moved in different directions.
ex: Physiotherapy aims to restore the full range of motion in the affected shoulder.

def: Relating to the ability of a limb to support the body's weight.
ex: The patient remained non-weight-bearing on the left leg for six weeks.

def: To help a patient begin to move or walk again after injury or surgery.
ex: We aim to mobilise the patient the day after hip replacement to prevent complications.

def: A rigid casing applied to a limb to keep a broken bone immobilised while it heals.
ex: A plaster cast was applied and the patient was advised to keep it dry.

def: A rigid support used to immobilise and protect an injured limb or joint.
ex: A wrist splint was fitted to support the sprained joint.

def: The application of a sustained pulling force to a limb to align bones or relieve pressure.
ex: The patient was placed in traction while awaiting surgery for the femoral fracture.

def: The surgical stabilisation of a fracture using plates, screws or rods placed inside the body.
ex: The surgeon performed open reduction and internal fixation of the ankle.

def: A minimally invasive procedure using a camera to inspect and treat the inside of a joint.
ex: A knee arthroscopy was arranged to trim the torn meniscus.

def: The surgical removal of all or part of a limb.
ex: Poorly controlled diabetes led to a below-knee amputation.

def: Treatment that restores movement and function through exercise and manual techniques.
ex: He was referred for physiotherapy to rebuild strength after the fracture healed.

def: Relating to the branch of medicine dealing with the bones, joints and muscles.
ex: The patient was referred to the orthopaedic team for surgical review.

def: An enlargement of a body part caused by inflammation or a build-up of fluid.
ex: There was marked swelling and bruising around the injured ankle.

def: Discolouration of the skin caused by bleeding underneath from a blunt injury.
ex: Extensive bruising over the thigh suggested a significant soft-tissue injury.

def: Difficulty and reduced ease in moving a joint or muscle.
ex: The patient complained of early-morning stiffness lasting over an hour.

def: An abnormal shape or position of a body part.
ex: There was an obvious deformity of the wrist consistent with a Colles' fracture.

def: A sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle.
ex: Muscle spasm in the lower back made it difficult for him to straighten up.

def: Describing a limb that must not bear any of the body's weight.
ex: Keep the ankle non-weight-bearing and use crutches for the next four weeks.

def: The process by which the ends of a fractured bone heal and join together.
ex: Follow-up X-rays showed good union of the fracture at eight weeks.

def: The failure of a fractured bone to heal within the expected time.
ex: Persistent pain and a visible gap on X-ray confirmed non-union of the tibia.

def: Describing a limb that is able to bear the entire weight of the body.
ex: By her final review she was full weight-bearing and walking without aids.

def: A tear in the crescent-shaped cartilage that cushions the knee joint.
ex: A twisting injury on the football pitch left him with a torn meniscus.

def: Pain radiating along the sciatic nerve from the lower back down the leg.
ex: The patient described sciatica shooting from the buttock to the calf.

def: A condition in which the soft centre of a spinal disc pushes out and presses on a nerve.
ex: The MRI confirmed a slipped disc at the L5 to S1 level.

def: To put the body's weight through a limb.
ex: Ask the patient whether they are able to bear weight on the injured leg.

def: Exercises designed to maintain or restore how far a joint can move.
ex: The physiotherapist taught her gentle range-of-movement exercises for the shoulder.

def: A common injury mechanism in which a person breaks a fall with an extended arm.
ex: A fall onto an outstretched hand is the classic cause of a fractured scaphoid.

def: A limitation in how far a joint is able to move.
ex: On examination there was reduced range of motion in the affected knee.

def: Loss of vision in one half of the visual field of one or both eyes, typically from a lesion of the optic pathways.
ex: The right occipital infarct left him with a dense left homonymous hemianopia, so he repeatedly bumped into door frames on his affected side.

def: A neurological condition in which a patient is unaware of or denies their own deficit, such as a paralysis.
ex: Her dense anosognosia meant she insisted her plegic left arm was working perfectly and refused to engage with rehabilitation.

def: An inability to carry out learned purposeful movements despite intact motor and sensory function.
ex: The patient's ideomotor apraxia was evident when he could not mime brushing his teeth on command despite normal strength.

def: An inability to recognise or interpret sensory stimuli despite intact sensory pathways.
ex: His visual agnosia was striking: he could describe a key in perfect detail yet had no idea what it was until he held it.

def: A cerebellar impairment in judging distance or range of movement, causing overshooting or undershooting of a target.
ex: On finger-to-nose testing the dysmetria was obvious, with her fingertip consistently overshooting the examiner's target.

def: An impaired ability to perform rapid alternating movements, characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction.
ex: Asked to rapidly pronate and supinate her hand, she showed marked dysdiadochokinesia on the left, pointing to an ipsilateral cerebellar lesion.

def: An exaggeration of the deep tendon reflexes, typically indicating an upper motor neurone lesion.
ex: The brisk hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses localised the lesion above the anterior horn cell.

def: A rhythmic, involuntary series of muscle contractions provoked by sudden stretch, indicating upper motor neurone pathology.
ex: Sustained ankle clonus of more than five beats confirmed the pyramidal tract involvement suggested by her spasticity.

def: A velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone due to an upper motor neurone lesion.
ex: Progressive spasticity in both legs made his gait stiff and scissoring, and he required regular botulinum toxin injections.

def: A sudden, brief, involuntary jerk of a muscle or group of muscles.
ex: The startle-induced myoclonus in a rapidly deteriorating patient prompted urgent testing for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

def: A movement disorder characterised by sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal postures or repetitive movements.
ex: Her cervical dystonia pulled the head involuntarily to one side, a posture partially relieved by a sensory trick.

def: A movement disorder marked by brief, irregular, non-repetitive involuntary movements that flow from one body part to another.
ex: The fidgety, dance-like chorea of her hands, combined with a family history, pointed towards Huntington's disease.

def: A movement disorder featuring slow, writhing, continuous involuntary movements, usually of the hands and feet.
ex: The child's athetosis produced constant sinuous writhing of the fingers, characteristic of dyskinetic cerebral palsy.

def: A movement disorder of violent, flinging involuntary movements affecting one side of the body, classically from a subthalamic lesion.
ex: The sudden hemiballismus of his right arm and leg followed a small infarct of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

def: Abnormal, involuntary movements, notably those emerging as a complication of long-term levodopa therapy.
ex: After years of levodopa, his Parkinson's disease was complicated by peak-dose dyskinesia with writhing movements of the trunk.

def: An involuntary tendency to take short, accelerating steps while walking, seen in parkinsonism.
ex: His festination made him hurry forward with ever-quickening tiny steps as though chasing his own centre of gravity.

def: The sense of the relative position and movement of one's own body parts, mediated by the dorsal columns.
ex: Loss of proprioception in his feet meant he could only stay upright with his eyes open, giving a positive Romberg sign.

def: Pain provoked by a stimulus that would not normally be painful, such as light touch.
ex: The allodynia was so severe that even the weight of a bedsheet on her feet caused burning pain.

def: An increased sensitivity to pain, in which a normally painful stimulus provokes an exaggerated response.
ex: Central sensitisation produced marked hyperalgesia, so a pinprick that others would barely notice felt excruciating to her.

def: Sharp, often paroxysmal pain arising from a nerve, typically following its anatomical distribution.
ex: His trigeminal neuralgia caused lightning-like jolts of facial pain triggered by shaving or a cold breeze.

def: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root, producing pain, weakness or sensory change in its corresponding dermatome and myotome.
ex: The L5 radiculopathy from a prolapsed disc caused radiating leg pain and weakness of great-toe dorsiflexion.

def: Any pathological process affecting the spinal cord, typically producing upper motor neurone signs below the level of the lesion.
ex: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy explained her spastic gait, brisk leg reflexes and clumsy hands.

def: Loss or destruction of the myelin sheath surrounding nerve fibres, which slows or blocks conduction.
ex: The MRI showed periventricular demyelination consistent with multiple sclerosis.

def: A disorder affecting a single peripheral nerve, often from compression or entrapment.
ex: The commonest mononeuropathy is carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is compressed at the wrist.

def: The zone of hypoperfused but still salvageable brain tissue surrounding the irreversibly damaged core of an infarct.
ex: The goal of thrombolysis is to rescue the ischaemic penumbra before it is recruited into the infarct core.

def: Neuronal injury caused by excessive stimulation of glutamate receptors, leading to calcium overload and cell death.
ex: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity is a key mechanism of neuronal death in the hours following an ischaemic stroke.

def: Sustained narrowing of a blood vessel, which after subarachnoid haemorrhage can cause delayed cerebral ischaemia.
ex: Around day seven after her subarachnoid haemorrhage she deteriorated from cerebral vasospasm.

def: An abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricles of the brain, raising intracranial pressure.
ex: The obstructing tumour caused acute hydrocephalus, and an external ventricular drain was inserted urgently.

def: A disorder in which a fluid-filled cavity forms within the spinal cord, classically causing dissociated sensory loss.
ex: Her syringomyelia produced a cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation while light touch was preserved.

def: Muscular weakness, especially the fatigable weakness of the autoimmune disorder myasthenia gravis.
ex: The fatigable ptosis and diplopia that worsened through the day were classic for myasthenia.

def: The capacity of the nervous system to reorganise its structure and connections in response to experience or injury.
ex: Intensive rehabilitation exploits neuroplasticity, coaxing undamaged cortex to take over functions lost after a stroke.

def: The neural process of encoding and detecting noxious stimuli that may cause tissue damage.
ex: Nociception is the sensory detection of harmful stimuli, distinct from the conscious, emotional experience of pain.

def: An abnormal, often unpleasant sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked, such as burning or tingling.
ex: The painful dysaesthesia in his feet was described as a constant burning laced with electric-shock sensations.

def: A sudden, transient loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, characteristically associated with narcolepsy.
ex: His cataplexy caused his knees to buckle whenever he laughed heartily, without any loss of consciousness.

def: A chronic sleep disorder characterised by overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden attacks of sleep.
ex: Her narcolepsy caused irresistible sleep attacks in the middle of conversations and even while eating.

def: A reduced level of alertness and a blunted response to stimulation, less severe than stupor.
ex: By the time he reached the department his drowsiness had progressed to obtundation, and he roused only to painful stimuli.

def: Dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system, affecting functions such as blood pressure, heart rate and sweating.
ex: The dysautonomia of Guillain-Barré syndrome caused wild swings in blood pressure that demanded intensive monitoring.

def: Relating to or occurring during a seizure or acute neurological event such as a stroke.
ex: The ictal EEG captured rhythmic spike-and-wave discharges precisely as her arm began to jerk.

def: Relating to the period between seizures.
ex: Interictal spikes on the recording supported the diagnosis of epilepsy even though no clinical seizure occurred.

def: Tending to cause or capable of provoking epileptic seizures.
ex: Surgeons aimed to resect the epileptogenic focus in the right temporal lobe while sparing eloquent cortex.

def: Describing an abnormal extensor posturing of the limbs that indicates severe brainstem injury.
ex: The decerebrate posturing, with arms and legs rigidly extended, signalled ominous deterioration and brainstem compression.

def: Describing an abnormal flexor posturing of the arms with leg extension, indicating a lesion above the brainstem.
ex: He showed decorticate posturing, flexing his arms towards his chest in response to a painful stimulus.

def: Relating to the motor system outside the pyramidal tracts, dysfunction of which causes disorders of tone and movement.
ex: The antipsychotic produced extrapyramidal side effects, including a shuffling gait and a resting tremor.

def: Relating to or affecting the opposite side of the body.
ex: A lesion of the right motor cortex produces weakness of the contralateral, left-sided limbs.

def: Relating to or affecting the same side of the body.
ex: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia on the ipsilateral side, so a right-sided lesion produces right-sided incoordination.

def: Wasting or atrophy of muscle tissue, typically from denervation.
ex: The progressive amyotrophy of his hand muscles hollowed out the spaces between the metacarpals.

def: Abnormally reduced muscle tone, often felt as decreased resistance to passive movement.
ex: The floppy infant's marked hypotonia prompted investigation for a neuromuscular cause.

def: Describing a remote effect of a tumour on the nervous system, mediated by immune or hormonal factors rather than direct invasion.
ex: Her rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome proved to be paraneoplastic, driven by antibodies against an occult breast cancer.

def: A neurodegenerative disease characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau protein in the brain.
ex: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a tauopathy, its neurons clogged by misfolded tau rather than by amyloid.

def: A misfolded, infectious protein particle that propagates by inducing normal proteins to adopt its abnormal conformation.
ex: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by a prion that triggers a fatal, spongiform degeneration of the brain.

def: A sudden loss of brain function caused by an interruption of the blood supply to part of the brain, either by a clot or a bleed.
ex: The patient presented with left-sided weakness and slurred speech, and the CT confirmed an acute ischaemic stroke.

def: A stroke caused by a clot or narrowing that blocks blood flow to part of the brain, depriving it of oxygen.
ex: Because it was an ischaemic stroke within the treatment window, we proceeded with thrombolysis.

def: A stroke caused by bleeding into or around the brain when a blood vessel ruptures.
ex: The scan showed a haemorrhagic stroke, so thrombolysis was absolutely contraindicated.

def: A brief episode of stroke-like symptoms caused by a temporary reduction in blood flow to the brain, with full recovery within twenty-four hours.
ex: Her arm weakness resolved within an hour, and we diagnosed a transient ischaemic attack rather than a completed stroke.

def: Bleeding within the brain tissue itself, often due to hypertension or a ruptured vessel.
ex: The sudden severe headache and rapid deterioration pointed to a cerebral haemorrhage.

def: Bleeding into the space between the brain and the membrane that covers it, classically causing a sudden thunderclap headache.
ex: He described the worst headache of his life, so we urgently ruled out a subarachnoid haemorrhage.

def: A headache of extreme intensity that reaches its peak within seconds, raising concern for a subarachnoid haemorrhage.
ex: A thunderclap headache always warrants urgent imaging to exclude a bleed.

def: A sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain that can cause convulsions, altered awareness or unusual sensations.
ex: The witness said he collapsed and shook for about a minute, which is consistent with a seizure.

def: A chronic neurological condition characterised by a tendency to have recurrent, unprovoked seizures.
ex: After his second unprovoked seizure, she was started on medication for epilepsy.

def: A medical emergency in which a seizure lasts more than five minutes or seizures recur without recovery in between.
ex: He remained convulsing on arrival, so we treated him for status epilepticus with intravenous lorazepam.

def: A generalised seizure with a stiffening phase followed by rhythmic jerking of the limbs, often with loss of consciousness.
ex: The tonic-clonic seizure was followed by a period of confusion and drowsiness.

def: A warning sensation, such as an unusual smell, light or feeling, that precedes a seizure or migraine.
ex: She reported a strange rising sensation in her stomach as an aura before each seizure.

def: Relating to the altered state of consciousness, confusion or drowsiness that follows a seizure.
ex: He was drowsy and disoriented in the postictal period but gradually returned to baseline.

def: A recurrent, often one-sided throbbing headache that may be accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
ex: She takes a triptan at the onset of a migraine and lies down in a dark room.

def: An abnormal sensitivity to light that causes discomfort, common in migraine and meningitis.
ex: The combination of neck stiffness, fever and photophobia raised the suspicion of meningitis.

def: Inflammation of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, usually caused by infection.
ex: The non-blanching rash and neck stiffness made us treat for bacterial meningitis without delay.

def: Resistance and pain on flexing the neck, a classic sign of meningeal irritation.
ex: On examination she had marked neck stiffness and could not touch her chin to her chest.

def: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, most often viral, which can cause confusion, seizures and reduced consciousness.
ex: The altered behaviour and seizures with fever prompted treatment for viral encephalitis.

def: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system damages the protective covering of nerves in the brain and spinal cord.
ex: Her episodes of optic neuritis and limb weakness led to a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

def: A progressive neurological disorder characterised by tremor, rigidity and slowness of movement.
ex: The resting tremor, shuffling gait and mask-like face were typical of Parkinson's disease.

def: An involuntary rhythmic shaking of a part of the body, most often the hands.
ex: The tremor was most noticeable at rest and eased when he reached for an object.

def: An abnormal slowness in initiating and carrying out movements, a cardinal feature of Parkinson's disease.
ex: The bradykinesia made everyday tasks such as buttoning a shirt increasingly difficult.

def: A measurable reduction in mental abilities such as memory, attention or problem-solving.
ex: Formal testing confirmed mild cognitive impairment affecting short-term memory.

def: Complete paralysis of one side of the body, commonly following a stroke.
ex: The stroke left him with a right-sided hemiplegia and no movement in the arm.

def: Weakness rather than complete paralysis affecting one side of the body.
ex: She had a mild left hemiparesis but could still lift the arm against gravity.

def: A loss or impairment of the ability to understand or produce language, usually due to brain damage.
ex: Following the stroke he developed expressive aphasia and struggled to find his words.

def: Slurred or poorly articulated speech caused by weakness or poor control of the muscles used for speaking.
ex: His speech was slurred but grammatically intact, indicating dysarthria rather than aphasia.

def: A partial or complete loss of sensation in a part of the body.
ex: The numbness in her right hand followed the distribution of the median nerve.

def: A lack of muscle coordination that affects gait, balance and fine movements.
ex: His broad-based, unsteady gait and past-pointing were signs of cerebellar ataxia.

def: Double vision, in which a single object is perceived as two images.
ex: The diplopia worsened when he looked to the left, suggesting a nerve palsy.

def: Drooping of the upper eyelid, which may indicate a nerve lesion or a neuromuscular disorder.
ex: The unilateral ptosis and dilated pupil pointed to a third nerve palsy.

def: A change in a patient's alertness and awareness, ranging from drowsiness to unresponsiveness.
ex: The nurse escalated care when she noticed an altered level of consciousness and a falling GCS.

def: A problem with nerve function affecting a specific area, such as weakness, sensory loss or speech difficulty in one region.
ex: The headache alone was reassuring, but any focal neurological deficit would prompt urgent imaging.

def: An abnormal increase in the pressure inside the skull, which can compress the brain and become life-threatening.
ex: The headache worse on lying down, vomiting and papilloedema suggested raised intracranial pressure.

def: Swelling of the optic disc seen on eye examination, indicating raised pressure within the skull.
ex: Fundoscopy revealed bilateral papilloedema, confirming our concern about raised intracranial pressure.

def: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into the lower spine to collect cerebrospinal fluid for testing.
ex: We performed a lumbar puncture to confirm meningitis once imaging excluded raised pressure.

def: The clear fluid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord.
ex: The cerebrospinal fluid was cloudy with a high white cell count, consistent with bacterial meningitis.

def: A procedure to mechanically remove a clot from a large blood vessel, used in selected strokes.
ex: Because a large vessel was occluded, he was transferred urgently for mechanical thrombectomy.

def: The twelve pairs of nerves that emerge directly from the brain and control functions of the head and neck.
ex: We examined the cranial nerves to localise the lesion causing his facial droop.

def: A weakness or sagging on one side of the face, often an early sign of stroke or facial nerve palsy.
ex: Ask the patient to smile and check for facial droop as part of the stroke assessment.

def: Automatic muscle responses to a stimulus, tested to assess the integrity of the nervous system.
ex: The reflexes were brisk in the right leg, suggesting an upper motor neurone lesion.

def: A period during which a person is unaware and unresponsive to their surroundings.
ex: He had a brief loss of consciousness after the collapse but recovered fully within a minute.

def: A reduction in muscle strength that impairs the ability to move a limb normally.
ex: We graded the motor weakness in her arm as three out of five on the power scale.

def: A reduced or absent ability to feel touch, temperature, pain or position in part of the body.
ex: There was sensory loss below the level of the injury, marking the extent of the cord damage.

def: A mild traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head, often with brief confusion or memory loss.
ex: After the fall he had a headache and could not recall the event, consistent with concussion.

def: A localised area of skin and underlying tissue damage caused by sustained pressure over a bony prominence.
ex: The patient has developed a grade 2 pressure ulcer over the sacrum, so I've started two-hourly repositioning.

def: To move a patient into a different position to relieve pressure and reduce the risk of skin breakdown.
ex: We reposition immobile patients at least every two hours to protect the skin.

def: A specialised air or foam mattress that redistributes body weight to prevent pressure damage in high-risk patients.
ex: I've requested a pressure-relieving mattress for bed four as her Waterlow score is high.

def: The state of the skin being intact and healthy without breaks, breakdown, or damage.
ex: On assessment his skin integrity is intact with no signs of redness over the heels.

def: A protective cream applied to the skin to shield it from moisture, urine, or faeces and prevent breakdown.
ex: Apply barrier cream to the perineal area after each episode of incontinence.

def: The routine of inspecting, cleaning, and protecting skin over bony prominences to prevent pressure damage.
ex: Pressure area care is documented four-hourly on the turn chart.

def: The cleaning and moistening of a patient's mouth to maintain oral hygiene and comfort, especially when they are nil by mouth.
ex: She's nil by mouth, so please give mouth care every two hours to keep her lips moist.

def: A wash given to a patient who is confined to bed and unable to bathe themselves.
ex: I'll give him a bed bath before the doctors' round and change his gown.

def: To help a patient carry out personal hygiene and get dressed when they cannot manage independently.
ex: This gentleman needs staff to assist with washing and dressing every morning.

def: The management of a patient's bladder and bowel needs, including toileting, pads, and skin protection.
ex: Continence care includes prompted toileting and regular pad changes to protect her skin.

def: The routine cleaning and monitoring of an indwelling urinary catheter to prevent infection and blockage.
ex: Catheter care is carried out daily and the drainage bag emptied when two-thirds full.

def: A urinary catheter that remains in the bladder and drains urine continuously into a collection bag.
ex: He has an indwelling catheter draining clear urine at around fifty millilitres an hour.

def: A record of a patient's fluid intake and output used to monitor their hydration and renal function.
ex: Please keep a strict fluid balance chart and total it at the end of the shift.

def: The careful measurement and recording of everything a patient takes in and passes out.
ex: The doctor wants strict input and output on this patient while we assess her kidneys.

def: A tube passed through the nose into the stomach for feeding, giving medication, or draining stomach contents.
ex: We passed a nasogastric tube and confirmed placement with a pH test before feeding.

def: The delivery of liquid nutrition directly into the stomach or gut through a tube.
ex: She's on continuous enteral feeding overnight via her nasogastric tube.

def: To draw back stomach contents through a feeding tube to check its position or measure residual volume.
ex: Aspirate the tube and check the pH is below five point five before you start the feed.

def: An evaluation of a patient's ability to swallow safely without the risk of food or fluid entering the airway.
ex: Keep him nil by mouth until speech and language therapy have done a swallow assessment.

def: Drinks thickened to a prescribed consistency to make swallowing safer for patients at risk of aspiration.
ex: The speech therapist has recommended stage two thickened fluids for this patient.

def: To actively promote a patient's eating and drinking to maintain nutrition and hydration.
ex: Please encourage oral intake and record everything she manages on the food chart.

def: A protective covering applied to a wound to promote healing and prevent infection.
ex: The wound dressing is due to be changed today and the surrounding skin looks healthy.

def: To clean a wound and apply a suitable dressing to it.
ex: I'll dress the wound after lunch once the medication round is finished.

def: A method of carrying out a procedure that keeps the area free from contaminating micro-organisms.
ex: Always use an aseptic technique when redressing a central line site.

def: A sample taken from a wound with a sterile applicator to test for infection.
ex: The wound looks infected, so I've taken a wound swab and sent it to the lab.

def: Fluid that leaks from a wound as part of the healing or inflammatory process.
ex: There is a moderate amount of serous exudate soaking through the dressing.

def: Dead, yellowish tissue in a wound bed that needs to be removed for healing to progress.
ex: The wound bed is about fifty per cent slough, so we've applied a debriding dressing.

def: New red, moist connective tissue that forms in a healing wound as a sign of recovery.
ex: There's healthy granulation tissue at the base, so the wound is healing well.

def: The partial or complete reopening of a surgical wound along its incision line.
ex: She has some wound dehiscence at the lower edge, so I've escalated to the surgical team.

def: The safe moving and lifting of patients using correct technique and equipment to prevent injury.
ex: This patient is a two-person manual handling transfer with a slide sheet.

def: A mechanical device used to lift and move patients who cannot bear their own weight.
ex: We'll need the hoist to transfer her from the bed to the chair.

def: A structured evaluation of how likely a patient is to fall so that preventive measures can be put in place.
ex: I've completed a falls risk assessment and put a bed rail and low bed in place.

def: A device kept within a patient's reach so they can summon nursing staff when they need help.
ex: Make sure the call bell is within reach before you leave the bay.

def: A scored assessment tool used to estimate a patient's risk of developing pressure damage.
ex: Her Waterlow score is nineteen, which puts her in the high-risk category.

def: A documented plan setting out a patient's needs, goals, and the nursing interventions required.
ex: I've updated her care plan to reflect the new mobility restrictions.

def: To record an event, observation, or intervention in a patient's clinical record.
ex: Remember to document in the notes that the family were updated this afternoon.

def: The scheduled process of administering prescribed medications to patients across a ward.
ex: I'm just starting the eight o'clock drug round, so I'll be about an hour.

def: To give a patient a prescribed drug by the correct route, dose, and time.
ex: Always check the five rights before you administer any medication.

def: Describing medication that is given as required rather than at fixed times.
ex: Paracetamol is prescribed PRN for pain, up to four times a day.

def: The regular, structured checking of patients to address comfort, pain, position, and personal needs.
ex: During intentional rounding I check the four Ps: pain, position, personal needs, and placement.

def: To inspect the skin over bony areas for early signs of pressure damage.
ex: When you reposition him, check for redness over the heels and sacrum.

def: A phrase used to record that a patient has passed a stool.
ex: Her bowels were open this morning, type four on the stool chart.

def: To urinate, often recorded when monitoring a patient's output.
ex: He hasn't passed urine for eight hours, so I'll do a bladder scan.

def: A documentation phrase indicating a patient is calm, pain-free, and resting well.
ex: The patient was settled and comfortable overnight with no concerns.

def: To ensure a patient drinks enough fluid to maintain adequate hydration.
ex: Offer drinks regularly to keep her hydrated in this warm weather.

def: Having no fever; with a body temperature within the normal range.
ex: By the morning round she was apyrexial and her observations had returned to baseline.

def: A deficiency in the amount of oxygen reaching the body's tissues.
ex: Signs of hypoxia such as restlessness and confusion should always be taken seriously.

def: The percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen in the blood, measured to assess respiratory status.
ex: His oxygen saturation dropped to 88 per cent, so I applied supplemental oxygen and escalated.

def: Sweating profusely, often as a sign of illness or physiological stress.
ex: The patient was pale and diaphoretic, which made me suspect his condition was deteriorating.

def: Having a reduced level of alertness and a dulled responsiveness to stimuli.
ex: The patient became increasingly obtunded, so I performed a neurological assessment and escalated urgently.

def: Relating to or caused by an upright posture, as in a drop in blood pressure on standing.
ex: Her orthostatic hypotension meant I asked her to sit for a moment before mobilising.

def: New connective tissue and tiny blood vessels that form on the surface of a healing wound.
ex: Healthy red granulation tissue at the wound bed was a good sign of healing.

def: The involuntary loss of bladder or bowel control.
ex: Because of her urinary incontinence, I introduced a toileting regime and protective skin care.

def: To empty the bladder of urine.
ex: I asked the patient to void before the procedure and measured the amount passed.

def: The act of passing urine.
ex: She reported burning on micturition, which I documented and reported for review.

def: The production of an abnormally small volume of urine.
ex: His oliguria over the last four hours made me review his fluid balance urgently.

def: The need to wake and pass urine one or more times during the night.
ex: He complained of nocturia, so I ensured a commode was within easy reach overnight.

def: Of a catheter or device, left in place within the body for a period of time.
ex: The indwelling catheter was documented and its insertion date recorded to guide removal.

def: To walk or move about, especially after surgery or a period of bed rest.
ex: I encouraged the patient to ambulate to the door and back to reduce the risk of complications.

def: Of record-keeping, made at the time of, or as soon as possible after, the events described.
ex: Nursing notes must be contemporaneous, so I documented the incident immediately.

def: Free from contaminating micro-organisms, or using a technique that prevents infection.
ex: I redressed the wound using an aseptic technique to reduce the risk of infection.

def: The normal firmness and elasticity of the skin, assessed as an indicator of hydration.
ex: Her reduced skin turgor and dry mucous membranes suggested she was dehydrated.

def: Relating to the heart and blood vessels.
ex: Smoking raises the risk of cardiovascular disease.

def: Relating to breathing and the lungs.
ex: The patient was admitted with a respiratory infection.

def: Relating to the stomach and intestines.
ex: Nausea and diarrhoea point to a gastrointestinal cause.

def: Relating to the muscles and bones.
ex: The back pain was musculoskeletal, not cardiac.

def: Relating to the nerves and the brain.
ex: Slurred speech prompted a neurological assessment.

def: Relating to the kidneys.
ex: Poor urine output raised concern about renal function.

def: Chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart.
ex: The angina came on whenever he exerted himself.

def: An infection that inflames the air sacs of the lungs.
ex: She was treated for pneumonia with intravenous antibiotics.

def: To give a medicine or treatment to a patient.
ex: The nurse administered the injection into the upper arm.

def: To formally order a medicine for a patient.
ex: The doctor prescribed a week's course of antibiotics.

def: To watch a patient's condition closely over time.
ex: Monitor her blood pressure every hour.

def: A thin tube put into a vein to give fluids or medicine.
ex: A cannula was sited in the back of the hand.

def: A covering placed over a wound to protect it.
ex: The dressing was changed daily to keep the wound clean.

def: Skin damage caused by staying in one position too long.
ex: Turning the patient regularly prevents pressure sores.

def: A patient's ability to move around.
ex: Her mobility improved with daily physiotherapy.

def: The record of fluids a patient takes in and passes out.
ex: Keep a strict fluid balance chart for this patient.

def: A sudden beginning of symptoms.
ex: The acute onset of severe headache warranted a scan.

def: Of a disease, able to spread from person to person by contact.
ex: The infection is contagious, so the patient was isolated.

def: A phrase used to introduce a simpler explanation for a patient.
ex: Put simply, the valve isn't closing properly.

def: A polite way to ask a patient to wait a moment.
ex: Bear with me while I check your notes.

def: A senior hospital doctor who is an expert in a field.
ex: The consultant reviewed her on the morning ward round.

def: A doctor training in a speciality, senior to a junior doctor.
ex: Bleep the registrar if his condition changes.

def: A patient who is treated without staying overnight.
ex: She was seen as an outpatient in the fracture clinic.

def: A patient admitted to stay in hospital.
ex: He remained an inpatient for a week after surgery.

def: The room where surgical operations are performed.
ex: The patient was taken to theatre at short notice.

def: To fall down suddenly, often losing consciousness.
ex: A shopper collapsed and was rushed in by ambulance.

def: Not awake and not aware of one's surroundings.
ex: He was unconscious but breathing when found.

def: A feeling of spinning or being off balance.
ex: The dizziness eased once she sat down.

def: An area of red, irritated skin.
ex: A rash spread across the child's chest overnight.

def: Taken by mouth.
ex: Switch him from intravenous to oral antibiotics.

def: Applied directly to the skin or a surface.
ex: A topical cream reduced the inflammation.

def: The slow delivery of fluid or medicine into a vein.
ex: She was started on a fluid infusion.

def: A medicine that fights bacterial infection.
ex: Finish the full course of antibiotics.

def: A device that delivers medicine into the lungs by breathing it in.
ex: Show the patient how to use the inhaler correctly.

def: A warm, open way to check on a patient.
ex: 'How are you feeling this morning?' 'A bit better, thanks.'

def: A gentle, informal way to tell a patient you'll start a treatment.
ex: I'm just going to pop you on some oxygen.

def: An invitation for the patient to report any change.
ex: Let me know if the pain comes back.

def: The standard reassuring warning given before a needle.
ex: Just a sharp scratch now — all done.

def: A letter written to direct a patient to another clinician or service for further assessment or specialist management.
ex: I am enclosing a referral letter for your review of Mr Adams's worsening angina.

def: A letter summarising a patient's admission, treatment and follow-up needs, sent to the receiving clinician on discharge from hospital.
ex: This discharge summary outlines Mrs Lee's inpatient stay and the arrangements made for her ongoing care.

def: A letter accompanying a patient moved from one facility or ward to another, detailing their current status and care requirements.
ex: Please find enclosed a transfer letter as Mr Osei is being moved to your rehabilitation unit today.

def: A standard opening formula used to state the purpose of a referral letter in its first sentence.
ex: I am writing to refer Mr Thomas Grant, a 62-year-old retired teacher, for assessment of a suspicious breast lump.

word: I am writing to update you regarding
def: An opening formula used in an update letter to signal that new information about a patient already known to the reader follows.
ex: I am writing to update you regarding Mrs Patel, whose blood pressure has remained poorly controlled since her last review.

word: I am writing in response to your letter
def: An opening formula used in a response letter to acknowledge and reply to correspondence previously received.
ex: I am writing in response to your letter of 3 May concerning Mr Cole's recurrent chest pain.

def: A courteous opening used in a response letter to acknowledge the colleague who sent the original referral.
ex: Thank you for referring Ms Nguyen, whom I reviewed in clinic on 12 June.

def: The formal salutation used when the recipient's name is known, taking a comma and the surname before the letter body.
ex: Dear Dr Harrison, I am writing to refer a patient under your care.

def: The formal closing used when the recipient has been addressed by name in the salutation.
ex: I look forward to your assessment. Yours sincerely, Dr A. Fields.

def: The formal closing used when the recipient is addressed impersonally, as in Dear Sir or Madam.
ex: Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours faithfully, Dr J. Owens.

def: The subject line placed above the letter body to identify the patient, typically giving name, date of birth and address.
ex: Re: Mrs Dorothy Wells, DOB 14/02/1948, 12 Elm Road.

def: A set phrase used to draw attention to documents accompanying the letter.
ex: Please find enclosed the results of her most recent echocardiogram.

word: I would be grateful if you could
def: A polite request formula used to state the specific action being asked of the recipient.
ex: I would be grateful if you could review his anticoagulation and adjust the dose accordingly.
syn: I would appreciate it if you could

word: do not hesitate to contact me
def: A standard closing courtesy offering further contact, usually preceded by a conditional clause.
ex: Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me.

word: should you require any further information
def: A formal conditional closing offering additional details if the recipient needs them.
ex: Should you require any further information, I would be happy to provide it.

word: I trust this information is sufficient
def: A closing formula expressing confidence that the letter provides enough detail for the recipient to act.
ex: I trust this information is sufficient for you to arrange her outpatient follow-up.

word: for your review and further management
def: A phrase stating that the patient is being handed to the recipient for continued assessment and treatment.
ex: I am therefore referring him to you for your review and further management.

word: I would appreciate your assessment and management
def: A courteous request phrase specifying that the writer wants the recipient to evaluate and treat the patient.
ex: I would appreciate your assessment and management of her deteriorating renal function.

word: your prompt attention would be appreciated
def: A closing phrase used to convey urgency politely when a rapid response is required.
ex: Given the risk of airway compromise, your prompt attention would be appreciated.
syn: I would be grateful for your urgent review

def: A concise way to introduce a patient's relevant chronic conditions within a single sentence.
ex: Mr Reid is a 70-year-old man with a background of ischaemic heart disease and COPD.

def: A phrase identifying a patient with an established, previously diagnosed condition.
ex: She is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis, managed with methotrexate.

def: A standard formulation recording that the patient has no documented drug or other allergies.
ex: She has nil known allergies and takes no regular medication.

def: A phrase introducing the objective findings elicited when the clinician assessed the patient.
ex: On examination, she was afebrile with reduced air entry at the left base.

def: A phrase used in discharge and transfer letters to state the reason for the patient's hospital admission.
ex: Mr Blake was admitted with acute exacerbation of heart failure on 2 June.

def: A working diagnosis stated before confirmatory results are available, often used in referral letters.
ex: My provisional diagnosis is unstable angina, though I would value your opinion.

def: The range of conditions being considered to explain the patient's presentation.
ex: The differential diagnosis includes pulmonary embolism and pneumonia.

def: A formal phrase indicating that a medication or treatment was started during the episode of care.
ex: She was commenced on amoxicillin and showed rapid improvement.

def: Adjusted a drug dose incrementally against the patient's response to achieve the desired effect.
ex: His insulin was titrated according to capillary glucose readings.

def: Became progressively worse, used to describe a decline in the patient's clinical condition.
ex: Despite treatment, her respiratory function deteriorated overnight.

def: The list of drugs the patient is to continue after leaving hospital, set out in a discharge summary.
ex: Her medication on discharge is detailed in the enclosed list.

def: A phrase marking the patient's clinical state or arrangements at the point of leaving hospital.
ex: On discharge, she was mobilising independently and tolerating a normal diet.

def: A phrase referring to the patient's situation or baseline before entering hospital.
ex: Prior to admission, he had been independent in all activities of daily living.

def: A phrase indicating that the patient is scheduled to be seen again at a particular time.
ex: He is due for review in your clinic in two weeks' time.

def: Waiting for something, such as results or an appointment, that is still to come at the time of writing.
ex: She is currently awaiting the results of her CT scan.

def: A formal connector introducing the reason or evidence on which a clinical decision is based.
ex: In view of her recurrent falls, I feel a specialist assessment is warranted.

def: A formal opening connector referring back to previous correspondence or a prior interaction.
ex: Further to our telephone conversation this morning, I am writing to confirm the arrangements.

def: A phrase used to flag a particularly relevant or noteworthy detail to the reader.
ex: Of note, she has a documented allergy to penicillin.

def: The conventional demographic opener used to introduce a patient by age, often followed by occupation or relevant context.
ex: Mrs Iris Bell is a 65-year-old retired nurse who presented with sudden-onset breathlessness.

def: The full story of how the current problem developed.
ex: In the history of the present illness, note when the symptoms began.

def: Substances that cause a harmful immune reaction in the patient.
ex: Always check for allergies before prescribing.

def: When a symptom started and how long it has lasted.
ex: Ask about the onset and duration of the pain.

def: Things that make a symptom worse.
ex: Movement was an aggravating factor for the back pain.

def: Other symptoms occurring alongside the main one.
ex: Associated symptoms included nausea and sweating.

def: To examine a part of the body by feeling it with the hands.
ex: The doctor palpated the abdomen for any masses.

def: Painful when touched or pressed.
ex: The area over the wound was warm and tender.

def: The planned course of treatment and monitoring for a patient.
ex: The management plan included fluids, rest and a review in a week.

def: To send a patient to another professional or service for care.
ex: I am writing to refer this patient to your clinic.

def: Started on a medicine or treatment (formal clinical writing).
ex: The patient was commenced on antibiotics on admission.

def: A polite, formal opener for a request in a professional letter.
ex: I would be grateful if you could review her medication.

def: A formal way to introduce the subject of a letter or note.
ex: With regard to your recent referral, I have arranged a scan.

def: Routine measurements of a patient's vital signs (informally, 'obs').
ex: Her observations have been stable overnight.

def: Of a patient, not getting better or worse; steady.
ex: He remained stable throughout the night.

def: To ease a patient's worry with calm, clear words.
ex: She reassured him that the procedure was routine.

def: To get a patient's informed agreement before a procedure.
ex: Obtain consent before you take the blood sample.

def: Explained simply, without medical jargon, so a patient understands.
ex: In plain terms, the artery is narrowed and needs widening.

def: An abnormal mass of tissue arising from uncontrolled cellular proliferation, which may be benign or malignant.
ex: Imaging revealed a well-circumscribed neoplasm in the left lobe that the pathologist later classified as benign.

def: A malignant tumour arising from epithelial cells lining the skin, organs or glands.
ex: The biopsy confirmed an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast requiring wide local excision.

def: A malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissues such as bone, muscle, fat or cartilage.
ex: Unlike the far commoner carcinomas, a sarcoma originates in connective rather than epithelial tissue.

def: To spread from an original site to form secondary tumours elsewhere in the body.
ex: Melanomas are notorious for their capacity to metastasise early, even from thin primary lesions.

def: The formation of new blood vessels, which tumours co-opt to sustain their growth.
ex: Bevacizumab inhibits angiogenesis by targeting vascular endothelial growth factor, starving the tumour of its blood supply.

def: The loss of cellular differentiation and structural organisation characteristic of aggressive malignancy.
ex: Marked anaplasia on histology, with bizarre mitotic figures, signalled a high-grade, poorly differentiated tumour.

def: The process of abnormal, autonomous new tissue growth underlying tumour formation.
ex: Multiple endocrine neoplasia is an inherited syndrome predisposing to tumours of several glands.

def: A primary brain tumour arising from the glial supporting cells of the nervous system.
ex: Glioblastoma, the most aggressive glioma, carries a dismal median survival despite maximal therapy.

def: A malignant tumour arising from pigment-producing melanocytes, usually of the skin.
ex: An irregular, asymmetric mole with recent colour change was excised and proved to be a melanoma.

def: A tumour derived from immature precursor or embryonic cells, commonest in children.
ex: Neuroblastoma, an aggressive childhood blastoma, arises from primitive sympathetic nervous tissue.

def: The multistep process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer.
ex: Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognised as a driver of carcinogenesis in several organs.

def: A substance or agent capable of causing cancer.
ex: Tobacco smoke contains dozens of chemical carcinogens implicated in lung and bladder cancer.

def: A mutated or overexpressed gene that drives malignant cellular transformation.
ex: Activation of the RAS oncogene locks the cell in a state of continuous proliferative signalling.

def: An agent that induces heritable changes in DNA, often contributing to cancer risk.
ex: Ultraviolet radiation is a potent mutagen, generating the pyrimidine dimers that seed skin cancers.

def: Rapid reproduction and multiplication of cells.
ex: The Ki-67 index quantifies the proportion of cells undergoing proliferation and gauges tumour aggressiveness.

def: The degree to which tumour cells resemble their normal tissue of origin.
ex: Well-differentiated tumours tend to behave less aggressively than those showing poor differentiation.

def: A cancerous growth with the capacity to invade tissue and spread to distant sites.
ex: Weight loss, night sweats and lymphadenopathy raised a strong suspicion of underlying malignancy.

def: The initiation and development of a tumour from normal tissue.
ex: Inactivation of tumour-suppressor genes is a pivotal step in colorectal tumourigenesis.

def: Toxic to cells, especially describing drugs that kill rapidly dividing malignant cells.
ex: Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy damages healthy dividing tissues as well as the tumour, hence its side effects.

def: The treatment of cancer with cytotoxic drugs that target dividing cells.
ex: She tolerated four cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy with manageable nausea and reversible hair loss.

def: The use of ionising radiation to destroy or shrink malignant tissue.
ex: Postoperative radiotherapy to the tumour bed reduced the risk of local recurrence.

def: Radiotherapy delivered by placing a radioactive source within or close to the tumour.
ex: Prostate brachytherapy implants radioactive seeds directly into the gland, sparing surrounding tissue.

def: Treatment that harnesses the patient's immune system to recognise and attack cancer.
ex: Checkpoint-inhibitor immunotherapy has transformed the outlook for advanced melanoma.

def: Reduction of bone-marrow activity leading to fewer blood cells, often a dose-limiting toxicity of chemotherapy.
ex: Severe myelosuppression after the third cycle necessitated a dose reduction and growth-factor support.

def: Painful inflammation and ulceration of the mucous membranes, a common toxicity of cancer treatment.
ex: Oral mucositis made swallowing so painful that the patient required parenteral nutrition.

def: Surgical removal of as much of a tumour as possible to improve the effect of subsequent therapy.
ex: Optimal debulking of ovarian cancer, leaving no visible residual disease, strongly predicts better survival.

def: Breast-conserving surgery removing only the tumour and a rim of surrounding tissue.
ex: For a small, early breast cancer, lumpectomy followed by radiotherapy is as effective as mastectomy.

def: Surgical removal of the whole breast.
ex: Because the tumour was multifocal, the surgeon recommended a mastectomy rather than breast conservation.

def: Surgical removal of one or more lymph nodes, often to assess or treat tumour spread.
ex: Axillary lymphadenectomy was undertaken once the sentinel node proved positive for metastatic disease.

def: Treatment aimed at relieving symptoms rather than curing the underlying disease.
ex: A short course of radiotherapy provided effective palliation of the patient's bone pain.

def: The classification of a cancer's extent according to tumour size and spread.
ex: Accurate staging with CT and PET imaging determines whether curative surgery is appropriate.

def: Assessment of how abnormal tumour cells appear under the microscope, reflecting aggressiveness.
ex: Histological grading places the tumour on a scale from well to poorly differentiated.

def: A measurable biological molecule that indicates the presence, progression or treatment response of cancer.
ex: A rising CA-125 biomarker prompted imaging that confirmed ovarian cancer recurrence.

def: The process of cell division producing two identical daughter cells.
ex: An abundance of atypical figures of mitosis on the slide reflected the tumour's rapid growth.

def: Variability in the size and shape of cells or their nuclei, a feature of malignancy.
ex: Nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli contributed to the high histological grade.

def: The infiltration of malignant cells into adjacent normal tissue.
ex: Lymphovascular invasion on histology signalled a heightened risk of nodal spread.

def: A microscopic deposit of tumour cells at a distant site, undetectable by routine imaging.
ex: Adjuvant chemotherapy aims to eradicate occult micrometastasis left behind after surgery.

def: A physician who specialises in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer.
ex: The medical oncologist discussed the risks and benefits of systemic therapy with the patient.

def: Describing treatment given before the primary therapy to shrink a tumour and improve resectability.
ex: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy downstaged the rectal tumour enough to permit sphincter-preserving surgery.

def: The growth of dense fibrous connective tissue in response to an invasive tumour.
ex: The marked desmoplasia surrounding pancreatic adenocarcinoma impedes drug delivery to the cancer cells.

def: A germ-cell tumour containing tissues derived from more than one embryonic layer.
ex: The resected ovarian teratoma contained hair, cartilage and even rudimentary teeth.

def: A slow-growing neuroendocrine tumour that may secrete vasoactive substances such as serotonin.
ex: A midgut carcinoid presented with flushing and diarrhoea once it had metastasised to the liver.

def: The reduction of tumour burden, usually by surgical removal of malignant tissue.
ex: Aggressive cytoreduction combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy is used in selected peritoneal malignancies.

def: Derived from a single cell clone, as in engineered antibodies used to target cancer.
ex: Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, revolutionised the treatment of B-cell lymphomas.

def: An abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, a frequent feature of cancer.
ex: Widespread aneuploidy reflects the chromosomal instability that fuels tumour evolution.

def: An enzyme that lengthens chromosome ends and confers replicative immortality on cancer cells.
ex: Reactivation of telomerase allows malignant cells to divide indefinitely without shortening their telomeres.

def: Readily damaged or destroyed by ionising radiation.
ex: Seminomas are exquisitely radiosensitive, so radiotherapy achieves high cure rates.

def: Relatively unaffected by ionising radiation and thus difficult to treat with radiotherapy.
ex: Melanoma is often radioresistant, which limits the usefulness of conventional radiotherapy.

def: The process by which a normal cell becomes cancerous.
ex: Certain viruses contribute to oncogenesis by inserting their genetic material into the host genome.

def: Capable of giving rise to a colony of cells, as with the self-renewing cells that sustain a tumour.
ex: Radiotherapy must eliminate every clonogenic cell to achieve durable local control.

def: The rim of apparently normal tissue removed around a tumour, assessed for residual cancer.
ex: A positive resection margin indicates that tumour reaches the edge of the specimen and raises recurrence risk.

def: Present but not clinically detectable without special investigation.
ex: Occult blood in the stool prompted a colonoscopy that revealed an early caecal carcinoma.

def: A chemotherapeutic agent that causes blistering and tissue damage if it leaks from a vein.
ex: Doxorubicin is a potent vesicant, so its extravasation can produce disfiguring tissue loss.

def: A gene whose normal role is to restrain cell division and whose loss promotes cancer.
ex: Inheriting a defective copy of a tumour-suppressor such as BRCA1 confers a high lifetime cancer risk.

def: The original tumour at the site where the cancer first developed.
ex: The primary tumour was in the breast, with secondaries in the axillary nodes.

def: Deposits of cancer that have spread from the primary site to other parts of the body.
ex: He was admitted with bone pain from widespread secondaries.

def: A substance measured in blood or tissue whose level can indicate the presence or activity of a cancer.
ex: We monitor her CA-125 as a tumour marker to track response to treatment.

def: A measure of how abnormal cancer cells look under the microscope and how quickly they are likely to grow.
ex: It is a high-grade tumour, so we expect it to behave aggressively.

def: Describing cancer cells that closely resemble normal cells and tend to grow more slowly.
ex: The pathology report described a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with a favourable outlook.

def: Describing a tumour that can be removed surgically.
ex: The multidisciplinary team judged the tumour resectable and listed her for theatre.

def: A rim of healthy tissue around an excised tumour that contains no cancer cells, indicating complete removal.
ex: The good news is that the surgeon achieved clear margins.

def: A set period of chemotherapy treatment followed by a rest period, repeated as a course.
ex: He tolerated the first cycle of chemotherapy well, with only mild nausea.

def: Treatment that acts on specific molecules or mutations driving a particular cancer's growth.
ex: Because the tumour is HER2-positive, she is eligible for targeted therapy.

def: Treatment that blocks or lowers hormones that fuel the growth of certain cancers.
ex: For an oestrogen-receptor-positive tumour we usually add hormone therapy for five years.

def: The growth or spread of cancer despite treatment.
ex: The scan showed disease progression, so we switched to second-line therapy.

def: To show improvement, such as tumour shrinkage, as a result of therapy.
ex: The tumour is responding well to treatment, having halved in size.

def: Describing treatment intended to cure the cancer completely rather than merely control it.
ex: The intent of surgery here is curative, not palliative.

def: Specialist care focused on relieving suffering and supporting patients with a serious or terminal illness.
ex: I've referred her to the palliative care team for symptom control at home.

def: Describing an illness that cannot be cured and is expected to lead to death.
ex: His cancer is now terminal, and our focus is on comfort.

def: The length of time a person is expected to live, given their condition.
ex: Families often ask about life expectancy, and we answer honestly but gently.

def: The length of time after treatment during which a patient shows no signs of cancer.
ex: This regimen significantly improves disease-free survival at five years.

def: A standardised measure of how well a patient can carry out daily activities, used to judge fitness for treatment.
ex: His performance status is too poor to tolerate further chemotherapy.
