def: A group of specialists from different fields who jointly plan a patient's cancer care.
ex: Her case will be discussed at the multidisciplinary team meeting on Thursday.

def: To signal gently that difficult news is coming, so the patient can prepare emotionally.
ex: I fired a warning shot by saying the results were more serious than we had hoped.

word: I'm afraid the news isn't good
def: A gentle, direct opener used to introduce a serious or unwelcome diagnosis to a patient.
ex: I sat down, held her gaze, and said, 'I'm afraid the news isn't good.'

def: To tell someone distressing information in a careful and compassionate way.
ex: I took the daughter aside to break the news gently before she saw her father.

def: To gradually accept and adjust to a difficult reality such as a serious diagnosis.
ex: It will take time to come to terms with the diagnosis, and that's completely normal.

def: A patient's overall wellbeing and ability to enjoy daily living, weighed against the burdens of treatment.
ex: We decided to prioritise her quality of life over aggressive treatment.

def: The process of discussing and recording a patient's wishes for future care should they lose the capacity to decide.
ex: We began advance care planning while he was still well enough to express his wishes.

def: A recorded decision that cardiopulmonary resuscitation should not be attempted if the heart stops.
ex: After a frank conversation, the family agreed to a do-not-resuscitate order.

def: Care given in the final period of a terminal illness, focused on comfort and dignity.
ex: The hospice provides excellent end-of-life care for patients like him.

def: A facility or service providing specialist care and support for people with a terminal illness.
ex: A bed became available at the local hospice for the last few weeks of his life.

def: A sudden flare of pain that occurs despite regular background pain relief.
ex: We prescribed a short-acting opioid for episodes of breakthrough pain.

def: Swelling of a limb caused by a build-up of lymph fluid, often after removal of lymph nodes.
ex: She developed lymphoedema of the arm following axillary node clearance.

def: The ideal refractive state in which parallel light rays focus precisely on the retina without accommodation.
ex: With no refractive error on either side, the young patient enjoyed emmetropia and needed no correction.

def: A condition in which the two eyes have unequal refractive power.
ex: The child's marked anisometropia risked amblyopia in the more hypermetropic eye if left uncorrected.

def: An inequality in the diameters of the two pupils.
ex: New anisocoria with ptosis prompted urgent imaging to exclude a third-nerve palsy from an aneurysm.

def: An abnormal white reflection from the pupil, classically signalling retinoblastoma in children.
ex: The grandmother noticed leukocoria in a flash photograph, and examination confirmed an intraocular tumour.

def: Posterior displacement of the eyeball within the orbit.
ex: The blow-out fracture caused enophthalmos as orbital contents herniated into the maxillary sinus.

def: Enlargement of the eyeball in infants due to raised intraocular pressure in congenital glaucoma.
ex: The enlarged, cloudy cornea of buphthalmos alerted the paediatrician to congenital glaucoma.

def: A developmental disorder in which one or both eyeballs are abnormally small.
ex: The neonate's unilateral microphthalmos was associated with a coloboma of the optic disc.

def: An accumulation of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye.
ex: After blunt trauma a layered hyphaema filled a third of the anterior chamber, and the pressure was watched closely.

def: A layer of white cells or pus settling in the lower anterior chamber, indicating severe intraocular inflammation.
ex: A dense hypopyon in the setting of a corneal ulcer suggested bacterial keratitis and possible endophthalmitis.

def: An adhesion binding the iris to adjacent structures, either the lens or the cornea.
ex: Recurrent uveitis had formed posterior synechia, tethering the pupil margin to the anterior lens capsule.

def: A progressive thinning and conical protrusion of the cornea causing irregular astigmatism.
ex: Corneal topography confirmed keratoconus, and the patient was referred for collagen cross-linking.

def: Surgical transplantation or grafting of corneal tissue.
ex: After the graft failed, she underwent penetrating keratoplasty to restore corneal clarity.

def: A wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva encroaching onto the cornea.
ex: Years of sun exposure produced a pterygium that advanced towards the visual axis and was excised.

def: A benign yellowish conjunctival deposit adjacent to the cornea that does not cross the limbus.
ex: The nasal pinguecula was a harmless degenerative change requiring only lubricants for occasional irritation.

def: A painless granulomatous swelling of the eyelid from a blocked meibomian gland.
ex: The firm, non-tender chalazion persisted despite warm compresses and was incised and curetted.

def: An acute, tender infection of an eyelid gland, commonly known as a stye.
ex: The patient presented with a painful external hordeolum pointing at the lash line.

def: Inflammation of the lacrimal sac, usually secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct.
ex: Acute dacryocystitis produced a red, tender swelling below the medial canthus with purulent reflux.

def: Overflow of tears down the cheek from excess production or impaired drainage.
ex: Chronic epiphora prompted syringing, which revealed a blocked nasolacrimal duct.

def: Inward turning of the eyelid margin so that the lashes abrade the ocular surface.
ex: Involutional entropion caused the lower lashes to rub the cornea, and surgical repair was arranged.

def: Outward turning of the eyelid margin, exposing the conjunctiva and causing tearing.
ex: Senile ectropion left the palpebral conjunctiva exposed and chronically inflamed.

def: Misdirection of eyelashes towards the eyeball, causing corneal irritation.
ex: Repeated trichiasis from scarred lid margins abraded the cornea and required epilation.

def: Incomplete closure of the eyelids, predisposing the exposed cornea to drying and ulceration.
ex: Facial nerve palsy produced lagophthalmos, so the cornea was protected with ointment and taping overnight.

def: Involuntary, forceful contraction of the eyelid muscles causing sustained closure.
ex: Benign essential blepharospasm forced the eyes shut intermittently and responded to botulinum toxin.

def: A manifest inward deviation of one eye relative to the other.
ex: The infantile esotropia was surgically corrected before it could entrench amblyopia.

def: A manifest outward deviation of one eye relative to the other.
ex: Her intermittent exotropia became more apparent when she was tired or daydreaming.

def: A latent tendency of the eyes to deviate that is controlled by binocular fusion.
ex: The cover test uncovered a heterophoria that only manifested when fusion was disrupted.

def: Paralysis of the ciliary muscle, abolishing accommodation.
ex: Cyclopentolate induced cycloplegia so that an accurate refraction could be measured in the child.

def: Examination of the anterior chamber angle using a mirrored contact lens.
ex: Gonioscopy revealed a narrow, occludable angle, confirming the diagnosis of angle-closure glaucoma.

def: Measurement of corneal thickness.
ex: Central pachymetry showed a thin cornea, which meant the true intraocular pressure was underestimated.

def: The systematic measurement and mapping of the visual field.
ex: Automated perimetry documented an arcuate defect characteristic of glaucomatous damage.

def: An objective technique for determining refractive error by observing the movement of a reflex from the retina.
ex: In a preverbal child, retinoscopy provided an objective refraction where subjective testing was impossible.

def: Surgical removal of the entire eyeball while leaving the extraocular muscles and orbital contents intact.
ex: Given the large choroidal melanoma, enucleation was recommended to prevent metastatic spread.

def: Removal of the intraocular contents while retaining the scleral shell and extraocular muscles.
ex: For the painful blind eye, evisceration offered a good cosmetic result with an implant in the retained sclera.

def: Radical removal of the entire orbital contents, including the eyeball, muscles and periorbital tissue.
ex: The invasive orbital malignancy necessitated exenteration to achieve clear surgical margins.

def: Surgical removal of the vitreous gel, typically to access or repair the retina.
ex: A pars plana vitrectomy was performed to relieve traction and reattach the detached retina.

def: A glaucoma-filtering operation creating a new channel for aqueous outflow to lower intraocular pressure.
ex: When drops failed to control the pressure, a trabeculectomy fashioned a guarded fistula beneath the flap.

def: Creation of a hole in the iris, usually by laser, to relieve or prevent angle closure.
ex: A prophylactic laser iridotomy was performed in the fellow eye to avert an acute attack.

def: The creation of a continuous circular opening in the anterior lens capsule during cataract surgery.
ex: A well-centred capsulorhexis ensured stable placement of the intraocular lens within the capsular bag.

def: The state of an eye containing an artificial intraocular lens after cataract removal.
ex: The glistening reflex confirmed pseudophakia, so her blurred vision was not due to a recurrent cataract.

def: Absence of the crystalline lens from the eye.
ex: Following complicated surgery he was left in aphakia and required a high-power contact lens to focus.

def: A congenital inability to perceive colour, accompanied by poor acuity and light sensitivity.
ex: Complete achromatopsia left the boy seeing only in shades of grey and intensely photophobic.

def: Impaired vision in dim light or darkness, commonly called night blindness.
ex: Progressive nyctalopia was the earliest symptom of his retinitis pigmentosa.

def: Distortion of the perceived shape of objects, with straight lines appearing wavy.
ex: The Amsler grid revealed metamorphopsia, prompting evaluation for a macular membrane.

def: A visual disturbance in which objects appear smaller than they actually are.
ex: Central serous retinopathy caused micropsia, so text seemed shrunken in the affected eye.

def: Loss of vision, especially without an obvious ophthalmoscopic lesion of the eye.
ex: Transient monocular amaurosis, described as a curtain descending, signalled carotid embolism.

def: A severe infective inflammation of the internal ocular tissues and cavities.
ex: Sudden pain and hypopyon days after surgery raised the alarm for postoperative endophthalmitis.

def: Benign, usually self-limiting inflammation of the episclera beneath the conjunctiva.
ex: The sectoral redness of episcleritis blanched with phenylephrine, distinguishing it from scleritis.

def: A painful, potentially sight-threatening inflammation of the sclera, often linked to systemic disease.
ex: The deep, boring pain of scleritis prompted a search for underlying rheumatoid arthritis.

def: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body, a form of anterior uveitis.
ex: Acute iridocyclitis produced a painful red eye with cells and flare in the anterior chamber.

def: A splitting of the neurosensory retina into two layers.
ex: Peripheral retinoschisis was distinguished from a true detachment by its smooth, dome-shaped elevation.

def: A congenital gap in an ocular structure resulting from failure of the embryonic fissure to close.
ex: An inferonasal iris coloboma gave the pupil a distinctive keyhole appearance.

def: Yellowish extracellular deposits accumulating beneath the retina, a hallmark of macular degeneration.
ex: Numerous soft drusen at the macula heralded an increased risk of progression to neovascular disease.

def: Abnormal new vessel formation on the iris, typically driven by retinal ischaemia.
ex: Rubeosis on the iris warned that neovascular glaucoma might soon follow the retinal vein occlusion.

def: An adhesion between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva binding the eyelid to the eyeball.
ex: Cicatrising conjunctival disease produced a symblepharon that restricted movement of the globe.

def: A congenital, usually bilateral absence or severe hypoplasia of the iris.
ex: The child's aniridia was associated with foveal hypoplasia and a mutation affecting the PAX6 gene.

def: Inflammation involving both the choroid and the overlying retina.
ex: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis left a pigmented scar adjacent to an active satellite lesion at the macula.

def: The sharpness or clarity of a person's vision, typically measured with a Snellen chart at a fixed distance.
ex: On presentation, her visual acuity was 6/12 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left.

def: A chart of letters in decreasing sizes used to test distance visual acuity.
ex: Ask the patient to read down the Snellen chart from six metres, covering one eye at a time.

def: A condition in which the eye fails to focus light precisely on the retina, causing blurred vision.
ex: Much of his reduced acuity was simply an uncorrected refractive error that improved with a pinhole.

def: A refractive error in which distant objects appear blurred because light focuses in front of the retina.
ex: The child's myopia had progressed enough to warrant a stronger prescription this year.

def: A refractive error in which near objects appear blurred because light focuses behind the retina.
ex: Uncorrected hypermetropia in a young hyperope can precipitate accommodative esotropia.

def: A refractive error caused by an irregularly curved cornea or lens, producing distorted or blurred vision at all distances.
ex: Her astigmatism was corrected with a toric contact lens rather than a standard spherical one.

def: The age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on near objects, due to stiffening of the crystalline lens.
ex: Most patients notice presbyopia in their mid-forties and start needing reading glasses.

def: The process by which the eye changes the shape of its lens to focus on objects at different distances.
ex: Test accommodation by asking the patient to focus on your finger as you bring it towards the nose.

def: The thin transparent membrane covering the white of the eye and the inner surface of the eyelids.
ex: The conjunctiva was injected and there was a stringy mucoid discharge suggestive of allergy.

def: The tough white outer layer of the eyeball that maintains its shape and protects the inner structures.
ex: A blue tinge to the sclera in an infant may point to an underlying connective-tissue disorder.

def: The transparent dome at the front of the eye that provides most of the eye's focusing power.
ex: Fluorescein staining revealed a small abrasion on the inferior cornea.

def: The clear fluid in the front chamber of the eye that nourishes the cornea and lens and maintains intraocular pressure.
ex: Obstruction of aqueous humour drainage at the trabecular meshwork raises the intraocular pressure.

def: The clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina and helps the eye keep its shape.
ex: As the vitreous humour liquefies with age, patients commonly report new floaters.

def: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts images into nerve signals sent to the brain.
ex: Fundoscopy showed haemorrhages scattered across the retina in a dot-and-blot pattern.

def: The small central part of the retina responsible for detailed central and colour vision.
ex: Because the macula was spared, her central vision remained surprisingly good despite the peripheral damage.

def: The tiny central pit of the macula that provides the sharpest visual acuity.
ex: Optical coherence tomography confirmed that the oedema extended into the fovea.

def: The point at the back of the eye where the optic nerve fibres leave the retina, seen as a pale circle on fundoscopy.
ex: The optic disc margins were blurred, raising the possibility of papilloedema.

def: The ratio of the central hollow of the optic disc to its total diameter, used to monitor glaucomatous damage.
ex: An enlarging cup-to-disc ratio over successive visits suggests progressive glaucoma.

def: Examination of the back of the eye, including the retina and optic disc, using an ophthalmoscope.
ex: Fundoscopy is easier once the pupils have been dilated with tropicamide.

def: A microscope with a bright adjustable light beam used to examine the structures at the front of the eye in detail.
ex: On slit-lamp examination there was a hypopyon and marked anterior-chamber activity.

def: The fluid pressure inside the eye, a key measurement in the assessment of glaucoma.
ex: His intraocular pressure was 34 mmHg, well above the normal range.

def: The measurement of intraocular pressure, most accurately performed with a Goldmann applanation tonometer.
ex: Applanation tonometry gave readings of 18 and 20 mmHg in the right and left eyes respectively.

def: A group of conditions in which the optic nerve is progressively damaged, often associated with raised intraocular pressure.
ex: Open-angle glaucoma is usually painless and detected only on routine screening.

def: A clouding of the eye's natural lens that causes gradual, painless loss of vision.
ex: The cataract had matured to the point where she could no longer read the newspaper.

def: The standard cataract operation in which ultrasound breaks up the cloudy lens so it can be removed and replaced with an implant.
ex: She underwent uncomplicated phacoemulsification with insertion of a monofocal intraocular lens.

def: An artificial lens implanted inside the eye to replace the natural lens, typically after cataract removal.
ex: The intraocular lens was calculated to leave him slightly myopic for comfortable reading.

def: A progressive disease of the macula causing loss of central vision, most commonly related to ageing.
ex: Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults.

def: A sight-threatening emergency in which the retina peels away from the underlying tissue at the back of the eye.
ex: The sudden curtain across his vision and shower of floaters pointed to a retinal detachment.

def: Small shapes or specks that drift across the visual field, caused by opacities in the vitreous gel.
ex: A sudden increase in floaters accompanied by flashing lights warrants urgent review.

def: The perception of flashes of light in the absence of an external light source, often signalling vitreoretinal traction.
ex: The photopsia she described in the temporal field raised concern about a retinal tear.

def: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, producing redness, discharge and irritation, and usually viral, bacterial or allergic in origin.
ex: Bilateral watery discharge and a preauricular node suggested viral conjunctivitis rather than a bacterial cause.

def: Inflammation of the uvea, the middle pigmented layer of the eye, presenting with pain, redness and photophobia.
ex: Anterior uveitis is often associated with HLA-B27-related systemic disease.

def: Inflammation of the cornea, which may be infective and can threaten sight if it involves the visual axis.
ex: Contact-lens-related microbial keratitis needs urgent corneal scrapes and intensive topical antibiotics.

def: An area of reduced or absent vision surrounded by a field of normal or relatively well-preserved sight.
ex: She described a central scotoma that made it impossible to recognise faces.

def: Reduced vision in one eye that develops in childhood because the brain fails to process its images properly, despite no structural defect.
ex: Patching the stronger eye is the mainstay of treating amblyopia in young children.

def: A misalignment of the eyes in which they do not point in the same direction.
ex: The cover test confirmed a convergent strabismus in the right eye.

def: Abnormal forward protrusion of the eyeball from the orbit.
ex: Bilateral proptosis and lid retraction pointed towards thyroid eye disease.

def: A sign, elicited by the swinging-light test, in which the affected pupil dilates rather than constricts, indicating optic nerve or severe retinal disease.
ex: A relative afferent pupillary defect on the swinging-light test supported a diagnosis of optic neuritis.

def: The application of an orange dye that highlights corneal abrasions and ulcers as green areas under blue light.
ex: Fluorescein staining showed a dendritic ulcer typical of herpes simplex keratitis.

def: The total area a person can see when looking straight ahead, including peripheral vision.
ex: Formal visual field testing confirmed an arcuate defect consistent with glaucoma.

def: Dilation of the pupil, whether physiological, drug-induced or pathological.
ex: Pharmacological mydriasis with tropicamide is needed for a thorough dilated fundus examination.

def: Constriction of the pupil, which may result from bright light, certain drugs or neurological disease.
ex: Pinpoint miosis in an unresponsive patient should prompt consideration of opioid toxicity.

def: Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins causing redness, crusting and a gritty, irritable sensation.
ex: Lid hygiene and warm compresses are the cornerstone of managing chronic blepharitis.

def: A bright red patch on the white of the eye caused by a small bleed under the conjunctiva, usually harmless and self-limiting.
ex: Reassure the patient that a subconjunctival haemorrhage looks alarming but typically clears within two weeks.

def: To adjust the focusing power of the eye in order to see objects clearly at varying distances.
ex: As you get older the lens becomes less able to accommodate, which is why near tasks feel harder.

def: The clinical procedure of measuring an eye's focusing error to determine the lens power needed for clear vision.
ex: Your refraction shows a small change, so I'll update the prescription for your reading glasses.

def: To bend light as it passes through the eye's optical surfaces so that it focuses on the retina.
ex: A misshapen cornea will refract light unevenly, producing blurred and distorted vision.

def: The measurement of the curvature of the front surface of the cornea.
ex: Keratometry is essential before fitting contact lenses so the curve matches the eye.

def: The examination of the interior of the eye, particularly the retina, using an illuminated instrument.
ex: On ophthalmoscopy the optic disc and retinal vessels looked healthy.

def: The border region where the transparent cornea meets the white sclera.
ex: The redness was concentrated around the limbus rather than across the whole eye.

def: The clear gel-like substance that fills the large cavity between the lens and the retina.
ex: Those drifting specks are usually harmless strands within the vitreous.

def: Relating to the watery fluid in the front chamber of the eye that nourishes the cornea and lens.
ex: The aqueous fluid drains through the angle, and blocked drainage can raise the pressure.

def: The production and secretion of tears by the eye.
ex: Excessive lacrimation in the wind is a common and usually harmless complaint.

def: The inward turning of both eyes to keep a near object single and in focus.
ex: Poor convergence can make the words seem to swim together during prolonged reading.

def: The perception of depth that arises when the brain combines the slightly different images from each eye.
ex: I tested stereopsis using a booklet of three-dimensional patterns.

def: The brain's active ignoring of the image from one eye to avoid double vision.
ex: Suppression of the deviating eye explained why she did not report seeing double.

def: The unit used to express the focusing power of a lens or the degree of a refractive error.
ex: Your prescription has increased by half a dioptre in the left eye.

def: The act of directing and holding the gaze steadily on a particular target.
ex: Ask the child to keep fixation on the light while you watch the eye movements.

def: A rapid jump of the eyes from one point of fixation to another.
ex: His saccades were slow and inaccurate when shifting from one target to the next.

def: Relating to the coordinated use of both eyes together to form a single image.
ex: Good binocular vision lets the two eyes team up to judge distance accurately.

def: To make the pupil widen, either naturally in dim light or with drops for examination.
ex: I'm going to dilate your pupils, and your vision will stay blurry for a few hours afterwards.

def: In therapy, any meaningful everyday activity a person needs or wants to do, from self-care to work and leisure.
ex: We define occupation broadly, so cooking a meal or gardening counts as therapeutic activity, not just paid employment.

def: A person's motivation to act, shaped by their interests, values and sense of personal capacity.
ex: His low volition after the stroke meant he initiated few activities, so we focused on rebuilding motivation first.

def: The patterns of habit and routine that organise a person's daily occupations and roles.
ex: Re-establishing habituation through a consistent morning routine gave structure to her otherwise chaotic days.

def: The ability to conceive, plan and carry out a sequence of purposeful, coordinated movements.
ex: We assessed his praxis by asking him to mime brushing his teeth without the actual toothbrush present.

def: Difficulty planning and coordinating purposeful movement, affecting everyday motor tasks.
ex: The child's dyspraxia made handwriting and doing up buttons slow and effortful.

def: Skill and coordination in using the hands to manipulate objects, especially small ones.
ex: Reduced fine dexterity made it hard for her to pick up coins or fasten a zip.

def: The action of grasping or seizing an object with the hand.
ex: We graded activities to improve his prehension, starting with large blocks before moving to smaller pegs.

def: A grip in which the thumb opposes one or more fingers to hold a small object.
ex: His pinch strength was too weak to hold a pen, so we trialled a built-up grip.

def: Rotation of the forearm so that the palm faces upward or forward.
ex: Limited supination meant she could not turn her palm up to accept change from a cashier.

def: Rotation of the forearm so that the palm faces downward or backward.
ex: We practised pronation and supination so he could turn a doorknob and pour from a jug.

def: An externally applied device used to support, align or improve the function of a body part.
ex: A wrist orthosis held the joint stable and allowed him to keep typing at work.

def: Designed or modified to help a person carry out a task despite a limitation.
ex: An adaptive knife with an angled handle let her cut vegetables one-handed.

def: Relating to equipment or technology that supports independence in daily activities.
ex: We prescribed assistive equipment such as a long-handled sponge and a sock aid.

def: Relating to strategies that work around a deficit rather than restoring the lost function itself.
ex: We took a compensatory approach, teaching her to use a checklist to offset her memory difficulties.

def: The process of restoring or improving an impaired underlying skill or ability.
ex: Rather than compensation, we chose remediation, working directly to rebuild his grip strength.

def: The use of handling, cueing or positioning to encourage a desired movement or response.
ex: With gentle facilitation at the shoulder, she was able to reach forward for the cup.

def: The act of moving a person from one surface or position to another, such as bed to chair.
ex: We practised a sit-to-stand transfer from the bed to the wheelchair before discharge.

def: The set of tasks involved in using the toilet, including transfers, clothing and hygiene.
ex: Independent toileting was her main goal, so we installed a raised seat and grab rails.

def: Personal care activities such as washing the face, brushing teeth and combing hair.
ex: He managed grooming at the sink once we provided a tap turner and a long-handled comb.

def: The everyday activities of looking after one's own body, such as washing, dressing and eating.
ex: Our first goal was to restore self-care so she could dress and feed herself at home.

def: The ability to control bladder and bowel function voluntarily.
ex: A regular toileting schedule helped him maintain continence and preserve his dignity.

def: A loss of normal muscle tone, leaving a limb soft, floppy and difficult to move.
ex: In the early flaccidity stage we positioned and supported the arm to protect the shoulder joint.

def: A reduced awareness of, or failure to attend to, one side of the body or space.
ex: Because of visual neglect he left the food on the left half of his plate untouched.

def: The sense that detects movement and position of the body's parts through the muscles and joints.
ex: Impaired kinaesthesia meant she could not tell where her hand was without looking at it.

def: Relating to the sense of touch.
ex: We used varied tactile materials to help him relearn to identify coins by feel alone.

def: The regulation of one's response to sensory input to keep it at a comfortable, functional level.
ex: Poor sensory modulation meant loud classrooms overwhelmed the child within minutes.

def: Relating to the combined function of sensory input and motor output in producing movement.
ex: We designed sensorimotor activities that combined touch, balance and reaching in one task.

def: The ability to arrange the steps of a task in the correct, logical order.
ex: Difficulty with sequencing meant she poured the tea before adding the teabag.

def: The ability to begin a task without external prompting.
ex: Poor initiation meant he would sit passively until someone cued him to start washing.

def: Relating to the higher mental skills of planning, organising, and self-monitoring behaviour.
ex: His executive difficulties showed when he could not plan a shopping trip or budget for it.

def: The capacity to sustain physical or mental activity over time without excessive fatigue.
ex: Her sitting endurance was only ten minutes, so we built up tolerance gradually.

def: The strategy of balancing activity and rest to manage limited energy or fatigue.
ex: We taught pacing so she could spread housework across the day instead of exhausting herself at once.

def: The study of designing tasks and environments to fit the person and reduce strain.
ex: A workplace ergonomics assessment led us to raise his monitor and change his chair.

def: The measurement of the range of motion available at a joint using a calibrated instrument.
ex: Goniometry showed his elbow extension had improved by fifteen degrees since the last review.

def: Considering the whole person, including physical, mental, social and environmental factors.
ex: A holistic assessment revealed that his isolation, not just his weakness, was limiting recovery.

def: The loss of physical fitness and function that follows a period of inactivity or bed rest.
ex: After three weeks in bed, deconditioning left her too weak to stand at the sink.

def: A state of reduced physical reserve that leaves an older person vulnerable to sudden decline.
ex: Given his frailty, even a minor infection could set back his independence considerably.

def: Short-term, goal-focused support that helps a person relearn daily skills and regain independence.
ex: A six-week reablement programme helped him regain confidence in cooking after his fall.

def: The number of patients or clients a practitioner is responsible for at a given time.
ex: With a high caseload she prioritised the clients at greatest risk of falls.

def: Aimed at recovering lost function or ability rather than merely compensating for it.
ex: We took a restorative approach, retraining his balance so he could eventually walk unaided.

def: To restore a person to their fullest possible function and independence after illness or injury.
ex: Our aim was to rehabilitate her sufficiently to return to living alone with minimal support.

def: A seizure triggered by a rapid rise in body temperature in a young child, usually between six months and five years of age.
ex: The parents were reassured that a simple febrile convulsion does not cause brain damage and rarely leads to epilepsy.

def: The recommended timetable setting out which vaccines a child should receive and at what age.
ex: I checked the red book and your daughter is up to date with the immunisation schedule apart from the pre-school booster.

def: Having received all the vaccines appropriate for a child's age according to the national schedule.
ex: Before starting nursery, staff will want to confirm that he is up to date with his vaccinations.

def: A skill such as sitting, walking or talking that most children reach by a particular age.
ex: She is meeting all her developmental milestones and started walking unaided at thirteen months.

def: Poor weight gain or growth in an infant or young child that falls significantly below expected values.
ex: The baby was referred to the paediatric clinic for failure to thrive after dropping across two centile lines.

def: A line on a growth chart showing the percentage of children of the same age who fall below a given measurement.
ex: His weight has tracked steadily along the fiftieth centile since birth.

def: A chart used to plot a child's weight, length or head circumference against age to monitor growth over time.
ex: We plot every measurement on the growth chart to make sure she is following her expected trajectory.

def: The measurement around the widest part of an infant's head, used to monitor brain growth.
ex: The health visitor measures head circumference at each review to screen for hydrocephalus.

def: The process by which an infant's first teeth emerge through the gums, often causing irritability and drooling.
ex: The dribbling and gum-rubbing you describe are almost certainly just teething rather than illness.

def: Prolonged, inconsolable crying in an otherwise healthy and well-fed infant, typically in the first few months of life.
ex: The evening crying spells that settle with winding are consistent with colic.

def: A viral infection of the upper airway in young children causing a characteristic barking cough and hoarse voice.
ex: The barking cough and stridor at night were typical of croup, and we gave a single dose of oral dexamethasone.

def: A harsh, seal-like cough characteristic of croup in young children.
ex: Parents often describe the barking cough of croup as sounding like a seal or a dog.

def: A common viral chest infection of infants that inflames the smallest airways and causes wheezing and feeding difficulty.
ex: The three-month-old with bronchiolitis was admitted because he was only taking half his usual feeds.

def: The effort a child expends to breathe, judged by signs such as recession, nasal flaring and accessory muscle use.
ex: Increased work of breathing with intercostal recession prompted us to start oxygen.

def: The visible drawing-in of the skin between or below the ribs during breathing, indicating respiratory distress in a child.
ex: There was marked subcostal and intercostal recession, showing she was struggling to breathe.

def: Widening of the nostrils with each breath, a sign of increased respiratory effort in infants.
ex: Grunting and nasal flaring in the newborn suggested significant respiratory distress.

def: A short sound made on breathing out as a distressed infant tries to keep the airways open.
ex: Grunting in a newborn is a red-flag sign that should never be ignored.

def: A simple check in which a clear glass is pressed against a rash to see whether the marks fade under pressure.
ex: We teach parents the glass test so they know when a rash needs emergency assessment.

def: The cluster of signs such as neck stiffness, headache and photophobia suggesting irritation of the meninges.
ex: The child had photophobia and neck stiffness, raising concern about meningism.

def: The number of urine-soaked nappies a baby produces, used as a practical measure of hydration.
ex: How many wet nappies has she had in the last twenty-four hours?

def: A balanced mixture of water, salts and sugar given by mouth to replace fluid lost through diarrhoea and vomiting.
ex: Give oral rehydration solution in small sips little and often rather than large drinks.

def: A common childhood viral illness causing an itchy, blistering rash and mild fever.
ex: The crops of vesicles at different stages were typical of chickenpox.

def: A chronic inflammatory skin condition causing dry, itchy and inflamed patches, very common in children.
ex: We advised regular emollients and a short course of topical steroid for the eczema flare.

def: Sore, red skin in the nappy area caused by prolonged contact with urine and faeces.
ex: Frequent nappy changes and a barrier cream usually clear up simple nappy rash.

def: Treatment of neonatal jaundice using blue light to break down bilirubin in the skin.
ex: His bilirubin level crossed the treatment line, so we started phototherapy overnight.

def: Born before thirty-seven completed weeks of pregnancy.
ex: As a premature baby born at twenty-nine weeks, she spent six weeks on the neonatal unit.

def: A specialist ward providing intensive care for newborn babies who are premature or unwell.
ex: The baby was transferred to the neonatal unit for respiratory support after birth.

def: An injury to a child that is deliberately caused rather than the result of an accident.
ex: The spiral fracture in a non-mobile infant was suspicious for non-accidental injury.

def: The personal child health record given to parents to keep track of a child's growth, development and vaccinations.
ex: Please bring the red book to every appointment so we can update the growth chart.

def: A qualified nurse who supports families with the health and development of children under five.
ex: If you have any worries about her weight, the health visitor can weigh her at the clinic.

def: An additional dose of a vaccine given after the primary course to maintain immunity.
ex: He is due his pre-school booster, which covers diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and polio.

def: A highly contagious bacterial infection causing severe coughing fits followed by a characteristic whoop, dangerous in young infants.
ex: The coughing bouts ending in vomiting and a whoop were strongly suggestive of whooping cough.

def: A highly infectious viral illness causing fever, cough and a widespread rash, preventable by the MMR vaccine.
ex: The rise in measles cases reflects falling uptake of the MMR vaccine.

def: The combined vaccine that protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
ex: The first dose of the MMR vaccine is given at around one year of age.

def: To relieve the worries of a child's parents by explaining that the situation is not serious or is being managed.
ex: I was able to reassure the parents that the rash was viral and would settle on its own.

def: Clear guidance given to parents on what warning signs to watch for and when to seek further help.
ex: I gave safety-net advice to return immediately if she developed a non-blanching rash or became floppy.

def: Describing an infant with abnormally low muscle tone who feels limp when handled.
ex: A floppy, drowsy baby who is difficult to rouse needs urgent assessment.

def: Describing an infant who is refusing or taking much less milk than usual, often an early sign of illness.
ex: He has been off his feeds since yesterday and is much less alert than normal.

def: A temporary cessation of breathing.
ex: During the episode of apnoea we began ventilating the patient with a bag-valve mask.

def: The movement of air into and out of the lungs, whether spontaneous or supported by a device.
ex: We took over ventilation with a bag-valve mask when his own efforts became inadequate.

def: An inadequate flow of blood to the tissues, often an early feature of shock.
ex: The prolonged capillary refill was a clear sign of hypoperfusion.

def: The act of preventing movement of an injured part or the spine to avoid further harm.
ex: Spinal immobilisation was maintained throughout the extrication from the vehicle.

def: The process of freeing a trapped casualty, typically from a vehicle or collapsed structure.
ex: The fire crew managed a controlled extrication while we monitored the patient's vital signs.

def: The state of being physically trapped, for example by wreckage after a collision.
ex: Prolonged entrapment raised our concern about crush injury to the legs.

def: A localised collection of blood outside the vessels, forming a swelling within the tissues.
ex: A rapidly expanding haematoma at the neck prompted an urgent re-examination of the airway.

def: An involuntary and violent contraction of the muscles, often occurring during a seizure.
ex: The convulsion lasted about two minutes before the movements gradually subsided.

def: Relating to a severe, rapidly developing allergic reaction that can threaten the airway and circulation.
ex: The swelling lips and wheeze suggested an anaphylactic reaction to the insect sting.

def: Being in a dying state, with imminent risk of death.
ex: On arrival the casualty looked moribund, so the team moved straight to resuscitation.

def: Lying on the back with the face upward.
ex: We laid the patient supine on the trolley before starting our primary survey.

def: Lying face down on the front of the body.
ex: He was found prone on the pavement, so we log-rolled him carefully to assess the airway.

def: Lying down or reclining rather than sitting or standing.
ex: We kept the fainting patient recumbent with the legs slightly raised until colour returned.

def: The measurement of the oxygen saturation of the blood, usually using a probe on a finger.
ex: Pulse oximetry read low, so we increased the oxygen and rechecked the position of the probe.

def: Having no detectable pulse.
ex: The patient was unresponsive and pulseless, so compressions were started at once.

def: To lose the ability to maintain normal function, so that a previously stable condition deteriorates.
ex: A child can decompensate suddenly once their reserves are exhausted, so we watched her closely.

def: Unpleasantly cold, damp and sticky to the touch.
ex: His clammy skin and rapid pulse were early warning signs of shock.

def: Aggressive and inclined to resist or fight, sometimes as a sign of confusion or lack of oxygen.
ex: The head-injured man became combative, so we spoke calmly and considered why he was agitated.

def: The condition of being open and unobstructed, especially of an airway or vessel.
ex: A head tilt and chin lift restored the patency of the airway.

def: To understand and share the feelings that another person is experiencing.
ex: I can empathise with how frightening a diagnosis like this must feel when you first hear it.

def: To accept or admit that something, such as a patient's concern, is real and worth noting.
ex: I want to acknowledge that you've been waiting a long time in pain, and I'm sorry about that.

def: To confirm to someone that their feelings or reactions are understandable and legitimate.
ex: It helps to validate a patient's worry before explaining why the results are reassuring.

def: To reassure someone that their experience is common and to be expected rather than abnormal.
ex: I'll normalise the fact that many people feel tearful for a few days after surgery.

def: To restate what someone has said using different words to check you have understood correctly.
ex: If I can paraphrase what you've told me, the headaches are worst in the morning and ease by lunchtime.

def: To tell someone in advance what you are about to discuss or where they can find further help.
ex: I'll signpost you to a support service that can help with the practical side of your recovery.

def: To raise a difficult or sensitive subject for discussion for the first time.
ex: It can be hard to broach the topic of end-of-life wishes, so I try to do it gently.

def: To reveal information that was previously secret or private.
ex: Some patients only disclose that they've stopped taking their medication when you ask directly but kindly.

def: To make known private or sensitive information, often reluctantly.
ex: Reassure the patient that nothing they divulge will be shared without their permission.

def: To give someone professional guidance and support to help them cope or decide.
ex: I'll counsel you through what each option involves so you can choose what feels right.

def: To comfort someone who is sad, distressed, or grieving.
ex: There was little I could say to console the family, so I simply sat with them for a while.

def: To calm someone who is anxious or upset, or to ease a physical discomfort.
ex: A slow, quiet voice can soothe a frightened child far better than a rushed explanation.

def: To make a symptom, pain, or worry less severe.
ex: Even simply explaining what to expect can alleviate a lot of a patient's anxiety.

def: To reduce the intensity of a tense or agitated situation through calm communication.
ex: Lowering my voice and acknowledging his frustration helped de-escalate the confrontation at the desk.

def: To express thoughts or feelings in spoken words.
ex: Some patients find it hard to verbalise their pain, so I offer them a simple scale instead.

def: A sympathetic concern for another's suffering together with a wish to relieve it.
ex: Delivering difficult news with compassion matters as much as the accuracy of the information.

def: The quality of being open, honest, and straightforward in what one says.
ex: Professional duty of candour means we tell patients honestly when something has gone wrong.

def: A milder or vaguer word used in place of one felt to be too blunt or upsetting.
ex: Avoid the euphemism 'passed away' if the family is unclear; sometimes gentle plainness is kinder.

def: A person without professional or specialist knowledge of a particular subject.
ex: Explain the results as you would to a layperson, using everyday comparisons the patient can picture.

def: An expression of sympathy offered to someone who has suffered a loss.
ex: I offered my sincere condolences to the family before quietly leaving them together.

def: The state of having recently lost a loved one through death, and the grief that follows.
ex: We can arrange bereavement support if you'd find it helpful to talk to someone in the coming weeks.

def: Extreme emotional or physical suffering or discomfort.
ex: I could see she was in some distress, so I paused and let her take her time.

def: A feeling of anxiety or unease about something that may happen.
ex: A little apprehension before an operation is completely normal, and we'll be with you throughout.

def: Feeling anxious or fearful that something bad may happen.
ex: You seem a little apprehensive about the injection; would it help if I talked you through it first?

def: Feeling worried, nervous, or uneasy about an uncertain outcome.
ex: It's understandable to feel anxious while you wait for the results to come back.

def: Feeling unable to cope because of too much emotion or information at once.
ex: If you feel overwhelmed, we can stop and go over just one thing at a time.

def: Careful to say or do things without causing offence or upset.
ex: You need a tactful way to ask about alcohol without making the patient feel judged.

def: Honest and straightforward, even about difficult matters.
ex: I'll be candid with you: the recovery is likely to take longer than you might hope.

def: Paying close and considerate attention to someone.
ex: Being attentive, and not typing while she spoke, showed the patient I was really listening.

def: Willing and open to receive new ideas, suggestions, or information.
ex: Once his pain was controlled, he was far more receptive to talking about lifestyle changes.

def: Unwilling or hesitant to do something.
ex: If a patient seems reluctant to undress, offer a chaperone and give them privacy first.

def: Slow to act or speak because of uncertainty or nervousness.
ex: She was hesitant to admit she couldn't afford the prescription, so I raised it gently.

def: Having recently lost a close relative or friend to death.
ex: When you speak with a newly bereaved relative, slow your pace and allow long silences.

def: Meant to be kept private and not shared with others.
ex: Everything you tell me today is confidential unless there is a serious risk to your safety.

def: Having the effect of removing someone's fears or worries.
ex: A calm, reassuring tone at the bedside can settle a patient before you've said a word.

def: Relating to communication expressed through gesture, expression, or posture rather than words.
ex: Her nonverbal cues, the folded arms and averted gaze, told me she wasn't reassured at all.

def: A mild feeling of pain or physical unease.
ex: You may feel some discomfort as the cuff tightens, but it will only last a few seconds.

def: A sudden, brief, sharp pain.
ex: Tell me if you feel more than a mild twinge when I press here.

def: Describing pain that beats in a steady, pulsing rhythm.
ex: Would you describe the headache as throbbing, or more of a dull, constant pressure?

def: Feeling slightly sick, as though about to vomit.
ex: It's common to feel a little queasy after the anaesthetic, and it usually passes quickly.

def: Feeling sleepy and not fully alert.
ex: This may make you feel drowsy, so please don't drive until you know how it affects you.

def: Lacking energy and feeling sluggish or unusually tired.
ex: If you start to feel very lethargic or hard to rouse, that's something we'd want to know about.

def: Having difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath.
ex: Are you breathless just walking around the house, or only when you exert yourself?

def: Feeling faint, dizzy, or as though one might lose balance.
ex: Sit up slowly, because standing too quickly can leave you feeling lightheaded for a moment.

def: To become less intense, severe, or noticeable over time.
ex: The swelling should subside over the next few days, but do ring us if it worsens instead.

def: Able to be dealt with or kept under control without too much difficulty.
ex: Our aim isn't to remove every ache, but to keep the pain at a level that feels manageable for you.

def: To make a sudden facial or bodily movement in reaction to pain or distress.
ex: I noticed you wince when I lifted your arm, so let's be gentler with that shoulder.

def: To recover one's health and strength after illness or an operation.
ex: You'll need a few quiet weeks at home to recuperate before returning to work.

def: In a soft, careful, and kindly manner.
ex: I'll press gently, and you just tell me the moment it feels uncomfortable.

def: The study of how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and eliminates a drug over time.
ex: Renal impairment markedly altered the drug's pharmacokinetics, prolonging its half-life and mandating dose reduction.

def: The study of the biochemical and physiological effects a drug exerts on the body and its mechanism of action.
ex: The pharmacodynamics of the beta-blocker explain its negative inotropic and chronotropic effects on the heart.

def: A rapid diminution in the response to a drug following repeated or continuous administration over a short period.
ex: Repeated dosing of the decongestant produced tachyphylaxis, so successive applications yielded progressively weaker vasoconstriction.

def: Capable of causing malformations in a developing embryo or foetus.
ex: Thalidomide is the archetypal teratogenic agent, having caused severe limb defects in exposed infants.

def: Damaging or destructive to the kidneys.
ex: Aminoglycosides are markedly nephrotoxic, so serum creatinine must be monitored throughout the course.

def: A substance that binds to a receptor and activates it to produce a biological response.
ex: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle in asthma.

def: A substance that binds to a receptor without activating it, thereby blocking the action of an agonist.
ex: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist that displaces opioids from their receptors to reverse respiratory depression.

def: Relating to a site on a protein distinct from the active site, at which binding modulates the protein's activity.
ex: Benzodiazepines act at an allosteric site on the GABA-A receptor, enhancing the effect of the endogenous ligand.

def: A pharmacologically inactive compound that is metabolised in the body into an active drug.
ex: Enalapril is a prodrug that is hydrolysed in the liver to the active ACE inhibitor enalaprilat.

def: A substance produced by or involved in the metabolism of a drug or other compound.
ex: The active metabolite of the antidepressant has a far longer half-life than the parent compound.

def: A phase II conjugation reaction that attaches glucuronic acid to a compound to render it more water-soluble for excretion.
ex: Neonates conjugate bilirubin poorly because their glucuronidation capacity is immature.

def: A metabolic conjugation reaction adding an acetyl group to a drug, the rate of which varies genetically between individuals.
ex: Slow acetylation of isoniazid predisposes certain patients to peripheral neuropathy.

def: Relating to the recirculation of a substance between the liver, bile, intestine and portal blood.
ex: Enterohepatic recycling of the drug prolongs its action by returning excreted metabolite to the circulation.

def: The tendency of a compound to dissolve in fats and lipids rather than in water.
ex: The high lipophilicity of the anaesthetic allows it to cross the blood-brain barrier rapidly.

def: The volume of plasma from which a drug is completely removed per unit time by the body's eliminating organs.
ex: Hepatic clearance of the drug falls sharply in cirrhosis, necessitating a lower maintenance dose.

def: The amount of a drug required to produce a given effect, an expression of the dose needed rather than the maximal effect achievable.
ex: Fentanyl's high potency means microgram quantities produce analgesia equivalent to milligrams of morphine.

def: The strength with which a drug binds to its receptor.
ex: The antagonist's high affinity for the receptor allows it to outcompete the endogenous agonist.

def: A reduction in receptor responsiveness following prolonged or repeated exposure to an agonist.
ex: Continuous agonist exposure triggers desensitisation through receptor phosphorylation and internalisation.

def: A decrease in the number of receptors expressed by a cell, often in response to sustained agonist stimulation.
ex: Chronic opioid use causes receptor downregulation, contributing to tolerance and dependence.

def: Producing effects that mimic those of stimulating the sympathetic nervous system.
ex: The sympathomimetic amine raised heart rate and blood pressure by activating adrenergic receptors.

def: Blocking the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.
ex: The anticholinergic side effects included dry mouth, urinary retention and blurred vision.

def: Affecting the force of muscular contraction, especially of the heart.
ex: Dobutamine has a positive inotropic effect, augmenting cardiac output in decompensated heart failure.

def: Affecting the rate of the heartbeat.
ex: Atropine exerts a positive chronotropic effect by blocking vagal tone at the sinoatrial node.

def: Acting to expel or destroy parasitic worms.
ex: A single dose of the anthelmintic cleared the patient's intestinal helminth burden.

def: Acting to dissolve a blood clot by activating the fibrinolytic system.
ex: Prompt administration of a thrombolytic agent can restore coronary flow in acute myocardial infarction.

def: Serving to reduce anxiety.
ex: Benzodiazepines exert an anxiolytic effect by potentiating inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission.

def: A drug used to prevent or suppress epileptic seizures.
ex: The anticonvulsant stabilises neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels.

def: An agent that reduces the activity or efficiency of the immune system.
ex: Ciclosporin is an immunosuppressant that inhibits calcineurin to prevent transplant rejection.

def: A chemical compound foreign to a living organism, such as a drug, toxin or pollutant.
ex: Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolise a vast array of xenobiotics.

def: One of a pair of molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
ex: Only one enantiomer of the drug is pharmacologically active, while the other is inert or toxic.

def: A mixture containing equal amounts of the two enantiomers of a chiral compound.
ex: The drug is marketed as a racemate, though only the S-enantiomer confers therapeutic benefit.

def: The property of a molecule of being non-superimposable on its mirror image.
ex: The chirality of a drug molecule can profoundly influence its affinity for a stereoselective receptor.

def: An inactive substance formulated alongside the active ingredient to aid manufacture, stability or delivery.
ex: Lactose is a common excipient that acts as a bulking agent in tablet formulations.

def: The incremental adjustment of a drug dose to achieve the desired effect while minimising toxicity.
ex: Careful titration of the opioid infusion balanced adequate analgesia against respiratory depression.

def: Delivered through the skin into the systemic circulation, typically via an adhesive patch.
ex: A transdermal patch provides sustained release of fentanyl for chronic cancer pain.

def: A molecule that binds specifically to a receptor or other target macromolecule.
ex: The radiolabelled ligand was used to quantify receptor density in the tissue sample.

def: The active transport of a substance out of a cell, often mediated by membrane pumps that confer drug resistance.
ex: Overexpression of the efflux transporter expels the cytotoxic drug, rendering the tumour resistant.

def: The enhancement of one drug's effect by another that has little or no effect of its own.
ex: Alcohol produces marked potentiation of the sedative action of benzodiazepines.

def: A combined effect of two or more drugs that exceeds the sum of their individual effects.
ex: The synergism between the two antibiotics produced far greater bacterial killing than either alone.

def: The branch of pharmacology concerned with the determination of appropriate drug dosages.
ex: Paediatric posology must account for weight, surface area and immature organ function.

def: The science and practice of detecting, assessing and preventing adverse effects of medicines after they reach the market.
ex: Post-marketing pharmacovigilance uncovered a rare cardiac risk not seen in the clinical trials.

def: The concurrent use of multiple medications by a single patient, often raising the risk of interactions.
ex: Polypharmacy in the elderly heightens the likelihood of adverse drug interactions and falls.

def: A harmful and unintended response to a medicine given at a normal therapeutic dose.
ex: The rash was reported as a suspected adverse drug reaction to the newly started antibiotic.

def: An unwanted effect of a medicine that occurs alongside its intended therapeutic action.
ex: Nausea is a common side effect in the first few weeks of taking this medication.

def: An initial higher dose given to reach a therapeutic drug level quickly before switching to maintenance dosing.
ex: Give a loading dose of digoxin, then start the standard maintenance dose the next day.

def: Describing the treatment recommended as the initial choice for a condition.
ex: Amlodipine is a first-line agent for hypertension in patients over fifty-five.

def: Describing a treatment used when the first choice has failed or cannot be tolerated.
ex: We moved to a second-line antibiotic after the initial course did not clear the infection.

def: A medicine used to lower high blood pressure.
ex: Her blood pressure remains high despite three antihypertensives at maximum dose.

def: An anti-inflammatory drug based on the hormones produced by the adrenal cortex.
ex: A short course of oral corticosteroid was prescribed to settle the asthma exacerbation.

def: A medicine that relaxes and widens the airways to ease breathing.
ex: Give a nebulised bronchodilator to relieve the wheeze before reassessing her.

def: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug used to reduce pain and inflammation.
ex: Avoid NSAIDs in this patient because of his history of peptic ulcer disease.

def: A medicine that reduces stomach acid production to treat reflux and protect the gut lining.
ex: Co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor to protect the stomach while she is on long-term NSAIDs.

def: The way a medicine is given to the patient, such as by mouth or by injection.
ex: As she cannot swallow, we need to change the route of administration to intravenous.

def: Given directly into a vein.
ex: The patient was switched to intravenous antibiotics because of poor oral absorption.

def: Given by injection deep into a muscle.
ex: The adrenaline was given by intramuscular injection into the outer thigh.

def: Given by injection into the fatty tissue just beneath the skin.
ex: Insulin is administered by subcutaneous injection into the abdomen or thigh.

def: Taken one time every day.
ex: This antihypertensive is taken once daily, which helps with adherence.

def: Taken two times each day, usually morning and evening.
ex: Take one tablet twice daily with food to reduce stomach upset.

def: A change in a medicine's effect caused by taking it together with another drug, food, or substance.
ex: Check for a drug interaction before adding clarithromycin to his statin.

def: The range of drug concentrations in the blood that is effective without being toxic.
ex: We monitor lithium levels closely because its therapeutic range is very narrow.

def: Cleared from the body mainly by the kidneys.
ex: As the drug is renally excreted, we must reduce the dose in renal impairment.

def: A change to the amount of a drug given to suit the patient's needs or organ function.
ex: This medicine requires dose adjustment in the elderly and in renal impairment.

def: To hold back a dose of medicine temporarily rather than giving it as scheduled.
ex: Withhold the ACE inhibitor if her blood pressure drops below the parameters on the chart.

def: A defined period of taking a medicine from start to finish.
ex: It is important to complete the full course of antibiotics even if you feel better.

def: An abnormal immune response to a drug, ranging from a rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
ex: She developed an allergic reaction to penicillin with facial swelling and a widespread rash.

def: The medicine generally regarded as the best option for a particular condition.
ex: Amoxicillin remains the drug of choice for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia.

def: To increase treatment to a stronger drug or higher dose when the current regimen is inadequate.
ex: If her symptoms are not controlled, we will step up to a combination inhaler.

def: To reduce treatment to a lower dose or milder drug once the condition is well controlled.
ex: Once his asthma has been stable for three months, we can step down his inhaled steroid.

def: Sold under the drug's official chemical name rather than a brand name.
ex: Please prescribe the generic version, as it is far cheaper than the branded one.

def: The process of confirming an accurate list of all the medicines a patient is taking, especially on admission or discharge.
ex: On admission we carry out medication reconciliation to avoid omitting his regular drugs.

def: A single dose of a medicine to be given immediately.
ex: Give a stat dose of intravenous furosemide to relieve the acute pulmonary oedema.

def: A mistake made during the preparation or supply of a medicine, such as the wrong drug, strength, or quantity being issued to a patient.
ex: A near-miss log helps the pharmacy identify the root causes of recurrent dispensing errors before a patient is actually harmed.

def: A structured, private consultation in which a pharmacist reviews a patient's regular medicines to improve their understanding and adherence.
ex: During the Medicines Use Review, she realised the patient had stopped his statin because of unexplained muscle aches.

def: A specific piece of advice a pharmacist must convey when handing over a medicine, such as timing, administration, or a key side effect.
ex: The main counselling point for alendronate is to take it on an empty stomach and remain upright for thirty minutes.

def: A portion of a prescribed quantity that cannot be supplied immediately and is recorded as owed to the patient for later collection.
ex: We could only give her forty tablets today, so I've put the remaining twenty on an owing for Thursday.

def: The practice of dispensing a bioequivalent generic version of a medicine in place of the branded product that was prescribed.
ex: Generic substitution is permitted here, but I always warn patients that the tablets may look different from their usual ones.

def: The deliberate specification of a particular manufacturer's product on a prescription so that no generic alternative may be dispensed.
ex: For modified-release preparations we recommend prescribing by brand to avoid variation in release characteristics.

def: The unintended prescribing of two or more medicines from the same class or with the same action, increasing the risk of adverse effects.
ex: The screen flagged a therapeutic duplication because the patient was on both ramipril and lisinopril from two different clinics.

def: A standardised warning added to a dispensed medicine that gives the patient specific safety or administration instructions.
ex: Remember to apply the cautionary and advisory label warning that the antibiotic may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraception.

def: A pharmacy service offering follow-up support to patients newly started on a medicine for a long-term condition.
ex: I've signed him up for the New Medicine Service so we can check how he's tolerating the anticoagulant in a fortnight.

def: The provision of a prescription-only medicine without a prescription, at a patient's or prescriber's request, under strict regulatory conditions.
ex: She made an emergency supply of his inhaler after confirming he had been using it regularly for asthma.

def: A medicine subject to additional legal controls over its prescribing, storage, and record-keeping because of its potential for misuse.
ex: Every supply of this controlled drug has to be entered in the register on the day the transaction takes place.

def: A bound or approved electronic record in which every receipt and supply of Schedule 2 controlled drugs must be documented.
ex: The running balance in the controlled drug register didn't match the stock, so we had to investigate immediately.

def: The continuously updated stock total for a controlled drug, recorded after each receipt or supply to allow discrepancies to be detected.
ex: We reconcile the running balance against the physical count every week to catch any diversion early.

def: The planned and supervised process of reducing or stopping medicines that may no longer be of benefit or may be causing harm.
ex: We agreed on a deprescribing plan to taper her long-standing proton pump inhibitor over several weeks.

def: The process of compiling an accurate list of a patient's current medicines and comparing it against new orders at a transition of care.
ex: On admission, medicines reconciliation revealed that his usual levothyroxine had been omitted from the drug chart.

def: The particular physical form and composition in which a drug is presented, such as a tablet, suspension, or patch.
ex: For a child who can't swallow tablets, we'd usually recommend a liquid formulation of the antibiotic.

def: Describing a formulation designed to release its active ingredient slowly or at a controlled rate rather than all at once.
ex: Crushing a modified-release tablet can cause the entire dose to be absorbed at once, which may be dangerous.

def: Describing a tablet or capsule with a coating that resists stomach acid so the drug is released in the intestine.
ex: Because the tablets are enteric-coated, I advised her not to chew them or the coating's protection would be lost.

def: The stepwise reduction of a medicine's dose before stopping it, to avoid withdrawal effects or rebound symptoms.
ex: Abruptly stopping the steroid is unsafe, so we've drawn up a tapering schedule for the patient to follow.

def: The regular dose given to sustain a steady therapeutic level of a drug once the desired effect has been achieved.
ex: Once she's stabilised, we'll drop her to a maintenance dose taken once each morning.

def: A property of a drug for which the difference between an effective dose and a toxic dose is small, requiring careful monitoring.
ex: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index, so even small changes in diet or interacting drugs can be significant.

def: A symptom or sign during a consultation that signals a potentially serious condition and warrants urgent referral.
ex: Unintentional weight loss with a change in bowel habit is a red flag that means I can't just sell her something over the counter.

def: A medicine that may be sold only from a pharmacy under the supervision of a pharmacist, without a prescription.
ex: That strength of the antihistamine is a pharmacy medicine, so I need to ask a few questions before I can sell it.

def: A medicine that may be supplied only against a valid prescription from an authorised prescriber.
ex: I'm afraid the antibiotic you're after is a prescription-only medicine, so you'll need to see a prescriber first.

def: The instructions on a prescription telling the patient how and when to take the medicine, transcribed onto the dispensing label.
ex: The directions simply read 'as directed', so I had to ring the surgery to clarify the intended dose.

def: A prescription that meets all the statutory requirements for particulars such as the prescriber's signature, date, and patient details.
ex: I couldn't dispense it because the script wasn't a legally valid prescription without the prescriber's signature.

def: A device such as a blister pack that organises a patient's tablets by day and time to support adherence.
ex: Because he was getting confused with his boxes, we set him up with a monitored dosage system.

def: An arrangement allowing a patient to obtain successive supplies of a stable regular medicine without a new prescription each time.
ex: She's on repeat dispensing for her thyroid medication, so she just collects the next batch every month.

def: The overall pattern of unwanted effects associated with a particular medicine, considered when advising a patient.
ex: I chose to counsel her carefully because the side-effect profile of this SSRI includes nausea in the first fortnight.

def: The UK reporting system through which suspected adverse drug reactions and product defects are notified to the regulator.
ex: Any suspected reaction to a newly licensed medicine should be reported via the Yellow Card scheme, however minor.

def: A medicine compounded by the pharmacist to meet an individual patient's needs when no suitable licensed product exists.
ex: With no commercial liquid available, we had to make an extemporaneous preparation of the drug for the infant.

def: The date after which a medicine should not be used because its quality or potency can no longer be guaranteed.
ex: During the date check we pulled several boxes whose expiry date had passed from the front of the shelf.

def: The length of time a medicine remains stable and usable under specified storage conditions.
ex: Once reconstituted, the antibiotic suspension has a shelf life of only fourteen days in the fridge.

def: The pharmacist's recommendation of an appropriate over-the-counter treatment for a patient's presenting symptoms.
ex: After ruling out any red flags, she moved to counter prescribing and suggested a simple rehydration sachet.

def: To prepare and supply a prescribed medicine to a patient.
ex: Before I dispense this, I need to check the prescription against your allergy record.

def: An approved list of medicines that may be prescribed within a health system.
ex: That preparation isn't on our local formulary, so I'll suggest an approved alternative.

def: To restore a powdered medicine to liquid form by adding a fluid.
ex: You reconstitute the powder with cooled boiled water and shake it well before each dose.

def: An effect that occurs when one medicine alters the action of another.
ex: There's a known interaction between your anticoagulant and this painkiller, so avoid it.

def: To increase the effect or potency of another agent.
ex: Alcohol can potentiate the drowsiness caused by this sedative, so don't drink while taking it.

def: A reduced response to a medicine after repeated use, needing a higher dose for the same effect.
ex: Over time some patients develop tolerance, so the earlier dose no longer relieves the pain.

def: A state in which the body needs a medicine to function normally.
ex: To avoid dependence, we don't recommend using this sleeping aid for more than a fortnight.

def: A medicine used to reduce fever.
ex: An antipyretic can bring the temperature down, but keep the child well hydrated too.

def: A medicine used to relieve or prevent constipation.
ex: A gentle laxative may help while you're on this painkiller, which can slow the bowel.

def: A medicine that has a calming or sleep-inducing effect.
ex: Because this is a sedative, avoid driving until you know how it affects you.

def: The degree to which a patient follows the agreed treatment instructions.
ex: A weekly pill organiser can improve compliance for someone taking many medicines.

def: A prescribed plan setting out how and when medicines are to be taken.
ex: Let's simplify your regimen so all your tablets are taken at just two times a day.

def: To prepare a medicine by mixing ingredients to a specific formula.
ex: The pharmacist will compound the cream to the exact strength the specialist requested.

def: Sold under a manufacturer's registered brand name.
ex: You may know the proprietary name, but the label shows the generic ingredient.

def: A condition or reason for which a medicine is appropriately used.
ex: That antibiotic has a specific indication, so it won't help a common cold.

def: Building up in the body through repeated doses over time.
ex: Because the effect is cumulative, never double up if you miss a single dose.

def: Producing a combined effect greater than the sum of the separate effects.
ex: The two agents are synergistic, so together they control the pain more effectively.

def: The body's chemical breakdown of a medicine into other substances.
ex: Grapefruit juice can slow the metabolism of some medicines, raising their levels.

def: The removal of a medicine or its waste products from the body.
ex: Since excretion is mainly through the kidneys, the dose is lowered in renal impairment.

def: To plan and supervise the withdrawal of a medicine that is no longer needed.
ex: We may deprescribe some of these tablets, as several are no longer benefiting you.

def: Denoting a tablet that dissolves with bubbling to make a drink.
ex: Drop the effervescent tablet into a glass of water and drink it once it stops fizzing.

def: The act of walking or moving about, especially after injury, surgery or illness.
ex: Early ambulation after the operation helps reduce the risk of complications and speeds recovery.

def: The movement that raises the foot or hand upward, decreasing the angle at the joint.
ex: Limited dorsiflexion at the ankle was preventing her from clearing the ground during the swing phase.

def: The movement that points the foot and toes downward, away from the shin.
ex: Strong plantarflexion is needed for an effective push-off when walking or climbing stairs.

def: Describing a posture or gait adopted to avoid or reduce pain.
ex: He walked with an antalgic gait, spending as little time as possible on the painful leg.

def: An instrument used to measure the angle or range of motion of a joint.
ex: Using a goniometer, I recorded knee flexion of ninety degrees at the initial assessment.

def: The small accessory movements, such as rolling and gliding, that occur between joint surfaces.
ex: Restoring normal arthrokinematics of the joint often precedes work on functional range.

def: An abnormal collection of fluid within a joint or body cavity.
ex: A large effusion in the knee limited flexion and gave the joint a full, tense feel.

def: A hands-on technique using graded, controlled movement to improve joint or tissue mobility.
ex: Gentle mobilisation of the stiff shoulder was combined with active exercises to restore range.

def: The redistribution or removal of pressure or load from an injured or vulnerable area.
ex: Offloading the heel with a specialised boot allowed the pressure area to heal.

def: Explosive exercises involving rapid stretching and contracting of muscle to build power.
ex: In the final rehabilitation phase we introduced plyometrics such as hopping and jumping.

def: Describing a muscle contraction in which tension is generated without any change in muscle length.
ex: We started with isometric quadriceps holds because the knee was too painful to move.

def: Describing exercise performed at a constant speed against a variable, accommodating resistance.
ex: Isokinetic testing gave us an objective measure of the strength difference between the two legs.

def: Describing a muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens under load.
ex: Eccentric loading of the tendon is a well-established approach for chronic tendon pain.

def: Describing a muscle contraction in which the muscle shortens as it produces force.
ex: Lifting the weight uses a concentric contraction, while lowering it slowly is eccentric.

def: The tendency of a muscle or person to tire quickly with sustained or repeated effort.
ex: Increased fatigability meant he could manage only a few repetitions before the muscle gave way.

def: Looseness or excessive slackness in a ligament or joint.
ex: Testing revealed increased laxity of the knee ligament compared with the uninjured side.

def: An abnormally large range of movement at a joint beyond the usual limits.
ex: Her generalised hypermobility meant we focused on stability and control rather than stretching.

def: Describing an angulation in which the distal part of a limb turns outward, away from the midline.
ex: On squatting, her knee collapsed into a valgus position, placing strain on the inner structures.

def: Describing an angulation in which the distal part of a limb turns inward, toward the midline.
ex: A varus alignment of the knee concentrated load on the inner compartment of the joint.

def: An inward curvature of the spine, most commonly in the lower back.
ex: An increased lumbar lordosis was noted, and we worked on core control and posture.

def: A sideways curvature of the spine.
ex: The scoliosis produced a visible asymmetry of the shoulders and waist on standing.

def: The number of steps taken per minute during walking or running.
ex: Increasing her cadence slightly reduced the load on the knee during each running stride.

def: The driving force that moves the body forward, generated as the foot pushes off.
ex: Weak calf muscles reduced propulsion, giving him a short, laboured step on that side.

def: Exercise and preparation undertaken before surgery to improve fitness and outcomes.
ex: A short prehabilitation programme before the knee replacement helped her recover more quickly afterwards.

def: The measurement of muscle strength or grip using a calibrated instrument.
